In D) we see a warning with explanation, graph and the identified line in the source code that causes the issue, together with a suggestion for a solution. 3.6 REQ6: Easy Integration with Existing PPLs Lastly, it is important that our debugger can easily be applied to existing PPLs. This requires a light-weight API to send data during inference to the debugging and analysis backend. After sending initial information, INFERLoG HoLMEs only re- quires the PPL backend to make regular HTTP requests, either batched or after each MCMC iteration, sending the current infer- ence state as JSON. Since PyMC provides an API for making such callbacks, the integration was particularly easy. Some other PPLs offer similar APIs, but even if a PPL does not, the HTTP calls could be directly implemented in the language without significant chal- lenges. By implementing the HTTP interface within a language, most features of INFERLoG HoLMEs are immediately available. To get full support for contextualized workflows, the ConcretePPL in- terface inside INFERLOG HoLMEs must be implemented for a new language. This allows INFERLoG Houmgs to add additional informa- tion to the warnings that are specific to the given PPL. 4 Workflows in INFERLoG HoLMEs Exemplified To illustrate the accelerated workflows enabled by INFERLoG Hoimgs, let us revisit the SAT coaching example from Section 2 from the users perspective. Modeling. Suppose a user wants to investigate whether short- term coaching improves SAT scores, using a Bayesian model. They begin implementing a PyMC model, informed by their prior beliefs. At some point, they want to see how their model is structured. This is when they open INFERLoc Hogs, which shows the model code side-by-side with a visual representation of the model graph (Fig. 4 Step A). Live Feedback During Inference. When ready, they launch infer- ence. Immediately, live diagnostics appear (Fig. 4 Step B). As poste- rior samples stream in, the user can inspect evolving distributions, trace plots, and summary statistics in real-time. The user starts inspecting the progression of the different variables. When they look at an overview of the 6 variables the user notices a warning icon next to the acceptance rate, which is at only 30%. Focused Inspection. Since the acceptance rate is very low for HMC based algorithms and the traceplots are indicative of suboptimal convergence, the user opens the details view for one of the @ vari- ables (Fig. 4 Step C). The user immediately notices the orange text box that tells them that there is a potential funnel between 7 and 0, a shape that is often difficult to explore for MCMC based algorithms. --- PAGE BREAK --- ICSE °26, April 12-18, 2026, Rio De Janeiro, Brazil This leads them to inspecting the shapes in the conditionally dis- played pairplots between these two variables, which indeed look funnel-shaped. Warnings and Potential Solutions. While the user is inspecting the details page, they notice that there are 10 warnings for potential roblems discovered by INFERLOG Hoimgs. So the user heads over to the warnings view and opens the topmost warning (Fig. 4 Step D) for the 6 variable. This warning, again, raises the issue of the funnel tween 7 and 6 and shows that the resulting posterior is difficult for HMC algorithms to explore. It further includes the problematic ine of code together with a suggested change. The user accepts this suggestion and clicks on the button "Show me where" to jump to the exact line of code causing the issue and replaces it. Iterations. Since continuing inference after identifying a fault wastes time, the user stops inference early and restarts it with the applied changes in place. From there the user keeps iterating together with INFERLoG Hommes until all warnings are resolved and the inference results show no indication of non-convergence. 5 Study Design To evaluate our framework we conducted a study with 18 partici- pants. We formulate following research questions: (RQ1) Does our online and interactive framework effectively de- crease time spent debugging inference? (RQ2) Are online visualizations of MCMC posteriors considered useful by PPL users? (RQ3) Are the warnings raised at inference time considered useful by PPL users? To answer these questions each participant was asked to solve three inference debugging tasks in PyMC and to fill out two ques- tionnaires: one pre-study questionnaire and one post-study ques- tionnaire. RQ1 is answered quantitatively by evaluating the hypotheses stated in Table 2 with statistical tests. Null hypothesis Alternative hypothesis PPL users are able to re- solve more issues with the tool Hig: The tool does not im-| H1: pact how many issues PPL user can solve H2): The tool does not im-| H2: pact how fast PPL user can identify issues H3): The tool does not im-| H3: PPL users have faster it- pact how fast PPL users eration cycles with the iterate over the problem tool H4): The tool does not im-| H4: pact how effective PPL users spend their time PPL users are able to identify issues faster with the tool PPL users spend their time more effectively with the tool Table 2: Null and alternative hypothesis For RQ2 and RQ3 we adopt a qualitative methodology, basing our analysis on participants responses to the questionnaires and verbal statements they made while performing the tasks. Nussbaumer et al. 5.1 Study Setup The study was conducted as a controlled experiment with a duration of 1h:15m to 2 hours for each participant. Environment: The study was conducted fully online via a video conferencing tool. To avoid differences in inference runtime de- pending on hardware differences, we provided an online version of VSCode. The participants accessed the online IDE via https: //vscode.dev and all program code was executed on the same lab- server for every participant. Design & Baseline Condition: The study follows a within-subject design, where the task order was randomized and the first task serves as the baseline condition for each participant. For this base- line, participants were allowed to use any existing tool or resource of their liking, except INFERLOG Hoimgs, to closely reflect real-world workflows. With Task 2 and 3 we evaluated the tool condition, where the participants were allowed to use INFERLOG Hoimgs in addition to existing tools or resources. For the first task, we observed participants opting to use the following existing tools and resources during: prior and posterior predictive checks, ArviZ (plots + summary diagnostics), search engines, PyMC + ArviZ documentation and tutorials, ChatGPT. In general, we observed that participants had different workflows but often relied heavily on ArviZ and search engines. Interestingly, only one participant asked a large language model for help. Across all participants, INFERLOG Homes became the primary tool during Tasks 2 and 3, with many relying on it so extensively that they stopped using other tools and resources. Protocol: Before the experiment, participants were asked to fill- out a pre-study questionnaire to assess their background and famil- iarity with probabilistic programming. Afterwards the participants connected to the online environment and were given an introduc- tion notebook. Its main purpose was introducing participants to PyMC and relevant tooling around PyMC. Participants were told to take as much time as they needed and that they could always refer back to the notebook or use any other resource they wish. Once a participant gave the signal that they were ready, they could proceed to the first task. The participants were informed that they have to solve the tasks in order and cannot go back and forth between them. The task order was randomly assigned to each participant, and every participant had to solve the first task without INFERLOG Homes. However, they could use any tool or resource they had access to for all tasks. The time limit for each task was set to 30 minutes (subtracting setup issues), and participants had to decide for themselves when a task is finished. They did not receive any feedback on their progress during the study. After participants deemed the first task done (or reached the time limit) they received a ~5 minutes introduction to INFERLoG HoimgEs. Participants were now free to use INFERLOG Houmgs, if they wanted, for the following two tasks. Aside from the new tool, everything else stayed the same. Once the participant finished all three tasks, they were asked to fill-out a post-study questionnaire. Afterwards, the study concluded and participants received feedback on their task performance if they wished. --- PAGE BREAK --- Online and Interactive Bayesian Inference Debugging 5.2 Tasks A task in our study is defined by a probabilistic program given as a PyMC source file with pre-implemented model and inference routine. In these programs we have introduced sub-optimal or faulty implementation decisions. The objective for the participants is to determine whether there is an issue with the model and/or inference implementation or whether there is no issues at all. We have prepared three tasks in total: (A) Linear regression model with HMC inference routine. Fault: bad choice of step-size hyper-parameter of HMC. (B) Signal detection theory model [17] with HMC inference routine. Fault: Unused random variables, sub-optimal hyper- parameter choice for step-size and too short burn-in period and too small sample size. (C) Eight schools model [15] with HMC inference routine. Fault: Sub-optimal model parameterization, too short burn-in pe- riod and depending on burn-in period setting potentially auto-tune needs to be disabled. The tasks vary in difficulty: the simple model and poor inference result of task A makes it easier to identify and solve in comparison to the other more challenging tasks B and C. 5.3 Participants Probabilistic programming is a relatively small community and since our study targets PPL users and requires prior knowledge of Bayesian inference preferably in the context of probabilistic programming, recruiting participants became a challenging task. As our efforts for recruiting study participants in the forums of the three popular PPLs PyMC, Pyro, and Stan was unfortunately unsuccessful, we opted for a snowball sampling [18] strategy instead. Here, we considered three major pools: (1) Students who took a university course on Probabilistic Pro- gramming (8 participants recruited) (2) Probabilistic Programming and Bayesian modeling researchers (7 participants recruited) (3) Practitioners, e.g., other scientists, data analysts, etc. (3 par- ticipants recruited) 5.4 Result Validation and Statistical Tests To make our results verifiable, we conducted a series of statistical tests, where we set the significance level at 5%. 5.4.1 Ordinal Measurements of Uncensored Data. Due to the non- normality of our ordinal variables (confirmed with the Shapiro- Wilk test), we performed the Mann-Whitney U Test on these mea- surements. The Mann-Whitney U Test is non-parametric and thus makes no assumption on the distribution of our data. Following common practice, we further used Cliff’s delta for estimating the effect size [19, 20]. 5.4.2 Censored Data. Some of our data variables are right censored, which means that there may be events that did not occur within the study period. For instance, the Time to first issue detected is right-censored, because some participants were unable to detect the first issue within the given time limit. For these kinds of variables, statistical survival analysis can be adopted [21, 22]. We performed ICSE °26, April 12-18, 2026, Rio De Janeiro, Brazil Cox Proportional Hazards Regression [23] and a log-rank test [24] to estimate the effect of our framework on the "survival rate". In this context, survival refers to the event that a bug "survives" the detection efforts of the participant. Since our study measures a positive outcome (e.g. task solved) in contrast to many other studies using these methods, we will focus our attention on the cumulative densities cd(T), instead of the survival function s f(T), which is defined as cd(T) = 1 — sf(T). So instead of investigating the probability of a task remaining in- complete beyond time T (e.g., survival), we focus on the probability of the task being completed (commonly interpreted as death in survival analysis) prior to time T. 5.5 Threats to Validity 5.5.1 External Validity. Given that participation in a study is en- tirely voluntary and the participants received no material benefit from participation, it is possible that our sample is not represen- tative of the general population of PPL users. Furthermore, the use of snowball sampling may lead to a more homogeneous group of participants [19]. We mitigated these issues by reaching out to possible participants broadly and ensuring that our participants come from different backgrounds. We were especially careful, to not only recruit students but also researchers and professionals to have participants from the full spectrum of PPL users. Furthermore, we ensured that the recruited participants had no dependency on the researchers (e.g. all students have been graded before participating). 5.5.2 Internal Validity. We identified two main threats to inter- nal validity for this study. First, due to the necessarily artificial nature of the tasks and setup, it is possible that the tasks do not represent real world issues well. Second, the tasks may overly favor the usage of INFERLoG Hots, through aligning with its feature set. We mitigated both these threats through basing our examples on existing literature and known examples. Task C, for example, is a well known problem in probabilistic programming research, Task B is based on a tutorial task for the Pyro PPL [13] with the main issue being a copy&paste / typo, which was an actual mis- take made during task creation and evaluation and Task A is the prototypical linear regression example with a common issue of bad hyper-parameters. To further mitigate the effect of task alignment, we introduced multiple issues into Task B and Task C. For instance, while the funnel warning in INFERLoG HoLMEs was designed to detect funnel relationships as constructed by the centered eight school model in Task C, we introduced two additional issues in the program to reduce alignment. Nevertheless, it is possible that the effects measured in this study, are somewhat larger than they would be in real world scenarios with more subtle bugs. 6 Quantitative Results In this section, we present our quantitative analysis to answer the question RQ1: Does our online and interactive framework effectively decrease time spent debugging inference? For hypothesis H1, we further conducted a Bayesian analysis of the results, which allows us to quantify effects in relation to each other, in contrast to the standard statistical tests. We implemented a Bayesian logistic regression model, which represents the number of issues identified as a Bernoulli distribution. The effects are modeled as latent random variables and are summed up and passed through a sigmoid function, which outputs the probability p of the Bernoulli distribution. We base our analysis on re- sponses to the post-study survey and quotes from participants recorded during the study. 7.1 RQ2: Are online visualizations of MCMC posteriors considered useful by PPL users? To answer RQ2, we tried to separate the effect of online visualiza- tions and visualizations in general. We designed our questionnaire to differentiate between the selection of visualizations in the tool and the general idea of online visualizations during inference. 7.1.1 The tool provides a good selection of visualizations. As can be seen in Fig. 8, participants considered the selection of visualizations overwhelmingly positive and only a few participants were missing certain visualizations. One participant mentioned that they missed a clean overview of posterior statistics like Arviz [27] provides through the summary function. Another participant related their statement about missing visualizations towards the static model graph. They mentioned that they are "[...] always missing the formula how parameters are added or mutiplied in the graph view as well in the tools case also shape information". In another section of the questionnaire one participant made the remark that they "[...] would like for each visualization to have --- PAGE BREAK --- ICSE °26, April 12-18, 2026, Rio De Janeiro, Brazil an explanation of on how to read it in detail, maybe via a link to another page". We consider these points valid feedback and incorporating them into a future version of the tool should be straight forward without negatively impacting the tools usefulness. As before, we tried to separate the perception of the warnings in general and the perception of the warning during inference. 7.2.1. In general, warnings are considered helpful. From the re- sponses presented in Fig. 9, we see that a clear majority of par- ticipants strongly agreed that warnings helped them detect issues and only 2 participants "just" agreed and 1 participant somewhat agreed with the statement. While the statement "The warnings helped me solve issues" drew less strong agrees to it, the overall tendency is that the warnings are helpful in that regard as well. This sentiment is further supported when participants were asked, if the warnings helped them understand issues and if the warnings made issues clearer. In both cases the majority of partic- ipants either agreed or strongly agreed with the statement. One participant highlighted in the optional free form input field of the post study questionnaire that "they[the warnings] were quite in- formative [...]". Another mentioned that the warnings are "very helpful with nice explanations!" and one participant pointed out that "[...] they were very helpfull[sic!], as it is hard to find from the docs, which parameters might influence the behaviour in a certain way". During their third task (task C) one participant exclaimed: "oh that’s cool. Well let’s try it out, when the tool says that". This was subjected at the funnel/reparametrization warning described in Table 1. Nussbaumer et al. While the helpfulness of warnings during inference is still perceived posi- tive overall, participants agreed less strongly to it than to the gen- eral helpfulness of the warnings. One participant even disagreed, and another one somewhat disagreed to the statement that "the warnings helped me detect issues early in inference". 3 participants remained neutral on the question, and 4 somewhat agreed. The participant who disagreed with this, however, pointed out that they "L...] only really look[ed] at the warnings after inference". In contrast, another participant stated that, "[...] their dynamicity really reflects the changing nature of the sampling process and how it should be interpreted". We take from these results that the overall perception of warn- ings during inference is positive, but that their usefulness during inference is less clear than after inference. This could potentially be improved upon in future framework instantiations through better heuristics for raising warnings during inference. 7.2.3 Some users felt misguided or were missing information. Fig. 9 shows that most participants disagreed with the statement that they "[...] felt misguided by some warnings" and only one participant somewhat agreed to this. Nevertheless when asked whether they felt misguided by warnings during or after inference, specifically (multiple choice), 4 participants mentioned that they felt misguided by warnings during inference, 1 after inference and 14 that they never felt misguided. This suggests that the warnings system might need adjustments in some areas. This is also reflected by statements made by two participants. One participant expressed that "in task three it told [them] to re- formulate but it was missing what this would change" and another mentioned that "[...] it is somewhat counter intuitive, that e.g. the same warning appears 8 times, if the variable is of dim=8 [...]". Both statements express potential improvements we agree with. More detailed warnings could further improve usability and interpret- ability and reducing the amounts of almost duplicate warnings displayed could reduce clutter and improve clarity. 8 Related Work Debugging Probabilistic Programs: Gorinova et al. proposed a live, multiple-representation editor for probabilistic programs tar- geting novices. The editor features a code editor, a model graph and prior as well as posterior distribution charts [7]. They further showed effectiveness of multiple representations for probabilistic program comprehension in their study. Our work draws from their work and also features multiple representations. While in their work, live refers to dynamically updating the representations when --- PAGE BREAK --- Online and Interactive Bayesian Inference Debugging source code changes, our work features live updates in the con- text of inference. Furthermore, our work enables deep insights into the inference process and offers visual debugging aids as well as contextualized warnings and information on resolving potential issues that is model, inference algorithm and PPL specific. Hoppen et al.[29] proposed a debugger for probabilistic programs that, in contrast to our work, resembles classical step-by-step debugging workflows more closely. It allows setting breakpoints in a proba- bilistic program and shows current values as well as the distribution from which the value was drawn. Their work aims to improve com- prehension of probabilistic code execution and debugging classical logic errors stemming from e.g. random numbers of loop itera- tions. DEPP [30] is another debugger for probabilistic programs that is closer to our work which features a combination of static and dynamic analysis. In contrast to our work, their work does not describe a PPL independent approach, but relies on a custom PPL implemented by them. Furthermore, they do not provide on- line inference insights in their described systems, which is a key innovation in our approach. SixthSense [31] is another work tar- geting probabilistic program debugging. In contrast to our work, SixthSense aims to predict model convergence within a specified number of steps ahead-of-run. Similar to our work they offer warn- ings for likely causes. In contrast to our work, they aim at prediction. Our work on the other hand gives deep insights into the real in- ference process by providing information and analysis tools at- and after-run-time. ShinyStan [32] is an interactive diagnostic tool with a graphical user interface for analyzing Bayesian posteriors after inference. It features interactive plots and tables commonly used for identifying MCMC inference problems. In contrast to our work it does not feature online analysis of Bayesian inference and does not incorporate details from the model or inference algorithm. Our framework further suggests potential problems based on these informations to reduce the debugging exploration space. Bug Patterns in Probabilistic Programs and MCMC Diagnostic Work: Lieberman et al. [33] explain the necessity for a dedicated debugging framework for probabilistic programming. Hamada et al. [6] explores bug patterns in PyMC programs and extracts four common bug categories. Donovan et al. [34] gives general guide- lines with clear questions and answers targeted to novices for di- agnosing MCMC inference. Zitzmann et al. identifies the effective sample size as a possible stopping criterion for MCMC algorithms [35]. Vats et al. [9] presents important MCMC diagnostics, many of which are used in our approach, and an exemplary workflow incorporating these diagnostics. Gabry et al. show a visualization based debugging workflow [8], which was inspirational for the visualization selection in our work. [36] showed how funnels in probabilistic models can be identified and proposed an automatic reparameterisation. Before that, it was shown that there is no gen- eral optimal parameterisation and centered, as well as non-centered, have both potential case dependent benefits and drawbacks [37]. Other Work in Online Diagnostics and Visualizations: Tensor- board [28] is a well known tool for online diagnostics and visualiza- tions in deep learning and was an inspiration to the live inference analysis presented in this paper. Glinda [38] is a complete system ICSE °26, April 12-18, 2026, Rio De Janeiro, Brazil for supporting data science that features a domain specific lan- guage, live programming and a GUI. They showed the benefits of interactive plots and live updates in the domain of data science. 9 Conclusion In this work, we propose a novel approach to debugging proba- bilistic programs. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to realize online analysis of the Bayesian inference process. We further describe a holistic debugging approach combining model visualizations, statistics, and analysis plots with warnings and di- rections. We implemented this approach in INFERLoG Homes for MCMC methods and evaluated its effectiveness in a user study with 18 participants. The study showed that our approach marks a significant advancement for debugging probabilistic models that future work can build upon. Without Showing Me Anything”: Zero-Knowledge Software Auditing for Al-Enabled Systems FILIPPO SCARAMUZZA, Tilburg University, Netherlands and Eindhoven University of Technology, Netherlands RENATO CORDEIRO FERREIRA, Tilburg University, Netherlands, Eindhoven University of Technology, Nether- lands, and University of Sao Paulo, Brazil TOMAZ MAIA SULLER, Politecnico di Milano, Italy GIOVANNI QUATTROCCHI, Politecnico di Milano, Italy DAMIAN ANDREW TAMBURRI, University of Sannio, Italy and Eindhoven University of Technology, Nether- lands WILLEM-JAN VAN DEN HEUVEL, Tilburg University, Netherlands and Eindhoven University of Technology, Netherlands The increasing exploitation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled systems in critical domains has made trustworthiness concerns a paramount showstopper, requiring verifiable accountability, often by regulation (e.g., the EU AI Act). Classical software verification and validation techniques, such as procedural audits, formal methods, or model documentation, are the mechanisms used to achieve this. However, these methods are either expensive or heavily manual and ill-suited for the opaque, “black box” nature of most AI models. An intractable conflict emerges: high auditability and verifiability are required by law, but such transparency conflicts with the need to protect assets being audited—e.g., confidential data and proprietary models—leading to weakened accountability. To address this challenge, this paper introduces ZKMLOps, a novel MLOps verification framework that operationalizes Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs)—cryptographic protocols allowing a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing additional information—within Machine-Learning Operations lifecycles. By integrating ZKPs with established software engineering patterns, ZKMLOps provides a modular and repeatable process for generating verifiable cryptographic proof of compliance. We evaluate the framework’s practicality through a study of regulatory compliance in financial risk auditing and assess feasibility through an empirical evaluation of top ZKP protocols, analyzing performance trade-offs for ML models of increasing complexity. Additional Key Words and Phrases: zero-knowledge proofs, machine-learning operations, MLOps, software auditing, trustworthy Al, regulatory compliance, cryptographic verification 1 Introduction Al-enabled software systems—i.e., all those that embed components such as deep neural networks (DNNs) or large language models (LLMs)—have moved from academic efforts to mission-critical infrastructure in finance, healthcare, transportation, public administration, and more [4, 44]. Decisions made by these systems are increasingly safety-, ethics-, or money-critical, hence legislators worldwide have begun to demand verifiable accountability. For example, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act! classifies many industrial AI deployments as high-risk and requires evidence of 1Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, enforced from June 2024 Authors’ Contact Information: Filippo Scaramuzza, [EMAIL_REDACTED], Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands and Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, Netherlands; Renato Cordeiro Ferreira, Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands and Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, Netherlands and University of Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil; Tomaz Maia Suller, Politecnico di Milano, Milano, Italy; Giovanni Quattrocchi, Politecnico di Milano, Milano, Italy; Damian Andrew Tamburri, University of Sannio, Benevento, Italy and Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, Netherlands; Willem-Jan van den Heuvel, Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands and Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, Netherlands. Manuscript submitted to ACM 1 --- PAGE BREAK --- 2 Scaramuzza et al. compliance with strict transparency, robustness, and human-oversight obligations [25]. Similar requirements appear in sector-specific guidance from financial regulators (e.g., the Basel Committee) or in forthcoming U.S. executive orders. On the one hand, in conventional software engineering, auditors rely on a spectrum of verification and validation (V&V) artifacts, ranging from manual process audits and test suites to formal model-checking [14]. On the other hand, the above artifacts are only effective when the implementation logic is explicit and can be modelled deterministically. Yet modern AI models are opaque “black boxes” whose behaviour emerges from millions (or even billions) of learned parameters [54]. Probing those parameters directly may leak intellectual property or personal data, and disclosing training data often conflicts with data-protection laws and contracts. Thus, organizations face an intractable tension: regulators request deep transparency, but disclosing the very artifacts that enable transparency would compromise proprietary or privacy-sensitive assets [15, 16]. The consequences of this scenario are often dire. For example, let us look a few years back: in 2015, the Volkswagen emissions scandal [34] revealed that the company had deliberately programmed its diesel engines with a “defeat device” to circumvent environmental regulations. This software could predict—by way of computational intelligence—when the vehicle was undergoing laboratory testing and alter its performance accordingly, creating a substantial gap between public claims and real-world behavior; needless to say, the whole scenario caused worldwide havoc, financial loss, production hampering, and more. This precedent of engineered leception exemplifies a similar verifiability gap that exists in the domain of artificial intelligence, where the opaque, lack box” nature of many ML models complicates rigorous auditing [51]. In response to such scenarios, this paper introduces ZKMLOps, a novel framework for the systematic auditing of Machine Learning (ML) systems. The framework operationalizes Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) [72] within the Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) lifecycle [39], enabling an organization to furnish verifiable cryptographic proof that its systems adhere to specific requirements and regulations. A ZKP is a protocol that allows a prover to convince a verifier that a computational statement is true, without revealing any information beyond the statement’s validity. This property makes ZKPs uniquely suited to resolve the auditing dilemma. However, the theoretical availability of these primitives does not address the practical challenge of their systematic application. This integration allows for the verification of properties, such as the use of an approved model, a fair dataset, or any other arbitrary requirement, without revealing any underlying proprietary information or sensitive data. Consequently, ZKMLOps directly addresses the fundamental conflict between the need for transparency in auditing and for confidentiality in competitive and regulated environments. The research context in which we operate reflects an emergent MLOps Engineering discipline, a new subfield of Software Engineering that studies the challenges of operating and verifying ML-Enabled Systems (MLES) [39, 40]. The rimary novelty we introduce in this new field is a framework aimed at enforcing the legislation compliance standards in the scope of algorithmic auditing [49] with a structured assessment of an AI system against predefined norms. The key technical enabler in our contribution is founded on the cryptographic principles of Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) [30]. Over the past decade, succinct ZKP schemes such as Groth16 [32], Bulletproofs [10], and PLONK [26] have reduced roof sizes to the kilobyte scale and verification times to milliseconds, enabling practical deployments in blockchains and confidential computing. Similarly, the rapidly maturing sub-field of Zero-Knowledge Machine Learning (ZKML) has started to demonstrate how entire AI/ML evaluations can be proven in zero-knowledge facilities [72]. Nevertheless, there is still a consistent gap between protocol research and disciplined, repeatable software engineering lifecycles, rinciples, and automations that teams can adopt in production, to operationalize such advanced cryptographic tools within their MLOps initiatives. The proposed framework bridges this gap by integrating ZKPs with established software engineering theory and practice, evaluating this integration in action. For example, by leveraging software architectural Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- “Show Me You Comply... Without Showing Me Anything”: Zero-Knowledge Software Auditing for Al-Enabled System3 designs, the framework decouples the core auditing logic from the diverse implementations of ZKP protocols, thereby transforming a complex cryptographic procedure into a modular, repeatable, and maintainable engineering process. In summary, this paper makes three key contributions. First, we propose the ZKMLOps framework, a novel archi- tecture for integrating ZKP-based verification into the MLOps lifecycle. Second, we demonstrate the framework’s practicality by presenting a detailed use case for regulatory compliance in financial risk auditing, showing how our approach can be applied to solve a real-world problem. Third, we assess its feasibility through an empirical evaluation of various ZKP protocols. Quantifying these trade-offs confirms that a strategic selection of ZKP protocols makes the framework viable across a range of ML models, especially within asynchronous workflows that can accommodate intensive prover computation. 2 Background In this section, we present the necessary background on Trustworthy AI, auditing of AI systems, and ZKP to contex- tualize our work. We begin by defining Trustworthy AI and its core principles, including fairness, transparency, and accountability. Following this, we outline the practices of AI auditing, explaining its objectives and methodologies as a mechanism for ensuring that AI systems adhere to these principles. Finally, we introduce the cryptographic concept of ZKP, explaining how they function and their growing importance in enabling privacy-preserving verification in machine learning contexts. 2.1 Trustworthy Al According to the European Union [60], an ML-enabled system should meet four ethical principles: (i) respect for human autonomy, (ii) prevention of harm, (iii) fairness, and (iv) explicability. Based on these four principles, Liu et al. [45 survey the recent research efforts in this domain and identify six dimensions of trustworthy AI: (i) Safety and Robustness, ie., to be robust to the tiny perturbations of inputs and to be able to make secure decisions; (ii) Non-discrimination & Fairness, i.e., to avoid unfair bias toward certain groups or individuals; (iii) Explainability, i.e., to be able to be explaine to stakeholders; (iv) Privacy, i.e. to avoid leaking any private information; (v) Accountability, i.e., to be assessable by a third-party and assign responsibility for an AI failure; (vi) Environmental Well-Being, i-e., to be sustainable an environmentally friendly. This work focuses specifically on accountability, as it addresses the regulations on ML-enable: systems to follow these six dimensions. As stated by Li et al. [43], accountability runs through the entire lifecycle of an ML-enabled system and requires that its stakeholders justify their product design, software architecture, implementation, and operation as aligned with human values. From accountability are also derived the concepts of auditability and traceability, which require an ML-enable system to be reviewed, assessed, and audited [42]. Figure 1 shows these six dimensions and our focus on accountability. 2.2 Auditing of ML-Enabled Systems The auditing of an ML-enabled system—AI auditing for simplicity—can be defined along two axes: functionally and methodologically [51]. Functionally, AI auditing is a governance mechanism that can be managed by various actors. For instance, regulators may assess compliance with legal standards, technology providers can investigate how to mitigate technology-related risks, and stakeholders can make informed decisions about how they engage with specific companies. Methodologically, AI auditing is characterized by a structured process whereby an entity’s past or present behavior is assessed for consistency with predefined standards, regulations, or norms. Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- 4 Scaramuzza et al. Non- Discrimintation and Fairness Safety and Robustness Environmental Well-being Explainability PNecommelsiting \ Auditability Traceability Fig. 1. Extended representation of the six trustworthy Al dimensions [45] with a focus on Accountability [43]. The first known auditing procedure was employed during Roman times—the etymology of auditing stems from the Latin auditus, “a hearing’—and was used during official examinations of oral accounts [63]. As the ages passed, auditors began to verify written records as a governance mechanism to secure and enforce accountability, for example, in the form of financial audits. The rise of financial audits as we know them today stems from the Joint Stock Companies Act (1844), from the British Parliament, which required finance directors to issue audited financial statements to investors [70]. Nowadays, financial auditing and accounting have grown into one of the world’s largest industries, with an estimated market size of over $100 billion [51]. Another big family of audits is the safety audits. While financial audits seek to manage financial risks, safety audits aim at highlighting potential health and safety hazards, while assessing the effectiveness of the prevention mechanisms and countermeasures [2]. Safety audits have a history dating back to the Industrial Revolution in 19th-century Britain, where workers faced poor conditions and high risks of workplace accidents. As workers formed unions demanding better conditions, workplace safety auditing became a mechanism to hold employers accountable. Nowadays, a lot of these audits exist, spanning from workplace safety audits [28], food safety audits [17], and operational safety audits [38]. Analogously to financial and safety audits, algorithmic auditing has recently emerged as a practice to tackle the novel risks posed by ML-enabled systems. This type of audit provides a mechanism to independently and systematically assess the design, development, and deployment of these systems, ensuring they align with established standards and societal values concerning, for example, fairness, bias, and accountability [49]. Mékander et al. [51] identify two main drivers for the need for AI auditing, i.e., they serve as (i) a mechanism to implement legislation and (ii) a governance mechanism for private corporations. The first driver is a top-down pressure, as more and more regulations are being released, such as the EU AI Act [25] or Canada’s Directive on Automated Decision-Making [56], just to name a few. The latter is, instead, a bottom-up pressure, as organizations that design and deploy autonomous and self-learning technologies have incentives to implement and maintain appropriate governance mechanisms, for example, by subjecting themselves Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- “Show Me You Comply... Without Showing Me Anything”: Zero-Knowledge Software Auditing for AIl-Enabled SystemS to independent audits, they can assess and improve their software development process and quality management system [67]. Per definition, auditing requires a predefined baseline against which the audit’s subject can be evaluated, and depending on the audit’s purpose, this baseline can consist of either technical specifications, legal requirements, or voluntary ethics principles, and therefore three main categories of AI auditing exist: (i) technical, (ii) legal and (iii) ethical [51]. Technical approaches include procedures designed to quantify and assess technical properties of ML-enabled systems, including accuracy, robustness, and safety, both before market deployment and after. These procedures include well-known software engineering practices, like model evaluation and system validation & verification [9]. The term legal approaches, instead, refers to auditing procedures that assess whether the design and use of ML-enabled systems comply with relevant regulations. Lastly, the term ethical approaches refers to auditing procedures for which voluntary ethics principles serve as the normative baseline; for instance, ML-enabled systems may be audited against either a technology provider’s organizational values or ethics principles proposed by well-known institutions like IEEE [12]. In practice, these three types of approaches have loose boundaries. For example, to demonstrate legal compliance, auditors typically rely on technical methods for gathering evidence about the properties and impact ML-enabled systems have [37]. We place our contribution in this last scenario, where the verification of specific properties throughout the MLOps verification lifecycle can serve as a mechanism for legal compliance assessment. 2.3. Zero-Knowledge Proofs ZKPs provide a formal mechanism through which a prover can convince a verifier that a given statement is true, without revealing any information beyond the truth of the statement itself [30]. At the core of modern ZKP systems is the transformation of any arbitrary computations into arithmetic circuits defined over finite fields [50]. Any computable function can be rewritten as a sequence of additions and multiplications over a finite field Fp, where p is a large prime. The prover’s task is to demonstrate knowledge of a valid assignment to all the variables in the circuit, ensuring that all constraints hold. Formally, the prover proves the existence of a secret witness w that satisfies: C(x,w) =y where C denotes the arithmetic circuit, x represents public inputs, w is the private witness, and y is the public output of the computation. The ZKP convinces the verifier that there exists a secret w such that the circuit C satisfies C(x, w) = y = true, without revealing w. ZKPs were first studied in the setting of interactive proofs [50], where the prover and verifier engage in a sequence of challenge-response rounds. These protocols guarantee that a cheating prover cannot convince an honest verifier of a false statement, except with negligible probability. A significant step towards removing interaction was the Fiat-Shamir heuristic [24]. This technique transforms certain interactive protocols into non-interactive variants by replacing the verifier’s random challenges with the output of a cryptographic hash function applied to the transcript. While widely used and practical, this transformation’s security is typically proven in the idealized Random Oracle Model [6]. Blum et al. [66] later gave a precise mathematical definition of Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proofs (NIZKs) and showed how to build them with provable security guarantees in the standard cryptographic model, typically using a shared reference string that all parties can access. Both approaches result in a self-contained proof that can be verified without further interaction. Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- 6 Scaramuzza et al. To enable efficient proof generation and verification, many systems encode the execution trace of the computation into a polynomial P(x) over Fp: n P(x) = » cx" i=0 The prover commits to this polynomial using a polynomial commitment scheme [36], which ensures both binding (the committed polynomial cannot be altered later) and optionally hiding (its content remains secret). The verifier can then check whether the polynomial satisfies the required properties by querying a few evaluations at selected points. This drastically reduces the size of the proof and the cost of verification, achieving the property of succinctness. A key challenge in applying ZKPs to domains such as ML is handling non-linear functions, which are not naturally supported in arithmetic circuits. Neural networks, for example, often include non-linear activation functions like the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU (x) = max(0, x)) [5]. To represent such operations in ZKP-friendly form, systems typically use lookup arguments [35]. In a lookup argument, the prover shows that each non-linear operation maps an input to an output according to a precomputed table T: A(x,y) €T suchthat y = f(x) This allows incorporating non-polynomial logic into ZKPs while preserving succinctness and zero-knowledge. The table T encodes valid input-output pairs for the non-linear function, and the verifier only checks that the prover’s values appear in the table. 3 Related Work The literature has already investigated the applications of ZKP techniques to ML (ZKML). More specifically, the objective is to employ ZKPs in ML to prove that certain computations or operations within an ML system, such as inference, training, or data preprocessing, have been carried out correctly without disclosing the underlying data, model parameters, or internal workings [55, 73]. In particular, the current literature places strong emphasis on inference verification, which is the most extensively explored subfield of ZKML. Notable works include ZEN [22], vCNN [41],zkCNN [46], and [62]. In more recent years, the research community has also focused on other aspects, such as training [1] and online metrics verification [74], to name just a few. The literature also exhibits another trend, concentrating on use cases related to trustworthy AI [55], such as ZKAudit [68] and FaaS [65]. A more in-depth exploration of these approaches can be found in Figure 4 and Table 1. To the best of found knowledge, the existing literature has not addressed the practical application of ZKPs for auditing ML-enabled systems within the MLOps paradigm. However, a thorough search of the relevant literature yielded two related contributions. Waiwitlikhit et al. [68] propose ZKAupIT, a zero-knowledge audit framework enabling trustless verification of model training and data properties without revealing model weights or training data. The system consists of two main phases: ZKAupit-T, which proves that a model was trained via stochastic gradient descent on a committed dataset, and ZKAupit-I, which allows auditing arbitrary properties over the hidden data and weights through user-defined functions. The framework leverages ZK-SNARKs over AIRs, using the Halo2 [19] backend with optimizations such as rounded division, variable fixed-point precision, and softmax implementation in finite fields. The framework supports real-world models like MobileNet v2 and DLRM-style recommenders and allows audits such as censorship detection, copyright verification, and counterfactual analysis. Scaramuzza et al. [55] first survey the existing literature in ZKP protocols and identify five key properties (non-interactivity, transparent setup, standard representations, succinctness, and post-quantum security) critical for their application in ML validation and verification pipelines. Subsequently, they Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- “Show Me You Comply... Without Showing Me Anything”: Zero-Knowledge Software Auditing for AIl-Enabled System# perform a follow-up systematic survey analyzing ZKP-enhanced ML applications across an adaptation of the Microsoft Machine Learning Workflow model (Data & Preprocessing, Training & Offline Metrics, Inference, and Online Metrics), detailing verification objectives, ML models, and adopted protocols. This contribution, although relevant, misses a practical implementation or any guidelines for implementing such verification systems. 4 Research Methods Our approach is grounded on the following research question: RQ: How can Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) be operationalized to systematically audit the Machine Learning Opera- tions (MLOps) lifecycle? To address this question, we propose the ZKMLOps framework, the development of which is structured in four steps. These steps are depicted in Figure 2. First, we survey practical implementations of ZKP in ML contexts, such as SNARKjs, ezkl, and GKR, to ground our work in available code and concrete cryptographic backends. Second, we analyze representative use cases that highlight real-world needs for such proofs and, most importantly, define the main steps required for verification. These use cases include verifying inference results for proprietary neural networks and auditing datasets for fairness or bias without exposing sensitive data. Building on these first two steps, our main contribution is the design of a modular system architecture that generalizes these code examples into a flexible auditing framework. This architecture employs well-established patterns (e.g., hexagonal architecture, orchestrated saga) to support a variety of ZKP protocols and use cases across the MLOps lifecycle. Finally, we evaluate the framework’s practicality by showcasing a real-world use case and its feasibility by studying the performance of inference verification on different ML models using three different ZKP protocols. Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- 8 Scaramuzza et al. 5 Proposed Framework In this section, we present the ZKMLOps auditing framework and describe all of its building blocks, depicted in Figure 3. As anticipated in Section 2, the proposed framework’s design aims at allowing @ Trust Stakeholders to verify specific properties throughout the MLOps verification lifecycle, serving as a mechanism for legal compliance assessment. More specifically, this framework operates in the intersection between a methodic approach, i.e., with the adoption of guidelines for the operationalization of the first phase of the framework (@ , (2) , 3) , @ ), and more practical considerations, like the @ implementation of an Hexagonal Architecture[48], @ artifacts storage, @ scripts executing the different ZKP protocols, and an @ internal state-machine keeping track of the auditing workflow and coordinating the execution of every script with the required artifacts. 5.1 ML-Enabled System Verification Lifecycle: Guidelines for Protocol Selection Herein, we present the building blocks of the methodical part of the framework. In this first stage, the actor involved is the IT Solution Architect (SA), in collaboration with the ML Engineer (ML) [39]. The output of this stage is a document describing: (i) the purpose of the audit, (ii) the MLOps stage involved in the audit, (iii) the artifact (e.g., a model, a dataset, or a metric) that needs to be audited, and (iv) the protocol chosen. As we discuss in this section, the last item is strictly dependent on the previous ones, as every stage of the MLOps verification lifecycle has different implicit requirements, as well as the inherent implementation properties of the ML models. The production of this document allows for clear ownership and accountability over the implementation of a specific audit practice. In the first stage, the IT Solution Architect chooses a phase from the (1) MLOps verification lifecycle, based on the purpose of the audit. Scaramuzza et al. [55] propose a classification of the ZKP-Enhanced ML approaches from the white literature. Each of these approaches tackles a specific task of the MLOps verification lifecycle. Such classification is depicted in Figure 4. These four phases are derived from the TDSP Model [3], which phases have been grouped to allow more flexibility into: (i) Data and Preprocessing Verification, (ii) Training and Offline Metrics Verification, (iii) Inference Verification, and (iv) Online Metrics Verification. The Data and Preprocessing Verification phase includes the verification of properties related to dataset design choices and preprocessing operations, like model requirements, data collection, data cleaning and labeling, and feature engineering. The Training and Offline Metrics Verification includes the verification of the training process and the evaluation of model performance using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, or group and individual fairness, which are computed right after the training and before the deployment, thus the name “offline metrics”. This phase includes anything that fits into the Model Training and Model Evaluation phases. The Inference Verification phase focuses on ensuring the correctness of the inference computation process, and can happen only after the Model Deployment. Finally, the Online Metrics Verification phase involves the real-time verification of dynamic properties and metrics, such as model drift and live accuracy assessments, i.e., everything that fits into the Model Monitoring stage [3, 55]. In the (2) Model Selection stage, the ML Engineer supports the IT Solution Architect by providing details about the deployed model, choosing the right verification technique based on its requirements. In the survey from Scaramuzza et al. [55], they identify nine categories of models that have been successfully verified with ZKP in the literature. The results of the survey are shown in Table 1. These two phases can be summarised in a three-layered decision tree [47]. The root node represents the audit purpose, while the intermediate nodes represent the different stages of the MLOps verification lifecycle. The leaf nodes represent the models adopted. For each leaf node, a set of candidate protocols is listed. In this last phase, the Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- “Show Me You Comply... These properties are (i) non-interactivity, (ii) transparent setup, (iii) standard representations, (iv) succinctness, and (v) post-quantum security [55]. Non-interactive protocols compress proof generation into a single exchange, where the Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- 10 Scaramuzza et al. This significantly reduces overhead in asynchronous contexts, like auditing scenarios. The setup phase, in a ZKP protocol, refers to the preliminary step in which cryptographic parameters are generated before any proving or verification can occur. In a transparent setup, such parameters are derived solely from publicly available verifiable sources of randomness [59]. This is particularly appealing for applications requiring strong auditability and long-term trust guarantees. Zero-knowledge protocols do not operate directly on high-level programs or models; instead, they require computations to be transformed into formal representations that are compatible with their internal proof systems [20]. Having standard and flexible representations is crucial for enabling broader toolchain compatibility, developer accessibility, and seamless integration of ML models into various proof systems. Succinctness is a foundational property of many modern zero-knowledge protocols, particularly those intended for use in bandwidth-limited or resource-constrained environments. A protocol is considered succinct if the size of the proof and the time required for its verification scale only polynomially with the size of the input and output, independent of the complexity of the computation being proven [31]. Lastly, whether a zero-knowledge protocol is considered post-quantum secure depends entirely on the primitives it employs. In general, protocols built solely on collision-resistant hash functions (CRHF [8]) are believed to be more resilient in a quantum context, since no quantum algorithm is currently known to break CRHFs faster than brute force. After the elicitation of the system requirements and the choice of the ZKP protocol, the IT Solution Architect can now produce the final output of this process. We call this document the (@) ZKP Traceability Specification. This document contains all the discussed information, namely (i) The PuRPosE oF THE AuDIT, the (ii) DECISION TRACE that led to the choice of the specific protocol, consisting of the MLOps verification lifecycle phase and the deployed model, and (iii) the SELECTED PROTOCOL. As the name suggests, the storage of this protocol must allow the traceability of such a decision. The ZKP Traceability Specification falls into the definition of an ARCHITECTURE DECISION RECoRD [64], and can be Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- “Show Me You Comply... Without Showing Me Anything”: Zero-Knowledge Software Auditing for Al-Enabled Systerhs stored—following the guidelines from Richards et al. [52]—in an ADR Storage, i.e., a wiki or a shared directory on a shared file server that can be accessed easily with a wiki or other document rendering software from the other actors involved in the process. 5.2 Trustworthiness-as-a-Service In this section, we present the building blocks of the application-oriented dimension of the framework. This dimension, named Trustworthiness as a Service, represents the implementation of a service-oriented architecture that enables the systematic auditing of trustworthy ML-enabled systems by integrating arbitrary ZKP protocols in its workflow throughout the whole MLOps verification lifecycle. The architectural pattern employed is the hexagonal architecture @ , also known as onion or clean architecture [48]. This architectural pattern is designed to enhance the flexibility and maintainability of the codebase by ensuring the core business logic remains independent of external technology stacks, e.g., the diverse ZKP implementations and repositories. The operational logic, on the other hand, employs a SAGA PATTERN [53], where each audit workflow undergoes decomposition into smaller procedural steps within an internal state machine, across which an orchestrator manages the program execution with a STATE PATTERN [48]. According to the hexagonal architecture, the system is divided into three main components: core, ports, and adapters [48]. As one moves toward the core, the abstraction level increases. Specifically, the inner layer contains higher-level policies and broad business rules, while the outermost layers handle concrete implementation details. The core represents the most general and highest level of abstraction within the system. A detailed visualization of the hexagonal architecture is shown in Figure 5. Adapters are implementations of ports, and are managed employing a DEPENDENCY INJECTION PATTERN [57], where adapters are “injected” at runtime if needed in the specific audit workflow. The latter is defined through a configuration file and ingested through the Config port. In the Figure 5, two scenarios are shown: neural network inference correctness verification and bias verification over a proprietary dataset. These configuration files are derived from the ZKP Traceability Specifications and contain the scripts needed to perform every step of the verification and the related input and output artifacts. The inner hexagon, representing the © core, implements the business logic governing the auditing workflow. Specifically, it orchestrates the execution of the program through the four main ZKP steps of an internal state machine ©: setup, key exchange, proof, and verification. This is achieved by implementing the orchestrator with an ORCHESTRATED SAGA PATTERN [53] and a STATE PATTERN [27], where for every step, a set of pre and post conditions are checked, to verify whether the input and output artifacts have been correctly uploaded or generated in the artifact storage @ and that the steps are executed in the correct order. In this context, every running audit workflow is represented by an Audit, the incarnation of the Saga just mentioned. While the implementations and use cases vary considerably, the four steps are the foundational common components in every non-interactive ZKP protocol. Therefore, we abstracted these steps within the business logic, and we made the key-exchange step explicit: despite its conventional inclusion in the setup phase, we believe this separation is more suitable within a service-oriented context, in light of the asynchronous nature of the auditing workflow. Each of these steps is defined by a set of scripts, and each of them ingests and produces artifacts. The scripts and the pre- and post-conditions are defined in the above-mentioned configuration file. The outer hexagon, representing the oe) dependencies, implements an Anti-Corruption Layer against external dependencies [48] where the Ports AND ADAPTERS PATTERN is employed. More specifically, the system defines one inbound port and three outbound ports. The inbound port, Router, allows the business logic to be invoked by a set of REST APIs. This interface is implemented as dedicated adapters for every business logic, i.e., artifacts management and Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- 12 Scaramuzza et al. These actors are, for example, third-party auditors, regulators, end users, internal auditors, or federated learning collaborators. The only interaction these actors can have with the system is, as described above, through the interfaces exposed by the adapters. Ideally, this would be implemented with a GUI as a web app to ease the auditing process. 6 Example Use Case: Regulatory Compliance for a Proprietary Financial Risk Model In this use case, a Financial Institution aims to prove to an Auditing Company that the credit risk scores it produces via a machine learning model deployed as a service (MLaaS) are generated by the declared, approved model. The model is proprietary and trained on sensitive data, so its internal parameters must remain confidential. At the same time, Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- “Show Me You Comply... Without Showing Me Anything”: Zero-Knowledge Software Auditing for Al-Enabled Systerh3 regulatory compliance requires a verifiable process ensuring that the correct model was applied to approved input data without exposing the model itself. After receiving the Aup1T REQuEsT LETTER from the Auditing Company @, the IT Solution Architect and the Machine Learning Engineer determine the appropriate protocol for implementing the audit workflow (1) (2) (3) . In this context, a simplified version of the ZKP Traceability Specification produced is presented as follows: e PURPOSE OF THE AupIT: Verify that the financial institution’s deployed neural network model correctly computes credit risk scores on approved input data during the inference phase, without exposing proprietary model parameters. e Decision TRACE: Focus on the inference phase of the MLOps lifecycle. The approach ensures the deployed neural network’s outputs can be proven correct while maintaining confidentiality. e SELECTED PROTOCOL: ezk1. The protocol is non-interactive, has transparent setup, standard representation, succinctness, and is considered to be quantum secure. If this specific audit workflow is not yet implemented, the DevOps Engineer or the Developers can extend the existing architecture by following the already existing structure and define a new configuration file for the new audit workflow. Once the audit workflow is implemented, it follows the sequence diagrams shown in Figure 6. If the output is correctly generated by the declared model, the audit workflow concludes with a response compliant; otherwise, it shall return non compliant. In this scenario, the Financial Institution is required to share only the verification key generated during the Key Exchange step and the proof produced in the Proof step. No other information is disclosed, thereby ensuring verifiability of the process while preserving confidentiality and protecting intellectual property. This scenario showcases the effectiveness of the developed model. The auditor can have sufficient confidence in the proving procedure to formally conclude the audit workflow by issuing a compliance certificate. Meanwhile, the Financial Institution benefits by avoiding disclosure of any confidential information or intellectual property. From a societal perspective, such auditing mechanisms promote accountability and contribute to building the foundations of Trustworthy and Responsible AI. 7 Evaluation The objective of this evaluation is to assess the feasibility and performance of different ZKP protocols for inference verification, the most computationally intensive and critical phase within ML auditing pipelines [22]. The focus on inference is justified as it represents the most mature application of ZKPs within the MLOps verification lifecycle [55]. Furthermore, its relevance to real-time auditing scenarios and its inherent computational complexity make it the most pertinent stage for a practical performance analysis. The evaluation was conducted by synthesizing experimental results from a comparative study of top ZKP tools, including ezk1”, SNARK® (implemented via Circom’), STARK® (via Cairo°), and GKR (based on the work by Liu et al.[46]). As model complexity increases, this dynamic shifts. For the Small CNN and MNIST CNN models (Tables 3 and 4), SNARK becomes the leader in proof generation speed and consistently maintains its advantage in proof size. However, verification leadership is split, with STARK being the fastest for the Small CNN and ezk1 for the more complex MNIST CNN. In the case of the LeNet5 model (Table 5), the specialized GKR protocol predictably excels, delivering the best performance in both proving and verification. These results underscore a critical design consideration in ZKML: the trade-off between prover effort, verifier efficiency, and proof size. A tool like ezk1, for instance, demonstrates a profile that is particularly advantageous for asynchronous auditing workflows; while it may not be the fastest prover for complex models, its competitive verification times are ideal for scenarios where a powerful, centralized prover can handle the computational load, while numerous, potentially resource-constrained, verifiers require rapid validation. The key takeaway is not the dominance of a single tool, but the demonstrated feasibility of applying ZKP-based verification across a range of standard ML models. The existence of these distinct performance profiles provides developers with the flexibility to select a protocol that aligns with the specific constraints of their auditing application, thereby confirming the practical viability of integrating these advanced cryptographic techniques into the MLOps lifecycle. 8 Discussion We answer the RQ in Section 4 by proposing ZKMLOps. The framework operationalizes ZKPs by first offering a systematic process for selecting an appropriate ZKP protocol based on the audit’s purpose, the specific MLOps stage, and the artifact in question, e.g., a model, a dataset, or any arbitrary component of the Al-enabled system (see Section 5.1). Second, it provides a concrete, service-oriented architecture that transforms the complex, protocol-specific steps of generating and verifying proofs into a modular, repeatable, and maintainable engineering process (see Section 5.2 and Section 5.3). Our approach resolves the fundamental conflict between the need for transparency in auditing and the need for confidentiality in highly-regulated environments. The ZKMLOps framework changes the classical auditing dynamic by enabling verifiable, cryptographic proof of compliance without disclosing the underlying assets. This paradigm allows a financial institution, for example, to prove to an auditor that its deployed credit risk model is the one that was approved, without revealing the model’s parameters (see Section 6). From a societal perspective, this enables accountability and trust in AI systems by making auditing practical even for opaque "black box" models. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates the practical feasibility of integrating ZKP-based verification into the MLOps lifecycle for a range of standard ML models. The results, presented in Table 2 through Table 5, do not point to a single Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- “Show Me You Comply... Without Showing Me Anything”: Zero-Knowledge Software Auditing for Al-Enabled Systerh3 superior ZKP protocol. Instead, they highlight a set of trade-offs between proving time, verification time, and proof size with respect to the different models tested. The existence of these distinct performance profiles provides developers the flexibility to select a protocol that aligns with the specific technical and business constraints of their auditing application, confirming the viability of the ZKMLOps approach. Some ZK frameworks, such as ezkl [18], already leverage GPUs to accelerate both proving and verification, making ZK auditing feasible for larger models. The most important finding of our work from a Software Engineering perspectives, is how ZKP primitives can be integrated into existing engineering and organizational processes, like MLOps. We show how ingesting selected artifacts, generated in crucial phases of the MLOps lifecycle, within our framework can enable an additional degree of governance, like auditing and accountability. The development of the ZKMLOps framework was guided by several key design principles and software engineering patterns. The key principle was the decoupling of core business logic from external dependencies, which is essential for building a flexible, maintainable, and extensible system. Among the adopted patterns, the four most relevant were: the HEXAGONAL ARCHITECTURE, the ORCHESTRATED SAGA PATTERN, the STATE PATTERN, and the STRATEGY PATTERN. The relationship between these patterns is hierarchical and collaborative. The HEXAGONAL ARCHITECTURE provides the macro-level system structure. Inside its core, the SAGA PATTERN orchestrates the business process. The STATE PATTERN defines the steps of that process, and the STRATEGY PATTERN provides the concrete, interchangeable behaviors for each script execution, making the entire framework modular and adaptable to future requirements. 9 Threats to Validity and Limitations Following the guidelines from Feldt et al. [21] on the threats to validity for empirical software engineering, we selected four out of the seven threats proposed that better describe the limitations of the proposed work, namely: external validity, conclusion validity, internal validity, and construct validity. External Validity. We demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness through an illustrative use case in a domain with unique regulatory constraints and data sensitivities. The effectiveness of the ZKMLOps architecture may not directly transfer to other regulated fields, such as healthcare or autonomous systems, which present different compliance re- quirements and operational demands. We mitigated this threat through deliberate architectural choices. The adoption of well-known architectural patterns is intended to decouple the core auditing logic from domain-specific implementations, thereby enabling a high degree of flexibility. Conclusions Validity. The analysis focused exclusively on the inference verification stage, omitting other computa- tionally significant phases like training or data preprocessing. Furthermore, the evaluation employed relatively small machine learning models, which may not reflect the performance characteristics of larger, more complex architectures prevalent in industry. We addressed this threat by framing the evaluation’s purpose around demonstrating practical feasibility rather than optimizing for absolute speed. The key takeaway is that integrating ZKP verification into a structured MLOps pipeline is achievable for standard models, establishing a baseline for viability. This is particularly relevant in many compliance-driven auditing contexts, where the verification process can be performed asynchronously, prioritizing integrity over real-time speed. Internal Validity. The observed performance metrics could reflect the maturity and optimization level of the underlying cryptographic libraries rather than the inherent theoretical efficiency of the protocols themselves. We addressed this threat by executing all benchmarks within a strictly standardized experimental environment, ensuring that hardware and operating system variables remained constant across all tests. Moreover, by averaging results over multiple random initializations, we minimized the impact of transient system noise, thereby providing a robust comparison of the Manuscript submitted to ACM --- PAGE BREAK --- 18 Scaramuzza et al. practical performance of the available tools rather than a purely theoretical one. Construct Validity. The theoretical construct of trustworthiness includes multiple attributes, whereas our evaluation is confined to verifying the computational correctness of model inference, a specific aspect of auditing. We mitigate this threat by deliberately and transparently scoping our contribution. After introducing the wider context, the paper focuses specifically on accountability and auditing as a mechanism for legal compliance, rather than claiming to address all dimensions of trustworthiness. Furthermore, the proposed framework is architecturally designed for extensibility, allowing for the future integration of modules that could verify other constructs like fairness or data privacy. 10 Conclusions and Future Work In this paper, we introduced ZKMLOps, a novel framework for the systematic auditing of Machine Learning systems. Our work addresses the regulations on ML-enabled systems by focusing on accountability, from which the concepts of auditability and traceability are derived. We demonstrated that Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) provide the technical foundation to resolve the fundamental conflict between the need for transparency in auditing and the confidentiality required in competitive and regulated environments. ZKPs give verifiable cryptographic proof of compliance while pro- tecting proprietary models and sensitive data, by convincing a verifier (e.g., an auditing company) that a computational statement is true without revealing information beyond the statement’s validity. The central contribution of the ZKMLOps framework is to operationalize these advanced cryptographic tools within the MLOps lifecycle. The theoretical availability of ZKP primitives does not address the practical challenge of their systematic application. Our framework bridges this gap by integrating ZKPs with established software engineering patterns, decoupling the core auditing logic from the diverse implementations of ZKP protocols. This transforms a complex cryptographic procedure into a modular, repeatable, and maintainable engineering process. We demonstrated the framework’s practicality by presenting a use case for regulatory compliance in financial risk auditing. Furthermore, we assessed its feasibility through an empirical evaluation of various ZKP protocols, analyzing their performance trade-offs when applied to ML models of increasing complexity. This work thereby establishes a baseline for integrating advanced cryptographic techniques into real-world auditing workflows. Future work shall proceed in two primary directions. First, we plan to validate the framework in real-world settings through industry case studies to assess its performance and scalability. Second, we shall extend its capabilities by implementing auditing workflows for other trustworthy AI properties, such as verifying dataset fairness or model robustness against adversarial attacks. Data Availability and Replication Package The source code of the framework is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16125053. Our implementation satisfies the five core properties of a robust scientific contribution: it is re-runnable, repeatable, reproducible, reusable, and replicable [7]. We containerized the entire application to guarantee that the framework is both re-runnable on any host system and repeatable. This guarantee, combined with the adoption of well-established software engineering techniques, directly enables reproducibility and extendability. The repository also contains the code used to generate the benchmarks.
