As FGGM computes the adversarial CSI for potential victim CSIs within their normal ranges, the attack remains effective even if the victim CSIs change due to movement. B. Victim’s Observation To search for an adversarial input, attackers need to estimate the CSI values of target users. Prior works have primarily focused on scenarios where attackers know the exact CSI values of victims (9} {10}. This line of work typically involves downlink data transmission, where the base station broadcasts a CSI reference signal to users. users then estimate the CSI and provide feedback to the base station in plain text, which can potentially be intercepted by adversaries. One approach to mitigate this drawback is to encrypt the CSI feedback at the physical layer to maintain confidentiality from malicious users. Obtaining the exact values of victim CSI is more challenging in the context of uplink transmission in LTE/5G mobile systems, where users send the CSI reference signal to the base station. Since attackers are located in different locations than the base station, the CSI reference signals they measure will differ from the CSI measured at the location of the base station. In this work, our method estimates the boundaries of victim observations by leveraging the observation normalizer, which is an essential component of a DRL agent, aiding in stabilizing the training process Given that DRL observations often consist of multiple dimensions, each dimension bounded by an interval, the observation normalizer transforms each dimension to follow a standard Normal distribution. This normaliza- tion process is similar to data whitening in regression tasks to ensure that all components of the observations have an equal influence. Without the observation normalizer, training DRL algorithms for most continuous control tasks becomes impractical. The observation normalizer contains the mean and standard deviation of observations obtained during the --- PAGE BREAK --- training phase. Hence, these statistics can be leveraged to estimate the average observation values of a typical user. Let Lo and o, denote the mean and standard deviation of the observation vector for a user, which can be extracted from the observation normalizer of the trained SAC agent. We can bound the victim’s observations between [9+0905, where do is a scaling factor controlling the width of the bounds. Similarly, the search space for potential attackers can be defined within the same limits. IV. FORMAL GREY-BOX GRADIENT METHOD This section explain how to attack the DRL-based scheduler for MU-MIMO without knowing the exact values of observa- tions of victims. We begin by explaining our abstraction-based method to over-approximate the output of a DNN. Then, we formulate the network throughput degradation attack into a non-linear optimization problem, and solve it via stochastic gradient descent. A. Compute DNN Output Bounds via Polytope We opt for the polytope domain (e.g., DeepPoly (ip as it is a precise and computationally efficient domain for general DNN verification problems. Note that the notation utilized in this section is distinct from that used in other sections and is applicable solely within the context of this particular section. The polytope abstract domain works by: (a) representing the input ranges of the DNN as polytopes, (b) applying transformation rules to the affine and non-linear units of DNN to obtain polytope regions representing output values of those units, and finally (c) converting the polytope results into output’s lower and upper bounds. The resulting outputs are over-approximations of the actual outputs. This ensures the approximation remains conservative, meaning that the actual outputs are always contained within the predicted bounds. Specifically, the abstraction computes linear upper and lower bounds of the output of neural network N w.rt input x € X, where 2 is bounded input domain: Ar+b< N(x) <Ar+b, VreX, (8) where the output of neural network N(2) is bounded by linear function of input x. A,b denote the coefficients for the lower bound hyper-plane, whereas b. A are those of the upper bound hyper-plane. To get those of an L-layer feed-forward neural network JN, it propagates bounds of N(x) as a linear function to the output of each layer, in a backward manner. Optimization Problem to Degrade Victim Throughput The adversaries adjust their observations to cripple the throughput of the victims by minimizing the probability that victims are selected for data transmission, meaning the Q- value of any action a, € Ayic containing a victim. Specifically, let Ogay represent the local observations of the adversaries and let o,;, and Gy; denote the lower and upper bounds of the local observations of the victims, respectively. With these inputs, the --- PAGE BREAK --- adversarial cluster head computes the upper and lower bounds of the continuous proto actions (u and %) using polytopes over- approximation as follows: u,T = POLYTOPE(1(.|0; Ox); (Oadvs Qvic)» (Cadvs vic): (16) where 7(.|o;0,) represents the trained actor models, (Oadv; Qyic) ANA (Oady, Oyic) are the concatenations of adversarial inputs with the intervals of victim inputs. By leveraging the trained critic network Q(o, u; 9g), FGGM assesses the Q-value based on the inputs and proto actions. The final optimization problem for generating adversarial observations is as follows: minimize @, (17) Oadv such that 4,7 = POLYTOPE(Q(0, U; AQ), (Oadvs Qvics Ui)s (adv Bvics Ui))s (18) and Hadv — Sadvadv < Oadv < Hady + Sadvadv, (19) for all u <u <t, ~ 20 {2 € Avie, 0) where u,; is the proto action that corresponds to the discrete action a;, Ayic C A is the subset of actions that includes all actions containing victims, and [g,g| in the estimated interval of Q-values. The values of the observation for ad- versaries should be clipped to fall within the desired range [Hadv ~ Sadvadvs Hadv + Sadvadv]> Where [lady and aay are the mean and standard deviation of adversarial observations, and dady is a hyper-parameter to control the width of the search space. The objective is to minimize the upper bound of the Q-value for all possible actions containing victims. Given that ogay is differentiable, we can solve this problem using a standard gradient-based optimizer . Since this op- timization problem is non-linear, FGGM restarts many times to optimize Oaqy from multiple initial values. Note that polytope abstraction ensures that the upper bound is always higher than the lower bound, minimizing only the upper bound Q-value leads to the reduction of the lower bound, and it is sufficient for the attack. Furthermore, the cluster head only needs to solve this problem once at the beginning of the attack period and the group of adversarial users can reuse the optimized adversarial observations for all time steps. V. EVALUATION AND DISCUSSION We evaluate our adversarial attacks DRL-based MU-MIMO scheduler, and show that the proposed attack is effective in reducing network access probability and degrading throughput of victims. We focus our evaluation on the following research questions: : How does FGGM perform under various sizes of the search space for adversarial observations, and various sizes of bounds for observations of victims? : Can throughput degradation attack be per- formed more effectively if there are more adversarial users using FGGM? : What is the most significant consequence if the DRL-based scheduler is operating with 50% FGGM attackers? A. Experimental Design 1) Benchmarking Environment: To access our proposed attack, we created the target system based on a publicly available DRL algorithm for large-scale discrete action space (14), and trained this algorithm for the MU-MIMO scheduling problem (i). The CSI values of all users were simulated using Quasi Deterministic Radio Channel Generator (QuaDRiGa) software . We specifically examined a scenario where mobile users move at an average speed of 2.8 m/s with random directions. In this scenario, mobile users rebounded upon reaching the boundary, which is a circular area with a radius of 300 meters. Additionally, the environment utilized a 16- QAM modulation scheme, and the error vector magnitude of the received constellation is used to derive the signal-to-noise ratio. Further details on the hyper-parameters are presented Tab. I: Simulation parameters Parameter Values bandwidth 20 MHz carrier frequency 3.6 MHz slot duration lms number of time slots 500 number of users (L) {8, 16} number of antennas (/) {4, 16} maximum users per time slot (V) {4,4} proportional fairness coefficient 3 0.5 number of dimension of proto action D {3,8} number of nearest neighbor 1 {20, 20} number of hidden units in Actor 128 number of hidden units in Critic 256 number of hidden layers in Actor and Critic 2 activation function in Actor and Critic ReLU number of adversarial users (Laay) up to {4,8} number of FGGM/SPGD iterations 300 number of FGGM/SPGD restarts 10 number of SPGD samples 100 2) Baselines: The performance of our proposed attack FGGM is compared with that of conventional schedulers and other potential schemes for generating adversarial ob- servations. Conventional schedulers include policies such as Random, OptPF, optimal max rate (OptMR), optimal pro- portional fairness with user grouping (OptPFUG), and SAC. In each time slot ¢, the Random policy randomly selects one action from the action set A. OptMR and Opt PF policies exhaustively evaluate the action set A to determine the action that yields the highest data rate or proportional fairness score (Eq. 6). However, OptMR and OptPF are not scalable for more users as their computational complexities are O(2"), where L is the number of total users sharing the same resource block. Opt PFUG reduces the complexity by grouping users with channel correlation less than 0.5 in the same group and selecting the group providing the highest proportional fairness score. Similarly, SAC is a scalable method for MU-MIMO --- PAGE BREAK --- scheduling, as it takes a polynomial time to infer the set of users from the trained actor and critic networks (§II-C). Three adversarial attack schemes are considered: (1) Noise, (2) sampling-based projected gradient descent (SPGD), and (3) our proposed attack FGGM. Noise generates random CSI at each time slot ¢ for adversarial users to disrupt the SAC scheduler, regardless of the observations of the victims, and it represents the class of black-box attacks. SPGD is our adapted version of the origin PGD (24) to perform grey-box attack. It randomly generates samples of CSIs within the estimated bounds of the observations of victims and then solves the same problem in|§I for the generated set of samples. To ensure fairness in our comparison, SPGD and FGGM have the same number of iterations and number of restarts (T. 3) Evaluation metrics: We compare the performance of MU-MIMO schedulers and attack schemes via four main metrics; namely, proportional fairness, Jain fairness index (JFI), the selection probability of victims, and average data rate of victims. To compute these metrics, we run the simulator for 500 time slots using the same CSI trace from QuaDRiGa (23), and record the set of selected users as well as each of their instantaneous transmission rates. The proportional fairness per each time slot is calculated according to |E and the Jain fairness index at each time slot t is defined as: L : L Rt)? In general, both gradient-based grey-box attack methods showed significant improvements compared to Noise, and our proposed FGGM method surpassed SPGD in almost all searched numbers of attackers. In the presence of a grey-box attack, there is a correlation between the number of attackers and the reduction in selection probabilities and transmission rates of victims. In the most favorable scenario where adversarial users occupied half of the considered resource block, the worst transmission rate of victims reduced to half of that of the Noise attacking scheme. The rationale behind this trend is that higher number of attackers means smaller number of unknown inputs, leading to a smaller input domain. It enables FGGM to estimate the upper bound of Q-value more precisely, further diminishing the throughput and access probability of victims. D. RQ3: Impact under 50% Attack At this point, we discuss the impact of our attack to DRL- based MU-MIMO system under the best parameters obtained from the previous ablation studies. |Fi shows the disruption of the attack in our small setting of 8 users per resource block. We observed that without disruption, the SAC scheduler pro- vided nearly similar performance to Opt PF scheduler in terms of worst victim throughput, proportional fairness, and Jain fairness index. This suggests that our DRL-based scheduler has been well trained. However, the Noise attacker degraded the performance of SAC back to the same level as Random. The main reason is that our standard SAC algorithm for large-scale discrete action problems lacks adversarial training (25). and it also highlights the emergent need for robust DRL training. As shown in SPGD degrades SAC by reducing the data rate from 88.5 MB/s to just under 52.3 MB/s, while FGGM, with the formal verification technique, further halves the throughput of the victim, at an impressive 70%, which is about 26.6 MB/s. as the number of users and attackers doubled, the pattern remained the same. For instance, the FGGM sig- nificantly reduced the worst victim delivered data rate and Jain fairness index. SPGD showed improvement from Noise, but FGGM was still stand out as the best attacking method. It demonstrates that minimizing the upper bound of the output Q-value is more effective than sampling a limited number of examples for a PGD attack. Fig. 6a] indicates that FGGM still reduced the victim’s throughput by 46% in compared with the reduced Jain fairness distribution of SAC but did not have any impact on proportional fairness distribution. This implies that training the DRL-based to maximize multiple fairness metrics may improve the robustness of the DRL agent against adversarial attacks. RQ3 Findings: Under 50% attack, FGGM reduce victim data rate from about 46% to 70%. In resource block with 8 users, data rates of DRL-based scheduler were crippled from 88.5 MB/s to merely 26.6 MB/s. VI. RELATED WORKS We review several algorithms that are based on DNN for solving resource allocation problems in MU-MIMO, with the emphasis on their potential unsanitized inputs. We then discuss related works on exploiting of these algorithms. A. DNN for Resource Allocation in MU-MIMO The multi-user scheduling problem presents a significant challenge in resource allocation due to its computational com- plexity. To reduce the complexity of traditional optimization- oriented methods, many papers advocate DNN-based wireless resource allocation algorithms for different problems. Recenly, DRL has been introduced as a solution to approximate the optimal allocation strategy [7]. For instance, in [26], the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm is utilized to optimize a fully connected neural network that maps the channel state in- formation (CSI) to the user set to maximize the sum rate. Alternatively, proposes a method where users directly report their CSI to the base station (base station), which trains a DRL model to select a subset of users for transmission to maximize the sum rate. Moreover, in , a real-time deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) model is developed with CSI as the main input for user selection during transmission. Similarly, 29) introduces a SAC network that utilized CSI for user selection. Conversely, in (30), previous achievable rates and channel correlation matrices derived from CSI is used to determine both the user set and their channel precoding strategy. Additionally, incorporates channel quality index, data amount, and data type as the state variables in the selec- tion algorithm across multiple layers. Lastly, ie) implements a vanilla SMART approach where CSI served as input for a DNN actor, showcasing one of the most effective methods for multi-user scheduling. In summary, the input of recently proposes DNN-based resource allocation algorithms in massive MIMO included the CSI, large scale fading coefficient, spectral noise, SINR, or transmission rate. Note that they can be modified by a group of adversarial users, and so the DNN output could be manipulated to achieve malicious goals. The next section provides an overview of existing attacks to the input of DNN- based resource allocation algorithms. B. Attacking Algorithms for Resource Allocation in MU- MIMO Recent works proposed attacks on DNN-based wireless re- source allocation algorithms such as power allocation, resource slicing, and multi-user scheduling. --- PAGE BREAK --- 2.0- 4 + + I Es 80- E 098 Es TL 2 I © wo. £ Tr E 096 ff =e s a & = S10- ‘c a 40- 2 £0.08 - = 3 | it & 20- 2 a Ro sony ” I 2 $s s ¢ & © & > ee € © & © & Ss iS ss $ SS So Se f RS xf ¥ S S gs € Ss F&F FF TF LF HK SG aS se & FF SF SF |S € € (a) Worst victim delivered data rate (b) Proportional fairness (c) Jain fairness index Fig. 5: Performance of all schedulers and attacking schemes in networks configuration with L = 8 M = 4, N = 4, and Lady = 4 100 - 80 - 60- MB/s 40 - 20- proportional fairness (a) Worst victim delivered data rate ¢ oe s ve sf < oS (b) Proportional fairness Jain fairness pl ptf pf Ly ¢ 9 ss ¢ are 2 ¥ s iS 5 ve os < ~ gs e RY g (c) Jain fairness index Fig. 6: Performance of all schedulers and attacking schemes in networks configuration with L = 16 M = 16, N = 4, and Lady = 8 In {10}, the authors conduct a white-box attack on a DNN- based regression model that learned a mapping from users’ geological positions to the optimal power allocation, obtained by solving the problem using traditional optimization tools. The threat model involves attackers overwriting the positioning information of nearby users so to manipulate the network input using fast gradient sign method (FGSM) |. PGD [24], and momentum iterative fast gradient sign method (MI-FGSM) Similarly, other works proposes gradient-based white-box attacks on the full input of the DNN, while main- taining the assumption of knowing the exact location of all users, which is impractical. To address this issue, a black-box attack based on universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) (37). However, the evaluation reveals that the black- box attack lacks of stealthiness as it is effective only with large perturbation magnitudes. Additionally, previous works allow the adversary to apply adversarial perturbations to the full input of the DNN. , a resource slicing attack based on Q-learning was carried out. To reduce the Q-learning resource slicing agent’s reward, they suggests to train another Q-learning agent as an attacker. This Q-learning-based attacker selects the resource block and sent a jamming signal within a limited energy budget. Subsequently, introduces a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) resource slicing system, where each agent represented a base station in a multi-cell architecture. These agents are trained using centralized training decentralized execution to map user requests to available channel resources, maximizing the system’s throughput. An attacker is also trained to select resources to jam in order to minimize the system’s global reward. Note that training an attacker is computationally intensive and may not effectively exploit vulnerabilities in trained resource slicing agents. In (9}. a black-box heuristic attack is proposed to target the heuristic selection of users in multi-user scheduling in massive MIMO networks. The advantage of this work is that only a few attackers need to manipulate the CSI in the networks. However, they assumes that attackers could passively listen and accurately determine the current CSI of normal users, without investigating how to attack the DRL-based multi-user scheduling system. In conclusion, our work differs from existing literature by assume that adversaries only manipulate a small fraction of the attacker’s input to DRL models, without the knowledge of local observations of normal users. CONCLUSION In this paper, we present FGGM, a technique designed to generate adversarial observations that compromise the func- tionality of DRL-based resource allocation algorithms. Unlike other previous attacking schemes, FGGM only controls a part of the observations, and does not require the exact knowledge of the other uncontrollable parts. Experimental results on DRL-based scheduler for massive MU-MIMO networks show that adversarial observations generated by FGGM effectively reduced the allocated resources to victims without the exact knowledge of their local observations. By constructing an objective function based on output bounds, the adversarial --- PAGE BREAK --- inputs have been optimized using stochastic gradient descent to achieve specific goals, such as minimizing the likelihood of the victim being selected for transmission. 20 REFERENCES Qing An et al. “A Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Re- source Scheduler for Massive MIMO Networks”. 2510.26065v1 [econ.TH] 30 Oct 2025 arXiv Price Levels in Heterogeneous-Agent Models Felix Héfer* Princeton University October 31, 2025 Abstract We study a model of the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level (FTPL) in a Bewley-Huggett-Aiyagari framework with heterogeneous agents. The model is set in continuous time, and ex post het- erogeneity arises due to idiosyncratic, uninsurable income shocks. Such models have a natural interpretation as mean-field games, introduced by Huang, Caines, and Malhamé and by Lasry and Lions. We highlight this connection and discuss the existence and multiplicity of stationary equilibria in models with and without capital. Our focus is on the mathematical analysis, and we prove the existence of two equilibria in which the government runs constant primary deficits, which in turn implies the existence of multiple price levels. 1 Introduction We study a heterogeneous-agent! economy with monetary and fiscal authorities who issue nominal government debt and levy taxes, respectively. Our framework is rooted in the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level (FTPL), but while at the core of many FTPL models lie representative-agent models, we introduce household heterogeneity in the tradition of Bewley-Huggett-Aiyagari [6, 19, 4]. Such heterogeneous-agent models have become central to modern macroeconomics, see for example Cherrier, Duarte and Saidi [9]. As emphasized by Kaplan, Nikolakoudis, and Violante [20], while representative agent models only allow stationary equilibria in which governments run primary surpluses, the models we consider has equilibria with primary deficits—a prominent feature of empirical data from the United States since 1970 and Japan. In such equilibria, the real interest rate on government debt r is less han the growth rate of the economy g. Household heterogeneity is driven by idiosyncratic endowment shocks, which, together with the rice-taking assumption of households, naturally lends itself to a mean-field game (MFG) interpretation. The MFG literature, initiated independently by Caines, Malhamé and Huang [15, 16, 17, 18], and Lasry and Lions [21, 22, 23], motivates our two-step equilibrium construction: we first establish the well-posedness of the household problem for given prices and policies and then impose market clearing. This mirrors the fixed-point structure of MFGs (see Carmona and Delarue [8])—a connection we make explicit in Section 1.2. Our goal is to provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for stationary heterogeneous-agent versions of the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level. Consequently, this manuscript’s focus is on the mathematical analysis of stationary equilibria, and our work complements the recent paper [20], which studies a Huggett model without capital. In particular, we establish regularity properties of households’ The author thanks Markus Brunnermeier and Sebastian Merkel for their invaluable guidance and support. Research partially supported by the National Science Foundation grant DMS 2406762. *Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, 08540, USA, email: [EMAIL_REDACTED] 1 Households are heterogeneous because of income shocks that are idiosyncratic to each household, not due to different utility functions or dynamics. This should not be confused with heterogeneity modeled through graphon games. --- PAGE BREAK --- Felix Hofer Price Levels in Heterogeneous-Agent Models optimal consumption rules and of the invariant cross-sectional distribution needed for the analysis. Our framework allows for both unbounded utility functions and general finite-state income processes. We further introduce an Aiyagari model with capital and characterize its stationary equilibria. In the version without capital, we refer to [20] for a discussion of extensions that ensure uniqueness of the price level. Our contributions are as follows. First, using the theory of constrained viscosity solutions, we analyze the household problem and prove the existence of classical solutions together with a comparison principle for general utility functions, including unbounded CRRA utilities. Second, we derive an explicit and sharp lower bound on the interest rate below which only non-monetary equilibria exist. Building on related work, we prove the existence and uniqueness of an invariant measure and continuity with respect to model parameters. An important ingredient to the equilibrium analysis is the fact that aggregate savings diverge as the interest rate approaches the households’ discount rate, which we also establish. We then discuss the existence and uniqueness of stationary equilibria in models with capital (Aiyagari) and without (Huggett). In particular, we establish the existence and uniqueness of equilibria in both models for a given primary surplus and the existence of two equilibria for small primary deficits. In the Aiyagari version, we additionally require smallness of the capital elasticity of output © guarantee the multiplicity of equilibria, and we numerically show non-existence for large primary deficits in both models. Finally, we prove that Aiyagari equilibria converge to Huggett equilibria as he capital elasticity of output tends to zero. After introducing the models in Section 1.1 and discussing their connection to mean-field games in Section 1.2, we state our main Theorems 1.18, 1.20, and 1.21 in Section 1.3 and discuss the related iterature in Section 1.4. It is commonly assumed in the economic literature that a continuum of households is given, often on the unit interval [0,1], and that each household i € (0, 1] carries their own independent idiosyncratic random process z}, see, for example, Bewley [6]. Aggregation is then taken with respect to the Lebesgue measure on i € [0, 1]. This approach is mathematically intricate and subtle measurability issues arise. While this approach can be made precise using Fubini extensions, we avoid these issues entirely by treating the problem as a mean-field game, and instead average over w € 2 randomness. Under appropriate assumptions, both approaches yield the same solution concept. In particular, identities such as [ 2)PCaw) -| 2 di 2 [0,1] can be proven using the exact law of large numbers, see for example Sun [31]. We emphasize that, in both the Huggett and Aiyagari model, households take prices (r*, w*) and a tax-and-transfer function r*(-) as given and then optimize over their consumption. In equilibrium, prices have to be consistent with the cross-sectional distribution of the optimally controlled state process (af, Z:)e>0 Via the market clearing conditions. This philosophy is precisely the idea underpinning the theory of mean-field games, and we discuss this connection in Section 1.2. Remark 1.2. To make the connection to mean-field games in the next section, we relax the above equilibrium definitions and only require the existence of an optimal control starting from a fixed initial condition (ao, 29) ~ G*. More precisely, instead of a feedback function c*(a, z) we consider an open-loop control (cf);>0 that is admissible starting from an initial condition (ao, zo) ~ G*. A priori, this makes the notion of equilibria dependent on the underlying probabilistic structure. Usually, one appeals to results on the law-invariance of the typical household’s problem, see, for example, [12, 14], to obtain a definition that is independent of the underlying probabilistic structure. In the cases we study, optimal controls are naturally of feedback form, and hence a law-invariance principle automatically holds. 1.2 Connection to mean-field games This section formulates the problem of finding stationary Huggett and Aiyagari equilibria as a mean- field game. In the mean-field literature, it is common to call a household that faces the optimal control problem (1.2) a representative household. This is motivated by the fact that one imagines a mean-field of households, each solving the same optimal control problem but with independent idiosyncratic noise processes. In macroeconomic theory, however, a representative household refers to a model without idiosyncratic shocks so that all households are identical, see [20], and we follow Acemoglu [1, Chapter 17.4] in replacing the phrase representative household by typical household. 1.3. In this equilibrium, any interest rate r* satisfies r* > —6. 1.4 Discussion and related literature This work sits at the intersection of three streams of literature: (i) the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level (FTPL), (ii) the continuous-time analysis of heterogeneous-agent models and (iii) the mathematical theory of mean-field games. 11 --- PAGE BREAK --- Felix Hofer Price Levels in Heterogeneous-Agent Models We contribute to the question of price-level determinacy within FTPL models. Building on Brunnermeier, Merkel, and Sannikov [7], who study uniqueness with idiosyncratic return risk in low-interest-rate environments, we adapt the setting to a framework where incomplete markets arise rom idiosyncratic, uninsurable income shocks in the tradition of Bewley-Huggett-Aiyagari. In the version of our model without capital, the recent preprint [20] coincides with our setup. We complement heir treatment with a mathematical analysis of the stationary problem and extending it to an Aiyagari model with capital. For further references in the macroeconomic literature, see [20], and for additional ackground on the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level, see Cochrane [10]. Our main results are as follows. In Theorem 1.18, we show that the price level in a stationary Huggett economy is unique for any given primary surplus 7 > 0. For small deficits (7 < 0 close to zero), wo equilibria emerge, whereas for sufficiently large negative 7 stationary equilibria may fail to exist. n the Aiyagari model with production (Theorem 1.20), we likewise establish existence and uniqueness or any given 7 > 0, and we prove the existence of two equilibria for small deficits and small capital elasticities of output. Exploiting a scaling property under CRRA utility, we also obtain uniqueness for a fixed interest rate; see Propositions 1.15 and 1.19. Finally, Theorem 1.21 shows that, as the capital elasticity of output tends to zero, Aiyagari equilibria (when they exist) converge to Huggett equilibria. Our emphasis is on rigorous mathematical analysis. We draw extensively on the theory of viscosity solutions and stochastic optimal control, relying in particular on the notion of constrained viscosity solutions introduced by Soner [28, 29]. We address the absence of a priori continuity of the value function at the boundary, prove a comparison principle, and establish C1 regularity of the value function. Using stability properties of viscosity solutions, we further show continuity of optimal feedback controls with respect to the interest rate. Building on Acikgéz [3] and Shigeta [27], we prove existence and uniqueness of an invariant cross-sectional distribution and show its continuity with respect to the interest rate. We also establish that aggregate savings explode as the interest rate approaches the households’ discount factor. Our “direct” proof is motivated by the discrete-time proof due to [3] and does not rely on martingale techniques as in [27]. Related work on the existence and uniqueness of stationary equilibria in heterogeneous-agent models includes the discrete-time analysis of [3] and the continuous-time treatment of [2]. Shigeta’s recent reprints [26, 27] establish existence and uniqueness of an invariant distribution in a related framework, and we build on several of those results. In contrast to the bounded-utility assumption there, our analysis accommodates more general—possibly unbounded—utility functions, more general borrowing constraints, and we prove a comparison principle in this setting. In the two-state income case |Z| = 2, Bayer, Rendall, and Walde [5] also proved the existence and uniqueness of an invariant measure. Structure of the remaining paper. In Section 2, we first fix an interest rate r < p, a wage w > 0, and a tax-and-transfer rate 7 < 1, and analyze the stochastic optimal control problem of a ypical household. In particular, we prove Theorems 1.8 and 1.9. In Section 3, we prove the existence and uniqueness of an invariant distribution of the optimal state process in Theorem 1.10. We also establish the lower interest rate bound (Proposition 1.11) and a scaling property under CRRA utility (Proposition 1.12). Continuity of the invariant distribution in the interest rate (Proposition 1.13) and he fact that aggregate savings diverge as the interest rate r approaches the discount rate p (Theorem 1.14) are also proved in Section 3. Finally, Section 4 uses the results established in Sections 2 and 3 to rove the statements about stationary Huggett and Aiyagari equilibria recorded in Propositions and Theorems 1.15, 1.18, 1.19, 1.20 and 1.21. 2 Household problem This section analyzes the optimal control problem of a typical household for given values of (r, w,7). 2510.26060v1 [cs.NI] 30 Oct 2025 arXiv JOURNAL OF I4TgX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020 Performance Analysis of Dynamic Equilibria in Joint Path Selection and Congestion Control Sina Keshvadi Abstract—Path-aware networking, a cornerstone of next- generation architectures like SCION and Multipath QUIC, em- powers end-hosts with fine-grained control over traffic forward- ing. This capability, however, introduces a critical stability risk: uncoordinated, greedy path selection by a multitude of agents can induce persistent, high-amplitude network oscillations. While this phenomenon is well-known, its quantitative performance impact across key metrics has remained poorly understood. In this paper, we address this gap by developing the first axiomatic framework for analyzing the joint dynamics of path selection and congestion control. Our model enables the formal characterization of the system’s dynamic equilibria-the stable, periodic patterns of oscillation-and provides a suite of axioms to rate their performance in terms of efficiency, loss avoidance, convergence, fairness, and responsiveness. Our analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off in protocol design between predictable performance (efficiency, convergence) and user-centric goals (fair- ness, responsiveness). We prove, however, that no such trade- off exists among efficiency, convergence, and loss avoidance, which can be simultaneously optimized through careful param- eter tuning. Furthermore, we find that agent migration can, counter-intuitively, enhance stability by de-synchronizing traffic, a theoretical result validated by our simulations. These findings provide a principled design map for engineering robust, high- performance protocols for the future path-aware Internet. Index Terms—Dynamic Equilibria, Path Selection, Congestion Control, Network Oscillation, Performance Analysis, Axiomatic Method I. INTRODUCTION The principle of end-host-driven path selection is ex- periencing a significant resurgence, forming the bedrock of next-generation network architectures designed to overcome the rigidity of today’s Internet. In the inter-domain, path-aware architectures like SCION are enabling enterprises to achieve unprecedented levels of security and availability by allowing endpoints to explicitly select network paths that bypass threats and performance bottlenecks [1]. Concurrently, within data centers and across the mobile edge, transport protocols such as Multipath QUIC (MPQUIC) leverage path diversity to deliver tangible perfor- mance gains, enhancing connection resilience and throughput by dynamically scheduling traffic over multiple available links [2]. Yet, this powerful capability introduces a critical, systemic risk: when a large population of self-interested agents indepen- dently and greedily selects paths based on perceived load, their uncoordinated actions can trigger persistent, high-amplitude load oscillations. This phenomenon threatens to undermine the very stability these advanced architectures aim to provide, a concern whose relevance is only amplified by the increasing scale and dynamism of modern network environments [3]. While this stability challenge is well-recognized, the vast body of prior research has predominantly concentrated on de- signing suppression mechanisms—strategies intended to guide selfish agents toward a stable equilibrium and prevent oscilla- tions from occurring in the first place [4]. Although critical, this focus on mitigation has left the underlying performance trade-offs of the instability itself largely unquantified. Key questions often remain unexplored: by precisely how much does oscillation degrade network efficiency during periods o traffic migration? How does it impact the fairness experienced by competing end-hosts? And what is the resulting cost in terms of convergence time and performance predictability? Answering these questions requires a framework capable o characterizing not just static equilibria, but the dynamic, and potentially non-convergent, behavior of the system. We argue that an axiomatic approach, which has been used to derive fundamental truths in areas from economics to routing protoco: design, provides the ideal lens for this investigation [5]. Our work, therefore, is the first to adapt and significantly extend the formal axiomatic method for single-path congestion contro: to the multi-path domain, providing a rigorous foundation for analyzing the joint dynamics of path selection and rate adaptation [6]. Our axiomatic analysis yields several insights that challenge the conventional understanding of path selection dynamics. Perhaps most notably, we establish that there is no funda- mental performance trade-off between network efficiency, loss avoidance, and the stability of traffic flows. These three critical goals, which collectively define predictable network operation, can be simultaneously optimized through principled protocol design. This co-optimization, however, reveals a deeper, inher- ent tension: we demonstrate that these performance metrics are fundamentally at odds with inter-agent fairness and a protocol’s responsiveness. Specifically, tuning a protocol for higher responsiveness—enabling agents to rapidly migrate to better paths—improves fairness but necessarily introduces greater load volatility and reduces overall throughput. This work therefore replaces the monolithic view of path selection’s instability with a nuanced, multi-faceted perspective, quantify- ing the precise conditions under which its effects are beneficial versus detrimental. In summary, this paper makes the following primary con- tributions: « A Generalized Analytical Framework. We develop a tractable model of joint path selection and conges- tion control that integrates key behavioral parameters— namely, agent responsiveness (m) and reset softness (r)— into a multi-path axiomatic system. ¢ Equilibrium Characterization. We detail our analytical model and its underlying dynamics in Section IV, followed by a characterization of its equilibria in Section V. We then formally define our axiomatic performance metrics in Section VI, use them to derive our key theoretical insights in Section VII, and validate our findings through simulation in Section VIII. We conclude in Section X with a discussion of limitations and future directions. Il. RELATED WORK The architectural principle of vesting path-selection intel- ligence in network endpoints has gained significant traction across a diverse array of networking domains, driven by the demand for greater performance, security, and flexibility. This trend is evident in proposals for multi-criteria routing, which empower applications to choose paths satisfying complex objectives beyond simple latency, such as economic cost or specific security postures [7]. In massive-scale data centers, fine-grained, source-driven traffic management is increasingly used to optimize for ultra-low latency and minimize flow com- pletion times for demanding applications [8]. The principle is also central to emerging network topologies; for instance, the highly dynamic nature of LEO satellite constellations necessitates source-based mechanisms for adapting to rapid changes in path availability and quality [9]. Finally, in next- generation inter-domain architectures such as SCION, end- host path control is a foundational element, enabling explicit trust establishment and resilience against prefix hijacks and routing anomalies [1]. While their specific goals vary, these systems are unified by the transfer of path-selection agency to the network edge. This architectural shift, however, invari- ably reintroduces the fundamental challenge of maintaining global network stability in the face of uncoordinated, greedy decisions made by a multitude of self-interested agents. The literature aimed at mitigating these load oscillations can be broadly classified into two main paradigms: centralized and end-host-based. Centralized approaches, typified by Software- Defined Networking (SDN)-based traffic engineering, rely on a logically unified controller with a global network view. This controller computes stable traffic distributions and installs for- warding rules that prevent the uncoordinated, greedy behavior that leads to oscillations in the first place [10]. In contrast, end-host-based approaches seek to achieve stability without central coordination by modifying the decision-making logic of the agents themselves. Such strategies include introducing inertia to discourage frequent path changes, using random- ized “hedging” strategies, or implementing more sophisticated adaptive algorithms that allow agents to converge to a stable state over time [11]. Despite their architectural differences, both research thrusts share the primary goal of oscillation sup- pression. Our work adopts a fundamentally different and com- plementary posture: rather than designing new mechanisms to prevent instability, our objective is to formally characterize and quantify its multifaceted performance consequences when --- PAGE BREAK --- JOURNAL OF I4TgX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020 it does occur, thereby providing a rigorous understanding of the system’s dynamic, oscillatory behavior. From a methodological standpoint, prior efforts to model path selection dynamics have navigated a trade-off between abstraction and specificity. Foundational work in selfish rout- ing has used the classic Wardrop model to analyze static traffic distributions, their efficiency (often termed the Price of Anarchy), and convergence properties [12]. However, these models cannot appropriately represent the congestion-control dynamics central to our analysis. At the other end of the spectrum, applied research in Multipath TCP, such as the design of protocols like LIA and OLIA, captures oscillatory phenomena but relies on ad-hoc reasoning and experimental validation, limiting its generality [13]. Our work adopts the axiomatic method, first applied to congestion control by Zarchy et al., as a compelling alternative that balances these extremes [6]. This aligns with a broader research program that has successfully applied axiomatic reasoning to other areas in computer science, including routing protocols and recommendation systems [14]. Finally, our work is distinguished from prior theoretical analyses of multi-path routing, such as the work by Wang et al. on the ’cost of not splitting in routing’ [15]. Their research captures the difference in network utility between selecting a single path versus concurrently using multiple paths. However, our work differs in several key aspects: we investigate the dynamic evolution of traffic rates rather than static allocations; we evaluate performance using a suite of axioms rather than a single utility metric; and our comparison is between a system with path selection and one with pre-determined paths, rather than between different modes of path selection. II]. BACKGROUND: THE AXIOMATIC METHOD IN CONGESTION CONTROL The axiomatic method for congestion control, introduced by Zarchy et al., provides a formal framework for analyzing and comparing the fundamental behavior of transport pro- tocols [6]. The approach is designed to move beyond ad- hoc, scenario-specific evaluations by establishing a set of first principles—or axioms—that represent universally desirable properties for any congestion control algorithm. In the canon- ical single-path context, these foundational axioms allow for a multi-dimensional characterization of protocol performance. They include: Efficiency, which requires a protocol to make full use of available bottleneck capacity; Fairness, which dictates how that capacity should be equitably shared among competing flows; Convergence, which demands that flow rates settle within a tight range of a steady-state value; and Loss Avoidance, which mandates the minimization of packet drops. Together, these axioms provide a formal basis for articulating and quantifying the inherent, and often conflicting, design trade-offs at the core of congestion control. The method borrows its philosophical underpinnings from classical economics and game theory, where axiomatic frame- works have long been used to formally define the properties of a “fair” or “desirable” outcome in systems with competing agents [16]. The evaluation process for a given protocol is methodical: first, a mathematical model is constructed to represent the interactions of agents universally adopting that protocol. Second, this model is analyzed to identify its long- term equilibrium state—the stable pattern of behavior to which the system dynamics converge. Finally, the properties of this equilibrium are measured against the predefined axioms, yield- ing a quantitative rating of the protocol’s intrinsic performance characteristics. For instance, to analyze a classic protocol such as TCP Reno, one would first formalize its well-known additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) behavior as follows: w(t +1) = { wi(t) +1 + -wilt) if L(t) <Cy if L(t) > Cy (no loss) (loss event) cwnd;(t) + a(r;(t)) B+ cwnd;(t) cwnd;(t+1) = { if Fall) S Cn if fx(t) > Cr (2) While this framework is powerful for analyzing protocols on a single, shared resource, its core assumptions are fundamen- tally challenged in a path-aware network. The ability of agents to dynamically select and migrate between paths introduces a new degree of freedom that has no analogue in the single- path model. This agent migration, driven by the rational, self- interested pursuit of uncongested links, intrinsically couples the load dynamics across all available paths. As a result, the system may not converge to a static equilibrium at all. Instead, the uncoordinated actions of agents can drive the network into a dynamic equilibrium characterized by persistent, periodic load oscillations. Such behavior lies outside the scope of the original axiomatic framework, which was designed to rate the properties of a fixed-point convergence, thus necessitating a direct extension to accommodate the unique dynamics of path- aware systems. Building on this foundation, our work introduces the nec- essary extensions to apply this rigorous method to the path- aware domain. Our primary adaptation is to shift the analytical focus from static fixed-points to the properties of the dynamic equilibria that characterize oscillatory systems. This allows us to reason formally about persistently fluctuating network states. In doing so, we also elevate Responsiveness—an agent’s propensity to migrate to a better path—to a first- class property, treating it not as an externality but as a core, tunable parameter of a joint path-selection and congestion control protocol. Consequently, our extended framework will evaluate protocol performance across a comprehensive suite of five axioms: the canonical properties of Efficiency, Fairness, Convergence, and Loss Avoidance, which we reinterpret for the dynamic context, alongside the newly incorporated dimension of Responsiveness. This scenario rests on the following three core assumptions: 1) Greedy, Load-Adaptive Selection. We assume agents are myopic and act greedily, always migrating to the path with the lowest instantaneous utilization. This behavior is a well-understood driver of instability in competitive routing games, as it encourages “herding” dynamics where agents rush en masse to a newly attractive resource, thereby congesting it and restarting the cycle [17]. Sequential Multi-path Usage. When an agent switches paths, we assume it migrates its entire traffic flow at once, rather than gradually splitting traffic. This maximizes the impulse of each migration event and thus the amplitude of the resulting load oscillations. This assumption is also a pragmatic approximation of real-world protocol behavior, as schedulers for Multipath TCP, for example, often concentrate the vast majority of traffic onto the single best-performing path at any given time [18]. 3) Disjoint and Similar Paths. We model the P paths as being resource-disjoint and homogeneous in terms of their bottleneck capacity and round-trip time. Model Limitations The clarity and analytical tractability of our model are predicated on several simplifying assumptions that necessarily define its scope. Our focus on a topology of homogeneous, parallel paths results in a system with implicitly synchronized feedback, which, while creating a tractable worst-case scenario for coherent oscillations, abstracts away the complexities of asynchrony and shared bottlenecks found in real networks. Furthermore, our framework is presently specified for the broad class of loss-based congestion control protocols. Ex- tending this axiomatic analysis to capture the fundamentally different dynamics of modern latency-based and model-based algorithms, such as BBR [20], represents a compelling and important direction for future research. Despite these limita- (no loss)tions, our model provides a robust and essential foundation for (loss evetteyiving the first-order principles that govern the performance of path-aware systems. bh be --- PAGE BREAK --- JOURNAL OF I4TgX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020 V. EQUILIBRIUM CHARACTERIZATION Having established the deterministic equations governing the system’s expected dynamics, we now analyze their long- term behavior. Our analysis reveals that the interplay between greedy path selection and congestion control does not drive the system toward a static fixed point, but rather toward a dynamic equilibrium. In the language of dynamical systems, such an equilibrium corresponds to a stable periodic orbit, or limit cycle, in which the system state—the vector of per-path agent counts and loads—evolves through a finite, repeating sequence of values [21]. Our objective in this section is to formally identify and characterize these periodic patterns. We will show that the system converges exponentially fast to one of two classes of dynamic equilibria: /ossless equilibria, where path capacities are always respected, and lossy equilibria, where they are periodically breached. The structure of both equilibrium types is determined by a remarkably consistent pattern of agent migration, which we formalize next. The structure of these equilibria is governed by a remark- ably consistent and self-organizing pattern of collective agent behavior, which we term a P-step oscillation. This is a dynamic pattern with a period of P time steps, in which the utilization-based ranks of the P available paths permute in a deterministic, round-robin fashion. The oscillation is driven by two coupled migration dynamics. First, the in-migration to the least-utilized path is consistently over-reactive: the sudden influx of agents is so large that this path invariably becomes the most utilized in the subsequent time step. This confirms that the myopic greedy strategy is not a Nash Equi- ibrium, as agents acting on momentarily correct information achieve a collectively pessimal outcome [17]. Second, the corresponding out-migration of agents from all other paths is order-preserving, meaning their relative utilization ranks are maintained. The composite effect is a perfectly predictable rank permutation: the path at rank p € [0, P — 2] moves to rank p+ 1, while the path at rank P — 1 jumps to rank 0. We formalize this cyclical rank evolution as follows: First, we define the rank of a path 7 at time t based on its expected load, which orders all paths from most utilized (rank 0) to least utilized (rank P — 1): rank(7,t) =p |{r’ € TL | La(t) > L.(t)}|=p. (9) With this, we can formally define the system’s core oscil- latory pattern. Definition 1 (P-step Oscillation). A system’s expected dynam- ics exhibit a P-step oscillation if there exists a time to after which the rank of any path m € II evolves according to the following rule for all T > 0: If rank(z, to) =p, then rank(z,to+T) = (p+T) (mod P). (10) A natural question is whether this P-step oscillation is a universal property of our model or a fragile artifact. We can test this by checking for logical consistency: if the hypothetical equilibrium flow volumes that result from assuming a P-step pattern are themselves inconsistent with that pattern (e.g., a rank-0 path has less flow than a rank-1 path), then our assumption must be invalid for those system parameters. We performed this consistency check across a wide range of parameters for responsiveness (p) and reset softness (7). The results, shown in Figure 3, demonstrate that the P-step pattern is remarkably robust. Inconsistencies only arise in a small, corner-case fraction of the parameter space, justifying our use of the P-step oscillation as the foundational dynamic pattern for the remainder of our analysis. This P-step oscillation pattern provides a deterministic map of agent migration, which allows us to solve for the agent equilibrium. Consider a path 7) that is at rank 0 at time to. For P — 1 consecutive time steps, it is not the least-utilized path, so it only experiences agent outflow, governed by the first case of Eq. (8a). At time to + P — 1, it reaches rank P—1 (the minimum). In the next step, to + P, it receives all agent inflow per the second case of Eq. (8a), returning it to rank 0. This complete cycle is characterized by the following first-order difference equation, which models the agent count for a specific path 7 at intervals of P time steps: ax (to + P) = (1— p)Pax(to) + pN qd) The predictable structure of the P-step oscillation allows for a full analytical characterization of the system’s lossless dynamic equilibrium. A key contribution of our work is the re-interpretation of these axioms for the context of a perpetually oscillating system. Unlike in a single-path model where metrics are evaluated at a static fixed point, our ratings are derived from the properties of the entire periodic cycle, such as its amplitude, minimum, and maximum values. We now proceed to formalize a metric for each of the five axioms previewed in our background: Efficiency, Loss Avoidance, Convergence, Fairness, and Responsiveness. We begin with Efficiency, which captures the productive use of network capacity. An MPCC protocol’s efficiency is determined by its ability to consistently utilize the available network capacity, ensuring that traffic migration does not lead to periods of severe under- utilization. We formalize this as follows: Axiom 1 (Efficiency). An MPCC protocol is said to be €- efficient if, once the system has converged to its dynamic equilibrium (for t > to), the utilization on any path 7 € II is guaranteed to never drop below the value e. The efficiency rating is therefore the minimum sustained utilization across all paths in the equilibrium cycle: €= min Ln(t) ~ t>to,nett C/P Higher values of € € {0,1] are more desirable. (20) The axiom of Loss Avoidance quantifies a protocol’s ability to respect link capacity limits, measuring the worst-case load overshoot that occurs during the peak of an oscillation. Axiom 2 (Loss Avoidance). An MPCC protocol is said to be -loss-avoiding if, in its dynamic equilibrium, the load L,(t) on any path 7 never exceeds its capacity C/P by more than a fraction X. The loss avoidance rating is therefore the maximum fractional overshoot observed across all paths during the equilibrium cycle: A= _max {0 t>to,7Ell Lower values of X > 0 are more desirable, with X = 0 indicating a perfectly lossless protocol. A protocol with poor convergence exhibits high-amplitude swings in traffic, leading to high performance volatility for the end-user. Axiom 3 (Convergence). An MPCC protocol is said to be Yconv-convergent if, in its dynamic equilibrium, the ratio of the minimum sustained load to the maximum peak load across all paths is given by Ycony. The Fairness axiom evaluates the equity of bandwidth allocation among competing agents, which is reflected in the distribution of their congestion window sizes at equilibrium. Simple metrics such as the ratio of minimum to maximum window size are ill-suited to a path-aware system where recent migrants naturally have small windows; we therefore use variance as a more robust statistical measure of distribution equality. Axiom 4 (Fairness). An MPCC protocol is said to be n-fair if, in the dynamic equilibrium, the variance of the congestion window sizes across the entire population of agents is equal to n. THEORETICAL INSIGHTS AND TRADE-OFFS Our axiomatic analysis of the system’s equilibria yields its first major theoretical insight, which challenges a com- mon assumption in network protocol design. We formally establish that there exists no fundamental trade-off be- tween Efficiency (c), Loss Avoidance (A), and Convergence (Yeonv). These three axioms, which collectively define a state of predictable, high-performance network operation, can be simultaneously optimized by a principled choice of protocol parameters. This optimum is achieved when the system is tuned to operate in a specific, critically-stable lossless equilib- rium where the peak of the traffic oscillation, LO, precisely matches the available path capacity, C,. In this state, the protocol is perfectly lossless (A = 0) by definition, while the oscillation’s minimal amplitude ensures both a high floor on utilization (maximizing ¢€) and a high ratio of minimum-to- maximum load (maximizing 7cony). Our analysis demonstrates that this optimal state is attainable through the joint tuning of a hard reset policy (i.e., a reset softness o — 0) and a carefully calibrated agent responsiveness (p). --- PAGE BREAK --- JOURNAL OF I4TgX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020 This co-optimization, however, exposes a more fundamental and unavoidable trade-off that lies at the heart of path-aware protocol design: the inherent tension between predictable performance (Efficiency and Convergence) and the twin goals of Fairness and Responsiveness. Our analysis reveals that a protocol tuned for high responsiveness (p — 1) naturally achieves a high degree of fairness. The constant flux of agent migration forces frequent congestion window resets across the population, preventing significant long-term window dispari- ties and resulting in a compact distribution with low variance (7 — 0). Yet, this same mechanism is profoundly detrimental to performance, as the perpetual window resets lead to chronic link under-utilization (low €) and large-amplitude oscillations (low conv). Conversely, a protocol with low responsiveness (p — 0) is highly efficient and stable, as ”sticky” agents can maintain large windows that saturate link capacity. This performance comes at the direct cost of fairness, as it creates a highly bimodal distribution of window sizes between long- tenured agents and the few recent migrants, yielding a large variance (7). Responsiveness (p) is therefore the primary axis along which a protocol designer must navigate this core dilemma. Beyond these internal trade-offs, our framework allows us to address a more fundamental question: what is the net perfor- mance impact of enabling end-host path selection compared to a static network with an optimal, fixed allocation of agents to paths? Our analysis reveals a nuanced answer, demonstrating that dynamic path selection can be both detrimental and, counter-intuitively, highly beneficial. A. Static Baseline for Comparison To quantify these effects, we first define the axiomatic rat- ings for our baseline: a static network without path selection, where N agents are optimally distributed, with a, = N/P agents on each path. This plot shows the minimum sustained efficiency (€) in a lossy regime as a function of responsiveness (p). The data confirms that as migration compounds the effect of a loss, efficiency degrades significantly, validating the “peril” of path selection in this state. These baseline ratings provide the formal ”ground truth” against which we compare the performance of our dynamic MPCC protocols. B. Performance Impact of Dynamic Selection The primary peril occurs in inefficient, lossy equilibria, where the out-migration of agents following a loss event compounds the window reduction, deepening the trough in utilization and degrading efficiency below that of the static baseline, as validated in Figure 8. However, our most striking finding is that path selection can offer a profound benefit by de-synchronizing agent behavior. In a static system, co- located agents tend to act in lockstep, creating highly corre- lated window increases that result in severe, periodic load over- shoots. Agent migration fundamentally disrupts this phase- locking. By constantly remixing the population on each path, it averages out the agents’ continuity times (7), thereby smooth- ing the aggregate traffic growth. This de-synchronization can dramatically dampen peak loads, leading to significantly better loss avoidance and stability than the more brittle, synchronized static system. C. Design Implications Taken together, these insights provide a formal design map for engineering next-generation, path-aware transport protocols. Our work suggests that designers should not view efficiency, stability, and loss avoidance as mutually exclu- sive goals to be compromised; instead, an optimal, lossless operating point exists and should be the target of a well- tuned protocol. The primary and unavoidable design choice, therefore, is not whether to achieve high performance, but how to position a protocol along the fundamental trade-off axis between that performance and the goals of fairness and responsiveness. The optimal setting for the responsiveness parameter, p, is thus context-dependent: a data center fabric might favor a low-p protocol to maximize stable throughput, whereas a mobile device could benefit from a high p to rapidly abandon failing links. Finally, our de-synchronization finding offers a new design principle: a controlled, non-zero level of agent migration can be viewed as a valuable tool for enhancing network stability and burst tolerance, reframing responsiveness from a purely end-user feature to a mechanism for improving collective network health. --- PAGE BREAK --- JOURNAL OF I4TgX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020 VIII. EVALUATION To validate our theoretical framework and demonstrate the accuracy of its predictions, we conduct a series of discrete- event simulations. The primary objective of this evaluation is to establish the fidelity of our central modeling abstrac- tion: the approximation of the full stochastic system by its deterministic expected dynamics. Verifying a close match between the behavior of the stochastic simulations and the predictions of our analytical model provides strong empirical support for the theoretical insights derived in the preceding section. To this end, we developed a custom simulator that faithfully implements the probabilistic agent migration and window evolution processes defined in Equation (3). Our core methodology is to run a set of stochastic simulations for a given configuration of network parameters (NV, P) and protocol parameters (p, 0,7, a(7)) and to compare the average trajectory of the simulated path loads and agent counts against the single trajectory predicted by our analytical model of the expected dynamics (Equation (8)). Figure 10 Replication: Simulated (gray) vs. Expected (color) MPCC Dynamics Fig. 9: Validation of the expected dynamics model. The colored lines show the deterministic prediction from our analytical model for path loads, while the faint gray lines show trajectories from individual stochastic simulations. The close correspondence of the analytical prediction with the mean of the stochastic runs validates our model’s fidelity. First, our simulations robustly confirm the high fidelity of our analytical model. Across a wide range of parame- terizations, the averaged trajectories of the stochastic simu- lations show a tight correspondence with the deterministic predictions of the expected dynamics model, as exemplified in Figure 9. With this validation established, we use our framework to quantitatively map the core performance trade- offs. Figure 10 plots the key axiomatic ratings as a function of agent responsiveness (p) for a scaled-up network of N = 500 agents. The results provide a vivid illustration of our theo- retical findings: both Efficiency (€) and Convergence (7cony) are monotonically decreasing functions of responsiveness. As agents migrate more frequently, the perpetual cycle of window resets suppresses overall throughput, leading to lower mean utilization and higher-amplitude oscillations. In stark contrast, the Fairness (7) rating improves with higher responsiveness, as the frequent migrations prevent large window disparities from emerging and drive the population-wide variance towards zero. The opposing trajectories of these ratings provide a clear, empirical confirmation of the fundamental design dilemma at the heart of path-aware protocols. Figure 9 Replication: Effects on Convergence and Fairness (2) change is 1m (migration probability) ‘m (migration probability) Fig. 10: Quantitative illustration of the core performance trade- off. Axiomatic ratings for (a) Efficiency, €, and (b) Fairness, 77, are plotted as a function of Responsiveness, p. The opposing slopes of the curves provide a clear visualization of the fundamental tension between these goals. Finally, our evaluation provides direct, quantitative evidence for the multifaceted impact of path selection when compared to an idealized static network. To specifically test our de- synchronization hypothesis from Section 8, we simulated a system where agents employ a CC algorithm with a bursty, slow-start-style increase function, a scenario prone to high traffic volatility. The results, shown in Figure 11, are striking. Introducing even a modest level of agent responsiveness (p > 0) dramatically improves the Loss Avoidance (A) and Con- vergence (7cony) ratings over the static baseline. This provides powerful empirical validation that agent migration acts as a natural shock absorber; by constantly remixing the distribution of agent continuity times, it smooths the aggregate traffic profile and prevents the large, synchronized overshoots that plague the more brittle static system. We find this stabilizing effect to be highly robust, persisting even when we introduce heterogeneity into the path capacities. While our model is necessarily a simplification, its core pre- dictions show a strong qualitative alignment with recent empir- ical measurements of deployed path-aware infrastructures. For example, performance studies in production SCION networks have observed that dynamic, performance-driven path selection can, in certain cases, induce significant traffic volatility on inter-domain links, particularly when multiple sources react to the same network event [22]. This finding provides a real- world analogue to the synchronized, over-reactive “herding” behavior that drives the oscillations in our model. Furthermore, the operational challenges reported in such studies reflect the essential trade-off between Responsiveness and Stability that our axiomatic framework formally derives. The practical need to balance the agility afforded by path selection against the imperative for predictable network performance confirms that our model, despite its abstractions, captures the first-order forces that govern these next-generation systems. IX. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS The theoretical insights and empirical validations presented in this paper carry significant implications for the future design --- PAGE BREAK --- JOURNAL OF I4TgX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020 Figure 8(b) Replication: Change in Loss Level im Lossless, a Lossy, a3 Em Lossless, as Lossy, as 120 200 60 ‘A (Change in Loss Rate) 20 m (migration probability) Fig. 11: The de-synchronization benefit of path selection. The plot shows the change in the Loss Avoidance rating (AA) when enabling path selection, compared to a static baseline. Negative values represent an improvement. For bursty traffic, path selection significantly reduces loss. and deployment of path-aware network protocols. Our central contribution is the formalization of the performance trade-offs governed by agent responsiveness, which suggests that param- eters like p (Responsiveness) and o (Reset Softness) should be elevated from latent implementation artifacts to first-class, explicit design parameters for any multi-path protocol. This points toward a future of tunable transport systems, where net- work operators or even applications can select a performance profile—for instance, prioritizing maximum stable throughput for data center workloads versus agile responsiveness for mobile clients—based on a clear, quantitative understanding of the consequences. Such a move aligns with the broader community’s push toward application-aware and policy-driven networking, where the monolithic, one-size-fits-all model of transport is superseded by more adaptable, context-specific solutions [23]. Our axiomatic framework provides the foun- dational science to inform these design choices, replacing ad- hoc heuristics with a principled methodology for navigating the complex performance landscape of path-aware systems. While our model provides a foundational understanding, its abstractions also define clear boundaries and motivate several rich avenues for future work. A primary direction is to extend our analysis to more complex and realistic network topologies, relaxing our assumptions to include heterogeneous paths with varying capacities and latencies, as well as scenarios with shared, non-disjoint bottlenecks. Another critical extension is the investigation of non-loss-based congestion control. Ap- plying our axiomatic framework to path-aware systems using modern latency-based protocols like Copa [24] or model- based protocols like BBR [20] is an important next step, as their fundamentally different feedback mechanisms may lead to entirely new stability dynamics. Finally, our assump- tion of simple greedy agents could be relaxed by exploring more sophisticated, learning-based path selection strategies. Investigating how a population of agents using reinforcement learning [15] would navigate the performance trade-offs we have formalized is a particularly compelling direction; indeed, our axiomatic ratings could serve as a multi-objective reward function to guide such agents, directly bridging fundamental theory with data-driven protocol design. Looking forward, we believe two research thrusts are partic- ularly promising. The first is to bridge our theoretical frame- work with direct empirical validation. Implementing a tunable MPCC protocol, with explicit controls for responsiveness and reset softness, and deploying it on a production-capable, path-aware testbed like SCION [1] is a crucial next step. Such an experiment would enable the real-world measurement of the performance trade-offs we have analytically derived, paving the way for context-aware transport services. The second thrust is to explore hybrid path selection strategies that aim to mitigate the fundamental trade-off through limited coordination. Our work characterizes the behavior of fully decentralized agents; introducing a small amount of explicit network signaling or information sharing could allow a system to dynamically modulate agent responsiveness to achieve both high performance and high agility [25]. Designing such minimally coordinated, *best of both worlds” systems is a significant and exciting challenge for the future of path-aware networking. X. CONCLUSION In this work, we addressed the critical stability challenge presented by the widespread adoption of end-host-driven path selection in next-generation network architectures. Motivated by a gap in the quantitative understanding of path-selection- induced oscillations, we developed and applied an axiomatic framework for joint path selection and congestion control. By modeling the system’s expected dynamics, we were able to an- alytically characterize the properties of the resulting dynamic equilibria. Our analysis culminates in the formal derivation of a fundamental trade-off, proving that a protocol’s fairness and responsiveness are intrinsically at odds with its ability to deliver efficient and stable performance. Our framework further reveals that efficiency, stability, and loss avoidance are not in conflict, and that agent migration itself can serve as a powerful de-synchronizing mechanism to improve, rather than degrade, network predictability. Ultimately, the contribution of this work is a shift from a qualitative intuition to a quantitative science for the design of path-aware protocols. By providing a formal language and an analytical framework to reason about these complex, dynamic systems, we have replaced ambiguous notions of instability” with a precise, multi-dimensional map of the core performance trade-offs. The impact of this formalization is both direct and practical: it equips protocol designers and network operators with the principled tools needed to engineer next-generation systems that are not only flexible and powerful, but also robustly stable and performant. As the Internet continues its evolution toward a more user-centric and programmable --- PAGE BREAK --- JOURNAL OF I4TgX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020 architecture, this foundational understanding of how to balance the freedom of decentralized path selection with the imperative for collective stability will be essential. 20. 21 22) REFERENCES D.
