The color gradient indicates cumulative damage amplification ratio, from low (blue, 1.5) to high (red, 2.5). The scatter plot reveals a fundamental trade-off: configurations achieving high mean trust (right side, 0.85-0.95) generally exhibit higher variability (upper-right quadrant), while configurations with low variability (lower region, SD < 0.05) typically have lower mean trust. The optimal region (marked in yellow) identifies configurations simultaneously achieving high stability (mean > 0.90) and low variability (SD < 0.08), representing approximately 5% of all configurations. These optimal configurations cluster with moderate cumulative amplification (orange colors, 1.7-2.0 range), validating that extreme parameter settings sacrifice either stability or predictability. The negative correlation between mean trust and cumulative amplification (r = -0.45) indicates that configurations creating strong damage accumulation effects inherently limit achievable trust levels. This stability analysis complements the Pareto frontier analysis (Figure 11) by revealing that optimal trust dynamics require balancing multiple competing objectives: negativity bias strength, hysteresis recovery potential, and stability- variability trade-offs. 35 --- PAGE BREAK --- Existence of optimal parameterizations: The Pareto frontier analysis identifies 375 configura- tions that simultaneously optimize multiple behavioral objectives, with the top-ranked configurations achieving perfect alignment with empirical negativity targets while maintaining balanced hysteresis and recovery properties. Practical implications for parameterization: For requirements engineering applications where precise parameter estimation is difficult, practitioners can select configurations from the Pareto- optimal set with confidence that key behavioral properties will emerge correctly. The robustness across 78,125 configurations provides assurance that qualitative trust dynamics are not critically sensitive to exact parameter values. This experimental validation provides comprehensive evidence that the computational trust model produces behaviorally plausible dynamics across diverse parameter configurations, establishing a solid foundation for the empirical case study validation presented in the following section. 9 Empirical Validation: The Renault-Nissan Alliance This section presents systematic empirical validation of the trust dynamics framework through detailed analysis of the Renault-Nissan Alliance (1999-present), one of the most significant and well-documented strategic partnerships in automotive history [18,24]. Following the dual-track validation methodology established in our foundational work [34], which achieved 45/60 validation score on the Samsung-Sony S-LCD joint venture, we apply structured qualitative-to-quantitative translation to convert rich case documentation into model parameters, then assess whether simulated dynamics reproduce documented trust evolution patterns across 25 years of relationship history. 9.1 Validation Methodology: Qualitative-to-Quantitative Translation Our empirical validation approach differs fundamentally from traditional statistical parameter estimation. We do not perform regression or optimization to fit time-series data. Rather, we employ a structured translation framework that converts qualitative case study evidence into quantitative model parameters through organized assessment rubrics, then evaluates whether the resulting parameterization produces dynamics qualitatively matching observed patterns. This methodology is appropriate for several reasons. The integration of conceptual modeling (i* framework) with computational trust models creates a novel field of inquiry where precise numerical trust measurements from real organizations do not exist. Traditional statistical validation would require trust time-series data that is not available in requirements engineering contexts. Our objective is to demonstrate that the model captures the qualitative mechanisms driving real-world trust evolution—negativity bias, hysteresis, cumulative damage—rather than to predict quantitative values of unmeasurable latent variables. Strategic alliances like Renault-Nissan generate extensive qualitative documentation from business historians, journalists, and management scholars describing relationship phases, critical events, and trust dynamics. This rich evidence supports structured parameter elicitation even though precise numerical trust values are not reported. Mixed-methods research traditions in social science routinely employ structured qualitative-to-quantitative translation through coding rubrics, ordinal scales, and consensus assessment panels. Our approach extends these established methodologies to computational model validation. 9.2 Case Overview: The Renault-Nissan Alliance (1999-2025) The Renault-Nissan Alliance represents one of the most significant cross-border automotive partner- ships in history, spanning 25+ years across five distinct relationship phases [19,24]. The partnership 36 --- PAGE BREAK --- began in 1999 when Renault acquired 36.8% of Nissan’s equity for $5.4 billion and dispatched Carlos Ghosn to lead Nissan’s turnaround from near-bankruptcy [40,43]. The alliance achieved remarkable success through the 2000s and 2010s, with both companies maintaining operational autonomy while achieving substantial synergies in platform development, component purchasing, and technology sharing [19,43]. By 2017, the alliance became the world’s largest automotive group by combined sales volume, surpassing Toyota and Volkswagen [24, 43]. However, the partnership entered severe crisis in November 2018 when Ghosn was arrested in Tokyo on financial misconduct charges that were widely perceived as orchestrated by Nissan executives seeking to prevent deeper integration with Renault [24]. This crisis revealed deep-seated mistrust and triggered a period of strained cooperation from 2018-2023 [27]. Current phases (2023-present) involve tentative recovery efforts under new leadership seeking to restore partnership functionality while maintaining organizational independence [28]. This case provides ideal validation material because of its extended duration enabling testing of long-term trust dynamics, multiple distinct relationship phases testing the model’s ability to capture phase transitions, major trust violation and subsequent recovery efforts testing hysteresis mechanisms, rich documentation from business historians and journalists providing detailed evidence of trust evolution, and high stakes ensuring thorough documentation of critical events. 9.3 i* Strategic Dependency Model Figure 13 presents the i* Strategic Dependency diagram for the Renault-Nissan Alliance, visualizing the structural dependencies that ground our quantitative trust dynamics analysis [40,43]. This diagram represents the mature cooperation phase (2002-2018) dependency structure before the 2018 crisis, when the alliance achieved its highest levels of integration and mutual reliance [19, 45]. The i* model reveals the structural foundation underlying trust dynamics in the alliance. Nissan’s initial high dependency on Renault’s financial resources (crit = 0.9 in 1999-2002) created substantial vulnerability during the crisis period, as the existential threat from potential partner withdrawal amplified trust sensitivity. Renault’s critical dependency on maintaining Nissan’s operational autonomy (crit = 0.9) became the focal point of the 2018 crisis when perceived integration threats violated this essential softgoal, triggering severe trust erosion. Both partners’ dependencies on market access (Europe for Nissan, Asia for Renault) and platform sharing created moderate structural coupling that persisted across all relationship phases. The quantitative interdependence coefficients derived from this i* model feed directly into the trust dynamics simulation through the interdependence amplification factor €. The moderate value of € = 0.50 reflects that while dependencies matter, they do not dominate the relationship—both organizations maintained sufficient independence to survive partnership dissolution, unlike cases of complete integration where € might approach 0.80-0.90. 9.4 Parameterization Methodology We translate the i* Strategic Dependency model and qualitative case evidence into quantitative trust dynamics parameters following the structured elicitation framework established in Section 5 of our foundational work [34]. 9.4.1 Interdependence Coefficient Calculation For Nissan’s dependencies on Renault in Phase 1 (Formation, 1999-2002): 37 --- PAGE BREAK --- Financial Market. This phase exhibits gradual trust building as Renault demonstrated commitment to Nissan’s autonomy while providing essential financial and strategic support. Ghosn’s visible success in executing turnaround plans (returning Nissan to profitability by 2001) without imposing French management control built credibility. The i* diagram shows Nissan’s high dependency on Renault’s financial resources during this phase (crit = 0.9), creating vulnerability but also strong incentives for Renault to demonstrate trustworthiness. Phase 2: Mature Cooperation (2002-2018, 40 periods) Extended period of successful partnership characterized by platform sharing (CMF architecture used across 14 vehicle models), component standardization (powertrain sharing), purchasing synergies ($5B+ annual savings), and mutual respect for operational autonomy. Both partners consistently delivered on commitments, leading to high trust levels documented in industry analyses describing the alliance as "gold standard" and "model for cross-border partnerships." This phase represents the baseline of mature coopetitive partnership before crisis, with trust levels approaching asymptotic maximum and the i* dependencies functioning smoothly. Phase 3: Crisis Period (2018-2019, 4 periods) Abrupt trust collapse triggered by Ghosn’s arrest in November 2018 on allegations of financial misconduct including underreporting compensation and misuse of company funds. The arrest was widely perceived by analysts and French government officials as Nissan’s strategic move to prevent deeper integration proposed by Renault and French government. Whether allegations were valid or pretextual, the action created severe reputation damage by violating the critical autonomy softgoal visible in the i* diagram (crit = 0.9). Partnership cooperation plummeted as organizations prioritized defensive positions and legal battles over joint initiatives. Phase 4: Recovery Efforts (2019-2023, 15 periods) Post-crisis period of attempted relationship restoration through new leadership (Makoto Uchida at Nissan appointed 2019, Luca de Meo at Renault appointed 2020) and renewed cooperation agreements including the May 2023 restructuring reducing Renault’s Nissan stake from 43% to 15% to achieve "balanced partnership." Despite stated commitment to alliance continuation, trust recovery was severely constrained by lingering mistrust and organizational memory of crisis. This phase tests hysteresis and trust ceiling mechanisms, with the i* dependencies remaining structurally present but cooperation limited by low trust preventing realization of potential synergies. Phase 5: Current State (2023-present, 8 periods) Recent developments including restructured governance, new joint ventures in electric vehicles and autonomous driving technology, and gradual rebuilding of operational cooperation. Trust remains substantially below pre-crisis levels but shows continued gradual improvement. Industry analyses describe relationship as "functional but constrained" and "cooperation exists but strategic integration limited compared to 2010s peak," validating that trust ceiling from reputation damage continues constraining partnership depth. 41 --- PAGE BREAK --- 9.6 Simulation Execution and Results We instanti ate the trust dynamics model with the elicited parameters and simulate trust evolution over 80 time periods (approximately 25 years with quarterly granularity) across the five phases. When observed trust data are available, this dimension uses quantitative goodness-of-fit metrics including root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and coefficient of determination (R?). In the absence of observed trust measurements, as in the present case study, this dimension assesses whether trust trajectories remain within plausible bounds and exhibit qualitatively reasonable evolution patterns. 46 --- PAGE BREAK --- ‘Trust Ceiling Mechanism: Hysteresis and Incomplete Recovery ‘Trust / Ceiling Level 0 10 20 30 40 50 o 70 ‘Time Steps Figure 18: Trust ceiling mechanism visualization demonstrating hysteresis effects in trust evolution. The graph plots actual trust trajectory (solid blue line) against dynamic trust ceiling function (red dashed line) derived from accumulated reputation damage Ri through relationship Ceiling(t) = .0— 0.6 - Ri;. Pink shaded region shows constrained trust space where actual trust cannot penetrate due to reputation damage constraints. During Phases 1-2 (periods 0-51), minimal reputation damage allows trust ceiling to remain at maximum (1.0), enabling trust to reach high stable levels ( 0.95-1.0). Phase 3 crisis (periods 52-55) creates severe reputation damage, causing trust ceiling to plummet o 0.40. Critically, even as Phase 4-5 recovery efforts (periods 56-79) gradually reduce reputation damage through decay parameter dr = 0.02, the trust ceiling rises only to 0.70 after 25 periods of sustained cooperation. The actual trust trajectory tracks closely below the ceiling, demonstrating chat trust remains persistently constrained by violation history even after extended recovery efforts. This provides direct visual evidence that trust cannot fully recover to pre-violation levels, validating he hysteresis mechanism central to trust dynamics framework. The gap between current trust ceiling ( 0.70) and pre-crisis achieved trust ( 0.95-1.0) explains observed alliance behavior where structural dependencies from i* diagram remain present but cooperation depth is substantially reduced compared to pre-2018 integration. 47 --- PAGE BREAK --- e The Behavioral Prediction dimension (0-15 points) evaluates whether trust responds appropri- ately to cooperation and violation phases identified in the historical record. This dimension awards 3 points for each phase where trust changes directionally consistent with the cooperation signal: specifically, trust should increase during cooperative phases (where actions exceed baseline expectations) and decrease during violation phases (where actions fall below baseline expectations). e The Mechanism Validation dimension (0-15 points) tests for emergence of three theoretically critical properties: asymmetric trust evolution where erosion occurs at least 1.5 times faster than trust building (5 points), hysteresis effects where trust fails to recover to at least 90% of pre-violation levels following documented crisis-recovery sequences (5 points), and reputation damage accumulation where cumulative violations produce reputation damage exceeding 0.3 threshold (5 points). e The Outcome Correspondence dimension (0-15 points) assesses whether final trust states fall within reasonable ranges (0.2-0.8) reflecting partial but incomplete recovery (7 points for reasonable states, 4 points otherwise) and whether phase transitions are clearly visible in trust trajectories with changes exceeding 0.05 threshold at documented transition points (2 points per visible transition). Statistical significance testing supplements this scoring framework through one-way ANOVA com- paring trust levels across phases (testing whether phase means are significantly different) and linear regression within each phase (testing for significant positive or negative trends consistent with documented cooperation or violation patterns). The Renault-Nissan Alliance validation achieved 49 of 60 possible points (81.7%), with full scores in Behavioral Prediction and Mechanism Validation demonstrating robust emergence of asymmetric trust dynamics, reduced scores in Trust State Alignment reflecting absence of quantitative observed trust measurements for empirical fitting, and moderate scores in Outcome Correspondence indicating clear crisis dynamics but limited visibility of certain phase transitions within the model’s temporal resolution. Case evidence shows that even organizational changes (new CEOs at both companies), governance restructuring (reduced Renault ownership stake), and new joint ventures cannot overcome reputation damage accumulated from 2018 violation, consistent with cumulative mechanism predictions. Statistical evidence: One-way ANOVA comparing mean trust across phases yields F'(4,75) = 35.05, p < 0.0001, confirming that phase means are statistically significantly different. Post-hoc tests show Phase 3 significantly lower than all others (p < 0.001), and Phases 4-5 significantly lower than Phase 2 (p < 0.01), validating the persistence of crisis impact and incomplete recovery predicted by hysteresis mechanism. 50 --- PAGE BREAK --- 9.7.4 Outcome Correspondence (9/15 points) Criterion: Do long-term outcomes match documented alliance status and performance? Assessment: The simulation predicts trust level of 0.45 in current period (2025), suggesting substantially compromised relationship compared to pre-crisis peak. Documentation confirms the alliance continues with structural dependencies from i* diagram still present but with reduced integration depth, separate strategic directions for electrification, and persistent organizational tensions limiting cooperation scope. However, some joint initiatives (EV platforms, hydrogen projects, continued purchasing cooperation) suggest slightly more functional cooperation than 0.45 might indicate, though these may reflect contractual obligations and sunk costs rather than high trust. We award 9/15 points reflecting strong but not perfect correspondence. Evidence: Recent analyses describe the alliance as "functional but fragile," "cooperation exists but strategic integration is limited compared to 2010s," and "trust damage from 2018 crisis continues to constrain partnership depth despite structural rationale for deeper integration visible in complementary capabilities." Financial performance shows continued benefits from platform sharing and purchasing synergies (validating that i* resource dependencies still function) but new strategic initiatives proceed separately rather than jointly (validating trust constraints on deeper cooperation). The 2023 governance restructuring reducing Renault’s ownership stake demonstrates trust damage requiring formal structural changes to signal reduced integration threat to autonomy softgoal. 9.7.5 Total Validation Score Overall Score: 49/60 points (81.7%) This validation score demonstrates that the trust dynamics model successfully captures the qualitative mechanisms and phase structure of the Renault-Nissan Alliance evolution across 25 years. The integration with i* Strategic Dependency analysis strengthens validation by grounding parameter elicitation in documented structural relationships and explaining why trust constraints matter (dependencies exist but cannot be realized without trust). The score exceeds our foundational work’s Samsung-Sony validation (45/60, 75%), reflecting both methodological maturation and the availability of exceptionally rich documentation for this case enabling more confident parameter elicitation and validation assessment. 9.8 Interpretation and Limitations 9.8.1 Validation Interpretation The 81.7% validation score indicates strong explanatory power: the model reproduces documented trust patterns across multiple decades and successfully captures crisis-recovery dynamics through theorized mechanisms (negativity bias, hysteresis, cumulative damage). The integration with i* dependency analysis demonstrates that structural dependencies alone cannot explain alliance outcomes—trust dynamics mediate whether structural complementarities can be realized. This is not a claim of 81.7% predictive accuracy in a statistical sense—we are not predicting numerical trust values that were measured. Rather, we demonstrate that application of our structured translation framework (from i* conceptual model to quantitative parameters to dynamic simulation) produces parameterizations that generate dynamics qualitatively matching observed patterns across 81.7% of assessed validation dimensions. The high score on mechanism validation (perfect 15/15) is particularly significant because it demonstrates that the model’s theoretical mechanisms—asymmetric updating, trust ceilings from reputation damage, gradual healing—are not merely mathematical abstractions but correspond to 51 --- PAGE BREAK --- real dynamics observable in major strategic partnerships. The trust ceiling visualization provides compelling visual evidence that these mechanisms function as theorized. The i* diagram provides structural grounding explaining why trust matters: all those dependencies remain present in 2023- 2025, yet cooperation depth is substantially reduced compared to 2002-2018, validating that trust operates as a distinct mediating mechanism beyond structural interdependence. 9.8.2 Methodological Strengths Several aspects strengthen this validation beyond our foundational work’s approach: Conceptual model integration: The i* Strategic Dependency diagram provides transparent audit trail from qualitative case evidence to quantitative interdependence parameter (€ = 0.50) through explicit dependency criticality ratings. This parallels TR-1’s methodology and demonstrates research program consistency. Multi-phase structure: Testing across five distinct relationship phases spanning 25 years provides much richer validation than single-snapshot assessment. The model must correctly predict not just average trust levels but phase transitions, crisis dynamics, and recovery constraints. Crisis-recovery testing: The 2018 crisis and subsequent recovery period provide a natural experiment for testing hysteresis mechanisms. The model correctly predicts that even after 5-7 years of renewed cooperation, trust remains substantially below pre-crisis levels, matching industry analyses and financial performance data. Transparent parameterization: Each parameter value links directly to specific case evidence through documented rubric assessments and i* dependency calculations (Equations 1-3), enabling other researchers to critique or replicate the translation process. Consistency with experimental validation: The elicited negativity ratio (3.0) precisely matches the median from 78,125-configuration experimental validation, demonstrating consistency between bottom-up (experimental) and top-down (empirical) validation approaches. Dual mechanism validation: The case validates both trust dynamics mechanisms (negativity bias, hysteresis) and the interdependence amplification mechanism from our foundational work. The i* dependencies explain why violations matter more (high criticality softgoal violation triggered crisis) and why recovery is difficult (structural dependencies create continued vulnerability requiring high trust). Figure 20 provides final visualization of the end-state trust configuration. 9.8.3 Limitations and Caveats Important limitations must be acknowledged: Single case study: While Renault-Nissan provides exceptionally rich validation material (25 years, five phases, crisis-recovery dynamics, extensive documentation), it represents one data point. Generalizability requires validation across multiple cases spanning diverse industries (technology platforms, healthcare systems, infrastructure projects), partnership types (joint ventures, alliances, consortia), and cultural contexts (Western, Asian, cross-cultural). Different organizational and cultural contexts may exhibit different trust dynamics requiring parameter adjustments. Parameter elicitation uncertainty: The qualitative-to-quantitative translation through rubric assessment involves interpretive judgment despite structured methodology. While the i* diagram provides objective dependency structure, criticality ratings involve assessment of case evidence that different researchers might score slightly differently. Sensitivity analysis could assess robustness to elicitation uncertainty—for example, testing whether A+ € {0.08, 0.12] and A_ € [0.25, 0.35] produce qualitatively similar dynamics. 52 --- PAGE BREAK --- Final Trust Matrix: Renault-Nissan Alliance (2025) 1.0 0.510 Renault Trustor (Source) Trust Level Nissan 0.0 Renault Nissan Trustee (Target) Figure 20: Final trust matrix heatmap showing end-state bilateral trust levels after 80 simulation periods (approximately 25 years, current state through 2025). We validate model outputs (cooperation patterns, relationship status, phase transitions) but not all intermediate state variables. Future research with organizational partners could attempt to collect trust perception data to enable more direct validation. Explanatory not predictive: The model explains documented patterns but wasn’t used to predict outcomes before they occurred. True predictive validation would require parameterizing from early alliance phases (1999-2010) and testing predictions against later developments (2018 crisis, recovery dynamics) without knowledge of actual outcomes. This would provide stronger evidence for model’s forward-looking utility. Simplified action modeling: We represent cooperation through scalar action values derived from phase descriptions (platform sharing, joint investments, governance cooperation). Real coop- eration involves multi-dimensional behaviors collapsed into single metrics. The i* diagram shows multiple dependency types (resources, goals, softgoals) that may respond differently to trust changes, but our model treats cooperation somewhat monolithically. Cultural and institutional factors: The Renault-Nissan case involves cross-border partnership between French and Japanese firms with substantially different organizational cultures and governance systems. These factors likely influence trust dynamics (Japanese emphasis on long-term relationships, French government ownership stake in Renault creating political dimensions). Our current model reats these as implicit context but doesn’t explicitly formalize cultural or institutional variables. Missing stakeholders: The i* diagram focuses on dyadic Renault-Nissan relationship, but the actual alliance involves additional stakeholders (French government as Renault shareholder, Japanese government regulations, dealers, suppliers). Some dynamics (particularly the 2018 crisis involving Japanese prosecutors) reflect broader stakeholder influences beyond bilateral trust. Despite these limitations, the empirical validation demonstrates that the trust dynamics frame- work grounded in i* dependency analysis captures real-world patterns across extended time hori- zons and successfully models crisis-recovery dynamics through theoretically grounded mechanisms. Combined with experimental validation across 78,125 configurations (Section 8), this provides com- prehensive evidence for the model’s behavioral validity and practical applicability to requirements engineering contexts involving strategic coopetition. The integration with i* conceptual modeling demonstrates successful bridge between qualitative analysis and quantitative simulation, addressing a critical methodological gap in requirements engineering research. 10 Discussion: Implications for Requirements Engineering Practice This section discusses how computational trust dynamics, now comprehensively validated through experimental robustness testing (78,125 configurations) and empirical case study analysis (Renault- Nissan Alliance achieving 81.7% validation score), inform requirements engineering practice, multi- agent system design, and socio-technical system analysis. 10.1 Requirements Engineering Applications Stakeholder relationship management benefits from validated trust trajectory analysis. Requirements analysts can use trust models to assess relationship health over project lifecycles with confidence in the model’s behavioral foundations. The experimental validation establishes that trust evolution exhibits consistent patterns across diverse parameter configurations: median negativity ratio of 3:1 (trust erodes three times faster than it builds), hysteresis recovery around 1.09 (trust recovers to approximately 109% of pre-violation levels after extended cooperation, but this takes 35+ periods), 54 --- PAGE BREAK --- and cumulative amplification of 1.97 (repeated violations produce twice the damage of equivalent single incidents). These validated behavioral properties enable quantitative prediction of trust dynamics. The Renault-Nissan empirical validation demonstrates that these mechanisms manifest in real strategic partnerships. Trust took three years (12 quarterly periods) to build from moderate to high levels during alliance formation, collapsed within one year (4 periods) during the 2018 crisis, and required 5-7 years (20-28 periods) to partially recover to approximately 45% of pre- crisis levels. Requirements analysts can use these empirically validated timescales to set realistic expectations: building high trust typically requires years of consistent cooperation, violations can destroy relationships in weeks or months, and recovery timescales are measured in years with incomplete restoration. Information disclosure strategies depend critically on trust levels. Trust gates willingness to disclose sensitive requirements information. The validated framework enables analysts to predict how trust building affects information flow, informing elicitation strategies. The experimental validation confirms that trust building rate has mean 0.031 per period with low variance (standard deviation 0.007), meaning trust accumulates predictably under sustained cooperation. Early investment in trust building activities including demonstrating confidentiality, showing competence, and delivering quick wins accelerates disclosure of business-critical requirements later in projects. Violation impact assessment becomes quantifiable with validated parameters. When requirement breaches, information misuse, or commitment failures occur, the framework quantifies trust damage and recovery timelines. The experimental validation establishes that single-period erosion has mean 0.291 (approximately 29% trust loss) with standard deviation 0.104, while time to 50% recovery has median 8 periods with mean 9.17 + 3.70. These validated metrics inform stakeholder management strategies. The Renault-Nissan case provides sobering evidence: a major violation (Ghosn arrest in 2018) reduced trust from 95-100% to 15-20% and required 5+ years to partially recover to 40-45%. This informs contingency planning for trust recovery, recognizing realistic timescales measured in years rather than weeks. Contract and governance design benefits from understanding empirically validated hysteresis effects. The Renault-Nissan case demonstrates that even after seven years of recovery efforts (2018- 2025), the alliance operates at substantially reduced trust levels compared to pre-crisis cooperation. This validates that contractual mechanisms enabling trust recovery including dispute resolution, renegotiation protocols, and third-party mediation are valuable even if rarely invoked, because recovery is slow and incomplete without structured support. The framework can evaluate different governance structures’ effectiveness at preventing violations versus facilitating recovery, informing organizational design for multi-stakeholder projects. 10.2 Multi-Agent System Requirements Trust-gated cooperation protocols enable autonomous agents in coopetitive environments including supply chain networks, trading systems, and service composition platforms. Our formalization, validated across 78,125 configurations and demonstrated in real partnerships, provides specifications for agent trust models integrating behavioral evidence processing, reputation tracking, and trust- dependent cooperation strategies. Requirements engineers can specify trust thresholds for different cooperation intensities, enabling agents to modulate behavior based on partner reliability. The validated negativity ratio of 3:1 suggests agents should weight negative evidence approximately three times more heavily than positive evidence to achieve realistic trust dynamics. Reputation system requirements benefit from the distinction between immediate trust and reputation damage validated in both experimental testing and empirical case study. Systems should 55 --- PAGE BREAK --- rack both current behavior for immediate trust assessment and violation history for long-term reputation. The experimental validation finds reputation decay rate has mean 0.03 with low variance, suggesting reputation systems should retain historical data for extended periods (33+ periods at this decay rate) rather than treating past and present equivalently. The Renault-Nissan case confirms his: reputation damage from 2018 crisis remained salient in 2025 documentation (seven years later), validating that violation memory persists for extended durations. Robustness to strategic manipulation emerges from validated asymmetric dynamics. The com- prehensive experimental validation establishes that across all 78,125 configurations, trust erosion consistently dominates trust building, with minimum negativity ratio of 1.0 and median 3.0. Agents cannot quickly rebuild trust after violations across the entire parameter space, limiting incentives or hit-and-run strategies. This property, now empirically validated through the Renault-Nissan case where recovery takes 5-7 years even with sustained effort, informs security requirements for multi-agent systems by reducing vulnerability to agents that cooperate briefly to build trust before defecting. 10.3 Integration with Broader Coopetition Framework This validated trust dynamics work integrates with our foundational framework [34] addressing interdependence and complementarity. The complete framework, now with empirical validation at 81.7% for trust dynamics (exceeding the 75% baseline from foundational work’s Samsung-Sony case), enables analysis of coopetitive relationships along three dimensions: The structural dimension through interdependence captures outcome coupling via the inter- dependence matrix from i* dependencies. This creates vulnerability to trust erosion through dependency amplification. The experimental validation establishes dependency amplification fac- tor has mean 1.271 + 0.070, meaning high-dependency relationships experience approximately 27% greater trust sensitivity to violations than low-dependency relationships. This affects value appropriation bargaining power and relationship resilience. The economic dimension through complementarity provides cooperation incentives via synergistic value creation, validated in our foundational work. However, trust gates realization of complementarity benefits. The Renault-Nissan case demonstrates this: despite substantial complementarities in platforms, powertrains, and global market access, the trust collapse in 2018 prevented realization of integration synergies for 5+ years. Low trust prevents actors from investing in partnerships even when synergies are objectively large, a mechanism now empirically validated. The behavioral dimension through trust evolution creates path dependence and feedback loops. Initial trust states and violation history fundamentally shape long-run equilibria, sometimes more than structural dependencies or economic complementarities. The experimental validation across 78,125 configurations establishes that trust ceiling mechanism consistently constrains recovery (hysteresis recovery metric mean 1.089 + 0.070), while the Renault-Nissan case provides concrete evidence: pre-crisis trust of 95-100% became constrained to 40-45% ceiling post-crisis despite strong complementarities and dependencies. Integrating these dimensions reveals emergent phenomena validated through both experimental and empirical methods. High structural interdependence creates trust vulnerability, amplifying damage from violations (validated experimentally with 1.27x mean amplification and empirically in Renault-Nissan where deep operational integration magnified crisis impact). Strong complementarity creates cooperation incentives, but only if trust is sufficient to overcome competitive pressures (validated empirically: Renault-Nissan had strong complementarities but couldn’t realize them during low-trust crisis period). Trust hysteresis means that structural changes including reducing dependencies or economic changes including increasing complementarities may not restore cooperation 56 --- PAGE BREAK --- if trust has eroded (validated empirically: new joint ventures in 2023-2025 achieved limited success because trust remained at 40-45% rather than recovering to pre-crisis 95-100%). Requirements engineers analyzing coopetitive systems should consider all three dimensions rather than treating them independently, guided by validated behavioral parameters and empirically confirmed mechanisms. A relationship with strong complementarity and weak dependencies might exhibit low cooperation if trust is damaged (Renault-Nissan case evidence). Conversely, weak complementarity might sustain cooperation if trust is high and reputation is pristine (validated experimentally through stability analysis showing configurations with high trust achieve cooperation despite modest synergies). 10.4 Methodological Contribution: Bridging Conceptual and Computational Modeling This research program makes a significant methodological contribution by establishing a defensible validation framework for computational models derived from conceptual modeling languages. The dual-track validation approach—experimental robustness testing across massive parameter spaces combined with structured qualitative-to-quantitative translation for empirical case studies—provides a template for bridging theory and practice in requirements engineering. The experimental validation demonstrates that key trust phenomena are robust emergent proper- ties rather than artifacts of specific parameterizations: across 78,125 configurations, negativity bias (range 1.0-9.0, median 3.0), hysteresis (range 0.79-1.17, median 1.11), and cumulative amplification (range 1.51-2.50, median 1.97) emerge consistently. This robustness provides confidence that the model captures genuine behavioral regularities. The empirical validation demonstrates that structured qualitative-to-quantitative translation through rubric-based parameter elicitation produces model parameterizations that generate dynamics matching real-world patterns. The Renault-Nissan case achieves 49/60 (81.7%) validation score, exceeding our foundational work’s baseline of 45/60 (75%) for Samsung-Sony, demonstrating both methodological consistency and improvement. This validation approach is appropriate for novel re- search domains where precise numerical measurements don’t exist but rich qualitative documentation does—a common situation in requirements engineering practice. Together, these validation tracks provide comprehensive evidence that computational trust models grounded in i* conceptual models and game-theoretic foundations can explain and analyze real-world strategic partnerships in requirements-intensive contexts. 10.5 Limitations and Future Work Our formalization has limitations that future research should address, now informed by validation findings. Deterministic dynamics assume trust evolution is deterministic given actions. Real trust formation involves uncertainty, misperception, and stochastic shocks. The experimental validation tested deterministic scenarios; incorporating stochastic noise in cooperation signals or trust updating would increase realism. The Renault-Nissan case suggests some randomness in violation timing (Ghosn arrest timing appeared strategic but exact timing was uncertain), supporting future stochastic extensions. Symmetric observation assumes actors perfectly observe partners’ actions. Requirements engi- neering contexts often involve information asymmetry where stakeholders have private information about their cooperation levels. The Renault-Nissan case reveals information asymmetries: Nissan executives’ perceptions of Renault’s integration intentions may have differed from Renault’s actual 57 --- PAGE BREAK --- intentions, contributing to crisis. Extending to partial observability through Hidden Markov Models or Partially Observable Stochastic Games would capture this reality. Homogeneous trust psychology applies identical trust updating rules to all actors. Real organiza- tions exhibit heterogeneity in trust responsiveness, negativity bias, and memory. The experimental validation used uniform parameters across actors; allowing actor-specific parameters would capture heterogeneity documented in organizational behavior research. Single trust facet models trust as unidimensional. Behavioral trust research distinguishes competence trust (belief in ability) from benevolence trust (belief in intent) [23]. The Renault-Nissan case suggests this distinction matters: even after crisis, both parties acknowledged each other’s technical competence while questioning benevolent intentions. Multi-faceted trust models would capture such scenarios. Limited empirical validation to single case study. While Renault-Nissan provides exceptionally rich validation material (25 years, five phases, crisis-recovery dynamics), generalizability requires validation across multiple cases. Future work should validate against additional strategic partnerships spanning diverse industries (technology platforms, healthcare systems, infrastructure projects), partnership types (joint ventures, alliances, consortia), and cultural contexts (Western, Asian, cross-cultural). Computational scalability becomes challenging for large actor networks. Value function iteration scales poorly to dozens of actors. The experimental validation tested dyadic relationships; for large networks including platform ecosystems with dozens of partners, approximation methods including reinforcement learning and simulation-based optimization may be necessary. Parameter sensitivity to elicitation uncertainty has not been systematically explored. While the experimental validation demonstrates robustness across parameter ranges, sensitivity to qualitative- to-quantitative translation uncertainty in empirical validation deserves attention. Future work could conduct multi-coder reliability studies and assess how parameter elicitation variations affect validation scores. Despite these limitations, the current framework provides substantial advances over existing approaches by integrating conceptual modeling, computational trust, and game-theoretic equilibrium analysis in a unified formalization validated through both experimental robustness testing (78,125 configurations) and empirical case study analysis (81.7% validation score). This comprehensive validation establishes confidence in the model’s behavioral plausibility and practical applicability to requirements engineering contexts involving strategic coopetition. 11 Conclusion This technical report developed computational foundations for trust dynamics in strategic coopetition, extending our foundational framework [34] with formal mechanisms for trust evolution based on behavioral evidence. Building on conceptual insights from [33] identifying trustworthiness as a critical dimension of coopetitive relationships, we provided definitive mathematical specifications and comprehensive validation of trust dynamics integrating with requirements engineering contexts. Our contributions include a layered trust model with immediate trust and reputation damage capturing dual-process cognition; asymmetric evolution dynamics reproducing negativity bias with validated three-to-one median erosion-to-building ratio (mean 3.47 + 1.93) robust across 78,125 parameter configurations; trust ceiling mechanisms formalizing hysteresis and incomplete recovery with validated hysteresis recovery of 1.09 + 0.07; integration with structural dependencies through interdependence amplification factor 1.27 + 0.07; trust-gated reciprocity coupling trust to strategic behavior; structured translation methodology from i* models to computational trust validated 58 --- PAGE BREAK --- hrough structured parameter elicitation rubrics; Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium extension for dynamic games with evolving trust; comprehensive experimental validation establishing robustness through 78,125-configuration parameter sweep with distributional analysis, sensitivity testing, and Pareto frontier identification; and empirical validation through Renault-Nissan Alliance case study (1999- 2025) achieving 49/60 validation score (81.7%), successfully reproducing documented trust evolution across five distinct relationship phases including formation, mature cooperation, crisis, and recovery periods. The dual-track validation provides comprehensive evidence for model validity. Experimentally, he framework demonstrates robust emergence of key trust phenomena—negativity bias (median ratio 3.0, range 1.0-9.0), hysteresis (median recovery 1.11, range 0.79-1.17), cumulative damage amplification (median 1.97, range 1.51-2.50), and dependency effects (mean 1.27x)—across the entire tested parameter space. These are not artifacts of specific parameterizations but inherent properties of the two-layer trust-reputation architecture. Empirically, the Renault-Nissan validation demonstrates that structured qualitative-to-quantitative translation produces parameterizations generating dynamics matching 25 years of documented partnership evolution, including gradual rust building (3 years to reach high levels), rapid erosion during crisis (one year to collapse), and constrained recovery (5-7 years to reach 45% of pre-crisis levels). The 81.7% validation score exceeds our foundational work’s baseline (Samsung-Sony 75%), demonstrating both methodological consistency and improvement. The framework enables requirements engineers to quantify trust trajectories over project timelines using validated parameters (building rate 0.031 + 0.007 per period, erosion 0.291 + 0.104 per violation); assess violation impact and recovery feasibility with empirically grounded timescales (median recovery time 8 periods, mean 9.17 + 3.70); design trust-building protocols grounded in validated dynamics including 3:1 negativity bias and cumulative amplification effects; integrate trust with dependency analysis through validated amplification factor 1.27x for high-dependency relationships; and specify trust requirements for multi-agent systems using behaviorally validated trust updating mechanisms and reputation tracking with slow decay (mean rate 0.03). By maintaining semantic richness of conceptual modeling while enabling quantitative analysis grounded in comprehensive validation, the framework bridges theory and practice in requirements- intensive coopetitive contexts. The dual-track validation methodology—combining massive-scale experimental robustness testing with structured qualitative-to-quantitative translation for empirical case studies—provides a template for validating computational models derived from conceptual modeling languages, addressing a critical methodological gap in requirements engineering research. This work contributes to a coordinated research program addressing five dimensions of coope- tition identified by Pant [33]. The foundational technical report [34] addressed interdependence and complementarity, achieving 45/60 (75%) empirical validation on Samsung-Sony S-LCD. This report addressed trust dynamics, achieving 49/60 (81.7%) empirical validation on Renault-Nissan Alliance while establishing experimental robustness across 78,125 configurations. Complementary research examines team production with loyalty mechanisms and reciprocity protocols for sequential cooperation, available as companion technical reports. The complete research program provides comprehensive computational foundations for analyzing and designing coopetitive socio-technical systems in requirements engineering and multi-agent contexts. Future research directions include incorporating stochastic elements and partial observability to capture uncertainty and information asymmetry documented in real partnerships; allowing heterogeneous trust psychology across actors to reflect documented differences in trust responsiveness; developing multi-faceted trust distinguishing competence and benevolence validated through cases like Renault-Nissan where these dimensions diverged; validating against additional longitudinal organizational cases spanning diverse industries, partnership types, and cultural contexts to establish 59 --- PAGE BREAK --- generalizability beyond current single-case empirical validation; conducting multi-coder reliability studies to assess parameter elicitation uncertainty and robustness of qualitative-to-quantitative translation; and scaling computational methods to larger networks using approximation techniques including reinforcement learning and simulation-based optimization. established in this technical report provides a solid foundation for these extensions, with empirical validation at 81.7% and experimental validation across 78,125 configurations demonstrating behavioral plausibility and parameter robustness sufficient to support both theoretical advancement and practical application in requirements engineering practice. competition, cooperation and incentives. 2510.24906v1 [cs.GT] 28 Oct 2025 arXiv 1 We consider a model in which a group of players seeks to split a fixed number of indivisi Fair Indivisible Payoffs through Shapley Value Mikotaj Czarnecki!, Michat Korniak!*, Oskar Skibski!, and Piotr Skowron! lUniversity of Warsaw, Banacha 2, 02-097 Warszawa, Poland °ETH Ziirich, Ramistrasse 101, 8092 Ziirich, Switzerland mc448206 @students.mimuw. edu. pl, [EMAIL_REDACTED], {oskar.skibski, p.skowron} @mimuw.edu.pl October 30, 2025 Abstract We consider the problem of payoff division in indivisible coalitional games, where the value of the grand coalition is a natural number. This number represents a certain quantity of indivisible objects, such as parliamentary seats, kidney exchanges, or top features contributing to the outcome of a machine learning model. The goal of this paper is to propose a fair method for dividing these objects among players. To achieve this, we define the indivisible Shapley value and study its properties. We demonstrate our proposed technique using three case studies, in particular, we use it to identify key regions of an image in the context of an image classification task. Introduction le objects among themselves. For each subgroup of players, hereinafter called a coalition, the exact or estimated number of objects they are entitled to is known. The goal of this paper is to develop a method for identifying a fair division while accounting for dependencies between players. Our setting models various scenarios. E.g., in kidney exchange programs [2] [10], hospi can be considered as players, with coalitions’ values representing the number of kidney exchanges they can perform through collaboration. The outcome of our algorithms can be interpreted as a recommended distribution of donors across different hospitals for a single round of the allocation process. Similarly, our algorithms can be used as apportionment methods for elections, where voters are allowed to approve multiple political parties [7] [5]. In this context, a coalition’s value would represent the number of seats it is entitled to, calculated as the percentage of votes cast on any subset of parties from the group, multiplied by the total number of seats. Our algorithms then determine a seat distribution among parties that can be considered fair both for voters, and the participating parties. outcome 0 for Yet another application involves selecting the most important features contributing to the f a machine learning model [17]. Depending on the app. We frame our problem as a coalitional game where the value of the coalition of all players i: can assess the contribution of each feature to the final ey regions that represent the distribution of importance sa ication, the values of individual coalitions may or may not be integral. To achieve a fair division, we introduce the indivisible Shapley value— an extension --- PAGE BREAK --- of the classic Shapley value that returns a vector of integer payoffs. Our method accounts for dependencies between players, and so prevents the overrepresentation of players that share common resources. To illustrate the idea of fairness, consider an apportionment scenario with three right-wing parties, A, B, and C, and two left-wing parties, D and E. Suppose there are three committee seats to distribute. The three right-wing parties are approved by 66% of voters and thus entitled to two out of three seats, while the two left-wing parties are approved by 33% of voters and entitled to one seat. Clearly, each right-wing party is entitled to 2/3 of a seat, while D and E are entitled to half a seat, each. If seats were assigned by simply rounding up the largest shares, all three seats would go to the right-wing parties, leaving 33% of the electorate underrepresented. Our method, however, would allocate two seats randomly among the right-wing parties and one seat to a left-wing party, resulting in an arguably more balanced and representative outcome. In coalitional games, the concept of a justified payoff for all groups is captured by the core. We show that in convex indivisible games with integer coalition values—where it is known that the Shapley value lies in the core—the indivisible Shapley value also belongs to the core. However, we demonstrate that such guarantees do not extend to general fractional or non-convex games. In our work we chose to focus on a deterministic algorithm. It yields desirable outcomes in settings such as elections where transparency and predictability are desired. Likewise, in machine-learning context determinism guarantees reproducibility and consistency. Additionally, we consider a setting where objects have the same value but are non-identical. We develop an algorithm to find an allocation corresponding to the indivisible Shapley value. Finally, we demonstrate our approach using three case studies: applying it as an apportionment method in approval elections, selecting key regions in an image classification task, and as a tool for a fair division of seats among political parties forming a coalition. Related Work The fair allocation of indivisible goods has been studied extensively in the literature. Most previous works conceptualize fairness through envy-freeness [23] [28], emphasizing individual-level comparisons. In contrast, we study fairness within the framework of coalitional games, which focuses on relationships and stability among groups of agents rather than individuals. Coalitional games are often defined using integer representations, for example in weighted voting games , matching games [4], and allocation games [12]. These formulations frequently employ integer parameters such as weights or capacities. However, the players’ payoffs or marginal contributions are not restricted to integer values, and the resulting Shapley values are typically non-integral. Our work differs in that we focus on coalitional games where both the representation and the resulting payoffs are explicitly integer-valued. Indivisible coalitional games can be viewed as a subset of Non-Transferable Utility (NTU) games [25]. However, it remains unclear whether previously proposed solution concepts yield fair or meaningful outcomes when applied specifically to indivisible games with integer payoffs. In particular, the Shapley NTU value, as introduced by McLean [25], is undefined in this setting, since no value exists that satisfies the Unanimity axiom (i.e., equally dividing the payoff in a unanimity game). 2 Preliminaries A (coalitional) game is a pair (N,v) such that N is the set of n players and v : 2% > Risa function that assigns a real value to every coalition S C N with v(0) = 0. Efficiency: )0,-y pi(N,v)=v(N) for every game (N,v) Null-player: y;(N,v) = 0 for every game (N,v) and player i € N which is a null-player, ice., v(S U {i}) = v(S) for every S C N \ {i} Additivity: y;(N,v+v') = yi(N,v) + yi(N, v’) for every games (N,v), (N,v’) and i € N, where (vu + v')(S) = v(S) + v'(S) for every S C N Symmetry: y;(N,v) = y;(N,v) for every game (N,v) and players i,j € N such that v(S'U {i}) = v(S U {j}) for every S CN \ {i,j} Efficiency states that payoffs of all players sum up to v(N). Null-player implies that a null-player get zero payoff. Additivity means the sum of payoffs in two games is equal to the payoff in the game obtained by summing both games. Symmetry states symmetric players gets equal payoffs. Among many characterizations of the Shapley value, one of the most important was proposed by Harsanyi . The Harsanyi dividend of coalition S' in game (N,v) is the surplus created by a coalition S. It is defined as the value of the coalition decreased by surpluses of subcoalitions: A,(8) = (8) - > A(L) if |S] > 4, TCS with A,(S) = v(S) for |S'| = 1. The Shapley value focuses on the fairness of the division. In general, the core can be empty. However, it is known that the core is not empty if the game is convex. A game is convex if it holds u(S U {i}) — v(S) < o(TU {i}) — v(L) for every ie N,SCTCN\ {i}. Roughly speaking, game is convex if the marginal contribution of a player to a coalition increases (does not decrease) with the coalition size. If a game is convex, then the Shapley value belongs to the core. A subclass of convex games is formed by positive games. A game is positive if all its Harsanyi dividends are non-negative: A,(S) > 0 for all S CN. 3. Indivisible Coalitional Games In this paper, we focus on a new class of coalitional games, named indivisible (coalitional) games. In such games, coalition represents the number of indivisible identical items (e.g., seats in parliament, kidney transplants). Formally, an indivisible coalitional game is a coalitional game (N,v) with v(NV) € N. As we argued in the introduction, depending on the application, values of all coalitions may or may not be integers as well. In the former case, i.e., if v(S) € Z for every S C N, we will call such games integer indivisible games. In the later case, we will call such games fractional indivisible games. --- PAGE BREAK --- The value of an indivisible coalitional game is an indivisible payoff vector x € ZN that assigns each player an integer. The goal of this paper is to extend the Shapley value to indivisible coalitional games. From Shapley’s axioms, we cannot demand Symmetry and Additivity. This is clear by looking at game w;,2} in which two players jointly create a value of one, but only one of them can receive payoff 1. If we assume that player 1 receives this payoff, then Additivity would imply that in game 2u,1,2} player 1 will receive the payoff of 2, which is clearly undesirable. The following two properties captures the idea we want the value to be as closed to the Shapley value as possible. Specifically, the Lower Quota states that the payoff of a player is no less than the floor of its Shapley value and the Upper Quota—that the payoff is no greater than the ceiling. Lower Quota: ;(N,v) > |SV;i(N,v)]| for every game (N,v) and player i € N. Upper Quota: y;(N,v) < [SVj(N,v)] for every game (N,v) and player i € N. Note that the Lower Quota and the Upper Quota imply Null-player. We define indivisible core as the set of indivisible payoff vectors that belong to the core. We note that the indivisible core might be empty even if the standard core is not; in fact, it might be empty even for integer indivisible games. Example 1. (Hailf-game) Consider an integer indivisible game with N = {1,2,3,4} and v(S) = [|S|/2]. Note that v(N) = 2. Fix an arbitrary payoff vector x = [x1,...,24] € RY and take two players with the smallest payoffs: i,j € N. Since v({i, j}) = 1 we know that 2; +2; > 1. This is only possible if « = [0.5,0.5,0.5, 0.5]. Thus, the core consists of only this one payoff vector and the indivisible core is empty. 4 4 Indivisible Shapley Value for Convex Integer Games We begin our analysis from convex integer games. As we already mentioned, we know that the core of a convex game is non-empty and that the Shapley value belongs to it [30]. However, as evidence by Example [I] this does not imply that any indivisible payoff vector is in the core. In this section, we show that there exists an indivisible payoff vector that satisfies Lower Quota and Upper Quota and at the same time belongs to the core and we define a method that finds such a vector. 4.1 Games with Shapley Values from the Unit Interval Let us first focus on games in which Shapley values of all players belong to (0,1) interval. From Efficiency, this implies that coalition is lower than the number of players: v(N) <|N]. Hence, to satisfy both Lower and Upper Quota, we need to select a subset of players that will receive value 1 and give 0 to the remaining players. At first, it seems natural to select players with the highest Shapley values. However, as we now argue, this is not a desirable approach. Example 2. This is, however, unfair to players 4 and 5 who are responsible for one good: the payoff vector (1,1, 1,0,0) is not in the core, as t4 +25 < v({4,5}). 4 Let (N,v) be any integer indivisible game such that SV;(N,v) € (0,1) for every ie N. Consider now a payoff vector which belongs to the core of the reduced game. For every convex and size-bounded integer game (N,v) and player i € N, there exists a 0-1 payoff vector x € {0,1}% in the core such that x; = 1 if and only if v(N) — v(N \ {é}) > 1. Our analysis indicates the following scheme for distributing coalition in convex integer games. We select a player whose marginal contribution to the grand coalition equal at least 1. We assign 1 to the selected player and create a reduced game. Based on Theorem [4.1] we know that the resulting game will also be a convex, size-bounded integer indivisible game. Thus, we repeat this step iteratively until coalition becomes zero. It remains to specify the order in which we consider players. Among the players with a positive marginal contribution to the grand coalition, we will always choose the remaining player with the highest Shapley value in the original game. In this way, while in many games players with the largest remainders will receive the additional units, we ensure that the payoff vector is in the core. 4.2 General Convex Integer Games To apply our method to general convex integer indivisible games, we need to perform two additional steps. However, since the size of the game grows exponentially with respect to the number of players, this assumption is not realistic. In this section, we present an algorithm that simulate the behavior of the indivisible Shapley value: approximates the Shapley value and then operates in polynomial time to determine the final outcome. We utilize the notion of the Shapley value matrix (SVj;(N,v))i,jen [14]. In this matrix, the Shapley value of a player is decomposed into a vector (SVj1(N,v),...,SVin(N,v)), where each element represents the synergy between two players: the contribution of player j to the value of player i: Au(S) a) |S? SVi;(N,v) = Ss i,jESCN Clearly, SVi(N,v) = Sojcn SVij(N,v). To avoid exponential blow-up, we rely only on the Shapley values and the Shapley value matrix as sources of information about the game and the dependencies between players. Our procedure operates as follows. First, we approximate the Shapley values and the Shapley value matrix by sampling random permutations. Then, in a loop, we select the player with the highest Shapley value and add 1 to this player’s payoff. To account for this increase, we decrease the player’s Shapley value by 1. However, if the Shapley value is smaller than 1, we also reduce the Shapley values of other players who have synergy with this player. Specifically, if the Shapley value of player i equals yp; < 1, we decrease the Shapley values of other players by (1 — y;) in proportions corresponding to their values S'V;;(N,v). Algorithm [5] outlines our procedure. Note that all players will receive their lower quota before we select a player with the Shapley value smaller than 1. The subsequent steps mimic the behavior of the indivisible Shapley value: whenever a payoff of 1 is assigned to a player, its contribution to others is removed from the game. In our algorithm for large games, this contribution is subtracted from the Shapley values of others players. If such a path exists, we extend the matching. Otherwise, this player cannot obtain an additional object without violating the core. Algorithm [7] presents our method. The following theorem shows that it finds an allocation corresponding to the indivisible Shapley value. Theorem 7.1. Given a list of object owners S, Algorithm |7 [A finds an allocation of objects (X1,...,Xn) such that (|Xi|)ien ts the indivisible Shapley value of game (N,vgs) and runs in time O(|S|(|S| + |N|)?/? + |S|[N|(|S| + |N])). Our algorithm runs in polynomial time with respect to the number of objects, and also to the value of the grand coalition in the corresponding game, or, after minor adaptation, to the number of non-zero Harsanyi dividends (see Theorem |C.4] in the appendix for details). This demonstrates that it is possible to compute the indivisible Shapley value in polynomial time for positive games represented as a list of non-zero dividends. Such a representation is obtained, for example, from marginal contribution nets without negative weights or literals [16]. --- PAGE BREAK --- T T T ™@ Gluckstein m™ = Laguiller Actual || Le | tl el ™ Besancenot. m Hue ™ Taubira ™ Jospin ™ Chevéenement MM Mameéere wT Sint Lepage mt Bayrou ™ Saint-Josse m Boutin L n m n m Meégret m Le Pen 0 20 40 60 80 100 Share of mandates (%) Figure 1: Share of mandates computed by various apportionment rules for the 2002 French presidential elections experiment data. 8 Case Studies In this section, we discuss three applications of our method: its use as an apportionment approach in approval elections, its application for identifying key regions in image classification tasks, and its role in ensuring a fair distribution of seats among political parties forming a coalition. 8.1 Approval-Based Apportionment Consider the problem of distributing a fixed number of parliamentary seats among political parties, where each voter i indicates a subset A; of approved parties [7] [5]. As discussed in the introduction, this can be viewed as an indivisible coalitional game, with parties being players and the value of a coalition S defined as the fraction of voters i with A; C S, multiplied by the total number of seats. Clearly, Indivisible Shapley Value can be used to distribute the seats among the parties, thus inducing an apportionment method. Below, we illustrate its behavior based on the data from the 2002 French presidential elections [24]. There, we interpret each presidential candidate as a political party[]] We treat each voter’s top three preferences, indicated in the dataset, as an approval vote. We compare the distribution of 100 seats computed by the Indivisible Shapley Value with the actual election outcome and the outcome produced by Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) [3], a rule exhibiting particularly strong properties pertaining to proportionality. Figure [I] presents the results. While PAV is known to select candidates fairly from the voters’ perspective, it can produce solutions that are arguably unfair to political parties. For example, if all voters approve the same two parties, PAV may allocate all seats to one party, since such a solution gives each voter the same number of representatives as evenly splitting the seats between the two. Our simulations indicate that this is likely in practice—in Figure [I] we see that smaller and extreme parties are underrepresented by PAV. The Indivisible Shapley Value, on the other hand, provides a fairer allocation from the perspective of parties, assigning seats in a manner that more closely reflects the actual vote distribution. At the same time, by using approvals the voters can indicate their willingness for a compromise, and so ISV was able to transfer some seats from the far-right to more moderate parties, compared to the actual outcome (with each voter voting for a single candidate). Interestingly, in this instance, our method satisfies EJR+, a strong axiom of proportional representation 6], indicating that being fair towards parties does not come at the cost of proportionally representing the voters. That said, the experiments on other datasets indicate that this property in principle must not not always be satisfied. 1While using approval ballots for committee elections is already well-established in the literature (73), their application to apportionment is a recent idea. Since, no datasets directly related to approval-based apportionment are available, we use datasets from presidential elections, where, intuitively, each candidate can be seen as representing their own party. 10 --- PAGE BREAK --- Figure 2: On the left, our method with a = 0.5; in the middle, a continuous Shapley value heatmap overlay; and on the right, the baseline method which selects regions with the highest Shapley values. 8.2 Key Regions in Image Classification Next, we apply Algorithm [5] for identifying key regions in an image classification task. We begin with a step-by-step explanation of the procedure on a single example. We use the image classification model EfficientNet BO [32] and dataset MinilmageNet that is a downscaled subset of ISVLRC ImageNet-1k [27], while retaining all 1,000 labels. We consider the image presented in Figure [2] which is classified as belonging to the brown bear class. In the first step, we use the skimage.segmentation.slic function from the scikit-image library [33] to divide the image into 247 regions using K-means clustering in the Color-(x, y, z) space [I]. We use the compactness parameter of 20. In order to identify key regions, we treat each region as a player and groups of regions as coalitions. The value of a coalition is defined as the probability that the model correctly classifies the image when the other regions are replaced with the average of 50 randomly selected images from the dataset. We approximate the Shapley value matrix using Algorithm [6] with 50,000 samples and estimate the Shapley value by summing the rows in the estimated matrix. We then increase the values by a constant to eliminate negative Shapley values and scale them, to ensure that the value of the grand coalition equals the number of regions we aim to select: v(.NV) = 10 in our case. Similarly, we modify the Shapley value matrix: adding a value to a player corresponds to adding this value to the diagonal of the matrix, while multiplication affects all matrix values. Figure [2] compares the results of our method for a = 0.5 with a Shapley value heatmap overlaid on the image and a baseline approach that simply selects regions with the highest Shapley values (which is equivalent to our method with a = 0.0). Red dots indicate the regions chosen by our method and the baseline. The heatmap colors represent feature importance: red for important regions and blue for negatively contributing ones. Our method identified a more diverse set of important features compared to the baseline method, which favored features with high synergy, selecting seven dots on the bear’s shoulders. The sum of Shapley values of features selected by our method was lower only by 27% than the sum for features selected by the baseline method, while their sum of synergies was lower by 67%. We applied Euclidean k-means clustering [22] (100 runs for each k € [2,9]) and selected the solution with the highest Silhouette Score [26]. The highest score was 0.58 for our method and 0.75 for the baseline method, both with three clusters. Overall, we conclude that our method trades off a small portion of the total Shapley value to achieve greater diversity, measured by lower total synergies and a lower Silhouette Score, indicating a less clustered selection of regions. Figure [3] presenting a comparison of both methods across different images can be found in Section [D.2]and statistics for them are provided in Section [D.1] We ran code for our case study on a supercomputer with nodes composed of Nvidia A100 GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs. Collecting 1000 samples for Shapley value matrix took us roughly one hour. 11 --- PAGE BREAK --- 8.3 Coalition formation The D’Hondt method is widely used to allocate seats in parliamentary elections. It is known o favor larger parties, a bias that becomes even more pronounced when the method is applied independently across multiple regions. Thus, smaller parties can increase their representation by orming a coalition and running on a single list, receiving more votes than the combined total of heir separate lists. The Indivisible Shapley Value offers a principled way to fairly distribute the seats gained by orming such a coalition. Specifically, we model a cooperative game in which the coalition parties are the players, and the value of any subcoalition is defined by the number of seats it would secure. As an example, we investigate the 2023 Polish parliamentary elections, in which three opposition arties — Civic Coalition, Third Way, and New Left — considered forming a coalition but ultimately ran separately. Using data from the Polish National Electoral Commission, we simulated various coalition scenarios by aggregating the votes received by each subcoalition across all regions. We found that all three parties would gain additional seats by forming a coalition. Without orming a coalition, Civic Coalition, Third Way and New Left received 157, 65 and 26 seats. n coalition after applying Indivisible Shapley Value they would receive 160, 72 and 33 seats, respectively. Notably, both the Shapley Value and its indivisible counterpart lie outside the core. We found that, in both the 2023 and 2019 Polish parliamentary elections, only games formed by coalitions of two parties are convex. This suggests that the most stable coalition would be formed y the New Left and Third Way. 9 Conclusions We proposed a novel model of indivisible coalitional games and defined an indivisible Shapley value, an extension of the classic Shapley value, assigning each player an integer. We proved it belongs to the core in convex integer games and proposed an algorithm that computes a corresponding allocation for non-identical objects. Morevoer, we introduced a method that mimics the indivisible Shapley value for large games and tested our approach on three case studies. There is a wide array of potential future directions. Solution concepts other than the Shapley value can be analyzed for our model. We find randomized algorithms allowing to achieve fairness in expectation a particularly interesting direction. Also, properties of our method can be studied in specific applications. Furthermore, it would be interesting to test concepts from the social choice literature in our setting.
