The combination of tilt analysis and lattice parameters provides a consistent and quantitative description of structural evolution in CsPbI3 and CsSnl3, in excellent agreement with experimental and computational literature. 4 Conclusion In this work, we have developed and validated MLIPs within the LATTE descriptor to investigate the structural dynamics and phase transitions of CsPbl3 and CsSnl3. By benchmarking against DFT datasets and experimental references, we demonstrated that the MLIPs faithfully reproduce energies, forces, and structural parameters, thereby reaching near-DFT accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. Importantly, our parity analysis and root-mean-square error (RMSE) benchmarks establish a quantitative foundation for deploying these models in large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Using this framework, we systematically explored temperature-dependent phase transitions and octahedral tilting behavior in both lead- and tin-based perovskites. Our simulations reproduced the sequence of cubic-tetragonal-orthorhombic transitions, capturing the order and transition temperatures with close agreement to experimental and theoretical studies. A key outcome is the identification of clear chemical trends: CsPbI3 exhibits larger octahedral tilts and higher transition temperatures compared to CsSnl3, reflecting the stronger bonding and enhanced stability of Pb-based perovskites. Conversely, the lower tilting magnitudes and reduced transition barriers of CsSnl3 highlight both its intrinsic instabilities and its potential tunability through compositional or interfacial engineering. Beyond their immediate application to CsPbI3 and CsSnlz, our results underscore the broader utility of MLIPs for investigating halide perovskites. The ability to bridge firstprinciples accuracy with molecular dynamics efficiency enables unprecedented access to long timescale and large system simulations, providing insights into anharmonicity, local disorder, and phase competition that are otherwise difficult to capture. This methodological advance paves the way for predictive modeling of lead-free 11 --- PAGE BREAK --- perovskites, where stability remains the primary bottleneck for practical photovoltaic applications. Looking forward, the integration of MLIPs with advanced sampling techniques, defect chemistry, and device-level modeling will allow us to address open questions regarding degradation pathways, stabilization strategies, and composition-structure-property relationships. In this respect, the present study not only provides a validated potential for CsPbI3 and CsSnls, but also establishes a robust framework for accelerating the discovery and optimization of next-generation, environmentally sustainable perovskite materials. 5 Data Availability The machine learning potential, training and test datasets and example scripts on how to run the potential in LAMMPS movies of phase transition and extra information that mentiend in the text of paper are available at : doi:10.5281/zenodo.17201948 Acknowledgements This work was supported by SISSA and computational resources from CINECA and local HPC facilities. 2510.24872v1 [cs.GT] 28 Oct 2025 arXiv What Are People’s Actual Utility Functions in Budget Aggregation? Ayelet Amster The Open University Israel ayelet.amster@ gmail.com Rica Gonen The Open University Israel ricagonen @ gmail.com ABSTRACT While participatory budgeting and budget-aggregation mechanisms require assumptions about how voters evaluate non-ideal budget allocations, little empirical evidence exists to validate which utility models accurately capture human preferences. We conducted structured polls with human participants to test whether real people’s preferences conform to commonly assumed utility functions such as f,, f and Leontief. Our results suggest that these models may have limited explanatory power for actual behav- ior: most participants showed inconsistent patterns across different metric comparisons, and standard assumptions of project symme- try and sign symmetry — core features of common distance-based metrics — received little empirical support. However, we find encouraging evidence for more fundamental preference structures: a large majority of participants showed con- sistency with single-peaked preferences, as well as with peak-linear utility functions, where utility changes proportionally with distance from the ideal budget. These findings have important implications for designers of bud- get aggregation mechanisms. While theoretical results demonstrate impossibility results for standard distance metrics regarding truthful- ness, Pareto-efficiency, and proportionality, our evidence suggests alternative modeling approaches may be warranted. More broadly, this work introduces a systematic methodology to empirically test the utility function assumptions that underpin budget aggregation theories, paving the way for more robust and realistic mechanism design. Lioz Akirav Ariel Univesity Israel lioz.akirav @ gmail.com Erel Segal-Halevi Ariel Univesity Israel erelsg!@ gmail.com 1 INTRODUCTION This research is motivated by the growing interest in participatory budgeting — a process by which the citizens can participate in decid- ing how to divide the budget of their city or state. One of the common models for participatory budgeting is budget proposal aggregation, in which each voter declares his or her ideal budget allocation, and all these declarations are aggregated by some algorithm to yield the actual budget. A simple aggregation algorithm is the arithmetic mean; however, despite its good axiomatic properties Elkind et al. [6], Intriligator [12], it provides strong incentives for voters to report false preferences in order to manipulate the outcome. This gave rise to more sophisticated aggregation algorithms that are truthful — can- not be profitably manipulated. Such algorithms use variants of the median rule Caragiannis et al. [4], Freeman et al. [8], Freeman and Schmidt-Kraepelin [9], Moulin [13] or Nash welfare optimization Brandt et al. [2]. In order to analyze the properties of an aggregation algorithm, it is necessary to have some assumptions about the voters’ preferences over non-ideal budgets. For example, suppose some voter thinks that the ideal allocation of a budget of 100 among three issues (50, 30, 20). Which of the following non-ideal allocations would this voter prefer: (41, 30, 29) or (43, 40, 17) or (43, 26, 31)? Different papers have different assumptions on this matter. Many papers assume that voters evaluate a non-ideal budget based on its distance from their ideal budget according to some metric, such as f; Caragiannis et al. [4], Freeman et al. [8] or & Freeman and Schmidt-Kraepelin [9]. In the above example, the ¢, distances are 18; 20; 22, so a voter with f, preferences would prefer (41, 30, 29). Note that different metrics may induce different preferences; the £, distances in the above example are (V162, V158, 186) so a voter with f preferences would prefer (43, 40, 17).! Recently, Brandt et al. [2] have argued in favor of utility functions called Leontief, that are not based on any metric: voters evaluate a non-ideal budget based on the smallest ratio of the amount given to any issue to their ideal amount. The smallest ratios in the above 17 example are # = 0.82; 25 = 0.85; Ed = 0.86, so the voter would prefer (43, 26, 31) as it provides the highest ratio. ‘With three issues, the fs distance is always 1/2 of the & distance, so the preferences induced by both metrics are the same. This is not true with four or more issues. --- PAGE BREAK --- Besides the different preferences in specific examples, different utility models yield substantially different combinations of proper- ties that can be satisfied simultaneously. As an example, Brandt et al. [2] prove that, for three or more issues and three or more voters, if voters’ preferences are based on f; or £. metrics, then no aggre- gation algorithm is truthful, Pareto-efficient and satisfies a weak fairness notion called proportionality. In contrast, if voters have Leontief utilities, then the algorithm maximizing the Nash welfare (the product of utilities) is group-strategyproof — which is stronger than truthful, and satisfies core fair share — which is stronger than both Pareto-efficiency and proportionality. These vastly different results invoke the following question, which is at the heart of the present research: What utility functions are actually used by real people when comparing different budgets? We aim to study this question using well-structured opinion polls. 1.1 Our contribution We have constructed a polling system in which subjects are asked for their ideal budget distribution among three issues (government offices or municipal projects). Then they are presented with pairs of non-ideal budget-distributions, and asked which of these two distributions they prefer. The pairs are carefully computed based on the ideal budgets, in a way that enables us to check various properties of the subjects’ underlying utility function. The structure and question design for each poll are detailed in Section A. Using our polling system, we initially checked which of the three common utility models (£;, £2, Leontief) best describes human pref- erences over budget-distributions. Our findings suggest that these models often fail to explain observed behavior (see subsection 5.1). Motivated by this gap, we investigate alternative structures: we iden- tify consistent patterns of single-peakedness (subsection 5.2) and peak-linearity (subsection 5.3), and propose a new utility function that better captures asymmetries in how participants perceive gains versus losses. This helps bridge the divide between theoretical mod- els and actual decision-making in participatory budgeting. The later polls (subsection 5.6, subsection 5.7) show that participants do not treat different projects or directions of change the same way — in- creases and decreases are valued differently, and some issues matter more than others. Based on these results, we define an asymmetric, weighted utility model (Equation 1) that reflects these differences between categories and directions. In addition, the biennial and triangle-inequality tests (subsection 5.7, subsection 5.8) show that people’s choices over time are not simply additive but follow clear and consistent patterns. Together, these findings link theoretical utility models with real human behavior and provide a stronger empirical basis for mechanism design in participatory budgeting. 2 RELATED WORK Participatory Budgeting (PB) enables citizens to directly influence how public funds are allocated. What began as a social innovation has evolved into a computational problem of combining individual preferences. The central challenge is to aggregate individual budgets into a single collective decision that is efficient, truthful, and fair. Prior research has primarily focused on two approaches: project selection and budget aggregation. 2.1 Project Selection In project selection, each project has a fixed cost, and voters sim- ply indicate which projects they support, effectively casting binary yes/no votes. Participants do not control the exact level of fund- ing; instead, aggregation rules determine which subset of projects is implemented. A prominent example is the Equal Shares (MES) rule Peters et al. [14], which distributes the budget equally among voters and allows them to allocate their share to supported projects. Projects that collect sufficient contributions are funded, ensuring that adequately large groups achieve representation. Various addi- tional algorithms and methods address this problem, such as those presented in Fairstein et al. [7]. 2.2 Budget Aggregation The second primary approach is budget aggregation. Here, each voter submits a complete allocation of the budget across projects or categories, represented as a budget vector summing to the total. A straightforward aggregation method is to average all voters’ vectors, producing an outcome that reflects the mean preference. However, this approach faces two main difficulties. First, it is vulnerable to manipulation, since strategic voters may benefit from misreporting their preferences. Second, the resulting mean allocation is often frac- tional (e.g., assigning 17.3% of the budget to parks), which requires rounding to discrete units in practice. Translating such continuous outcomes into feasible discrete budgets is far from trivial: naive rounding may violate budget constraints or distort proportionality among voters. Schmidt-Kraepelin et al. [16] develops a theoretical framework showing that discretization fundamentally changes the set of feasible mechanisms. An alternative to averaging is to aggregate by the coordinate-wise median. This method is generally less sensitive to strategic manip- ulation but introduces a new complication: unlike the mean, the coordinate-wise medians do not necessarily sum to the total bud- get. The moving phantom mechanism Freeman et al. [8] addresses this inconsistency by introducing carefully positioned “phantom” votes that shift continuously until the medians align with the budget constraint. Recent work has also explored alternatives to moving- phantom mechanisms. de Berg et al. [5] introduce several new truth- ful, anonymous, neutral, and continuous mechanisms that aggregate budget vectors without relying on the traditional moving-phantom approach. The theoretical literature on PB further investigates how assump- tions about voter preferences shape the design and properties of aggregation rules. A recurring theme is the inherent tension be- tween desirable axioms such as efficiency, proportionality, fairness, and strategyproofness, which cannot all be satisfied simultaneously Brandt et al. [3]. For instance, welfare-based rules such as UTIL can be strategyproof and Pareto efficient but often fail to deliver proportional representation Elkind et al. [6]. The Nash product rule under Leontief utilities, by contrast, achieves a compelling balance between efficiency, fairness, and group-strategyproofness Brandt et al. [3]. These results highlight that theoretical guarantees are highly sensitive to assumptions about voter utilities, underscoring the importance of empirical validation of which models best capture actual human behavior. This is the core focus of our research. --- PAGE BREAK --- 2.2.1 Thresholds and Satisfactory Budget Division. Beyond proportionality and justified representation, recent work introduces the notion of satisfactory budget division, where participants specify demands and satisfaction thresholds. The aim is to guarantee that each participant sees a sufficient number of their preferred projects funded. Although this problem is computationally hard in general, approximation algorithms and greedy heuristics can often yield sat- isfactory solutions Gourvés et al. [11]. Threshold-based approaches thus expand the design space by formalizing satisfaction guaran- tees that go beyond classical proportionality. This relates closely to subsection 5.6, where we examine whether participants prefer a single large decrease in one category balanced by increases in others, versus smaller decreases across multiple categories offset by a single increase. Suppose participants indeed base their preferences on the number of sufficiently funded projects. In that case, we expect survey responses to consistently favor the scenario with one large decrease over that with multiple smaller decreases. 2.3. Empirical and Experimental Research Empirical studies of PB distinguish between the frontend which is the interface and elicitation format used to collect preferences and the backend — the aggregation rule that combines these inputs. This distinction is useful for classifying experimental findings, as both projects shape voter experience and collective outcomes. 2.3.1 Data Elicitation Formats. The elicitation format strongly influences expressiveness, cognitive effort, and aggregation quality. Prior work has studied formats such as Knapsack Voting Goel et al. [10], Cumulative Voting Skowron et al. [18], k-Approval Voting, Threshold Approval, and others Benadé et al. [1], Fairstein et al. [7]. These studies highlight the trade-off between usability and expres- mpler formats reduce cognitive effort but capture coarser preferences. For example, Skedgel et al. [17] compares rete Choice Experiments (DCE) with Constant-Sum Paired Comparisons (CSPC). In their study, which focused on healthcare resource allo- cation, participants were asked to distribute a fixed budget among various health interventions or to choose between pairs of alterna- tives. The authors found that while DCE captures clear preferences with lower cognitive load, CSPC provides more detailed informa- tion about relative priorities and trade-offs between programs. Such findings underscore that elicitation design not only affects partici- pant experience but also determines the quality of the data available for aggregation. This insight is directly relevant to our poll format, described in section 4, which similarly combines repeated paired comparisons with budget allocation tasks to capture participants’ nuanced priorities. sivenes 2.3.2 Empirical Evaluation of Aggregation Rules. On the back- end, experiments evaluate how different aggregation rules perform in terms of fairness, efficiency, and robustness to strategic behav- ior. Studied rules include greedy algorithms, Equal Shares (MES) Fairstein et al. [7], utilitarian aggregation, and the Nash-product rule Rosenfeld and Talmon [15]. A further support is provided by recent experimental studies, which show how citizens perceive different aggregation rules in terms of fairness and legitimacy, highlighting important trade-offs for practical system design Yang et al. [19]. Empirical evidence complements theoretical results by showing how these rules operate with real human voters rather than abstract utility models, revealing gaps between axiomatic guarantees and observed behavior. 3. MODEL AND NOTATIONS In a budget allocation problem, there is a set A of m alternatives (also called issues or projects). The total budget is denoted by B. The set of all possible budget allocations is the simplex A(B) := {qe R” | q>0and Ya =B} j In our experiments, we always assume B = 100, meaning “100% (in other words, every number appearing in our polls should be interpreted as a percentage of the total budget). Hence, we represent the set of possible budget allocations simply by A. We assume that each person has a preference ranking over A, which can be represented by a utility function u : A > R. We further assume that wu can be described by the following two projects: e An ideal budget allocation — a unique vector p € A which the person thinks is the best way to allocate the budget of B among the m issues. e A utility model function — a function U : Ax A > R, such that for all q € A, u(q) = U(p,q). Whereas typically each person has a different utility function, we believe that different people may have a similar utility model function; this is the function that we aim to uncover in the present research. The polls were available in English and the participants’ native language. A total of 623 unique individuals par- ticipated, completing 950 polls instances in total. At our request, the company prioritized re-engaging individuals who had participated in previous polls and ensured a demographically representative sample for each poll of approximately 40 participants. Participants received points redeemable for money based on poll length, but the incentive was not tied to truthfulness. Participants first defined their ideal budget allocation across three issues (see Figure 1). Then participants were presented with one of two fixed sets of three issues: a national-level set (Health, Education, and Defense ministries) or a municipal-level set (schools, help for the needy, and cultural events). Finally, they answered 10-12 questions. These were mostly pairwise-choice tasks requiring them to select their preferred option from two non-ideal budgets (see Figure 2). Across 18 distinct polls that utilized 11 different pair-construction algorithms, we systematically tested various properties of partici- pants’ utility functions. These polls simulated decision-making in --- PAGE BREAK --- both national-level (11 polls) and local municipal (7 polls) budgeting scenarios. Each algorithm was designed to probe a specific hypothe- For instance, some polls directly compared preferences between common theoretical models (e.g., 1; vs. Leontief), while others tested for adherence to fundamental axioms, such as single-peakedness. The order of options in each pair was randomized. One survey varia- tion involved ranking three alternatives instead of pairwise selection (see Figure 3). Our approach builds on the distinction highlighted by Skedgel et al. [17] between "choosing" from pre-defined alternatives and "allocating" a budget. Our polls were designed to capture both aspects: participants first perform an allocation task by defining their ideal budget, and subsequently engage in a series of choosing tasks through the pairwise and ranking questions, allowing us to study preference trade-offs in both contexts. To ensure data quality, we applied several filters. The system required all participants to allocate their budget to at least two i: Additionally, in a few specific surveys, participants who assigned a value of 0 to an issue were prevented from proceeding due to algo- rithmic constraints. This was necessary as certain pair-generation strategies require non-zero values in the ideal budget to compute valid alternative allocations. Our most critical filter involved two “alertness checks” embedded in the question set (one as the first question and another in the middle), where one of the presented options was the participant’s own ideal budget. Any participant who failed to select their ideal budget in either check was immediately blocked from all subsequent polls. This filtering process yielded a final dataset of 461 reliable participants. We also verified that a negligible number of participants (<1%) consistently chose only the first or second option in all questions. Our poll design incorporated several key decisions to ensure data quality while minimizing cognitive load. We used exactly three issues to create a non-trivial trade-off space, avoiding the over- simplicity of a two-issue (one-dimensional) decision and the com- plexity of four or more issues. To encourage deeper consideration, we forced a choice (i.e., no indifference option was allowed), pre- venting participants from defaulting to an "equally bad" assessment of two non-ideal budgets. To further reduce cognitive load, numeri- cal values in the budgets were generally constrained to be multiples of 5. This was supported by an optional "Rescale" feature (see Fig- ure 4) that automatically adjusted inputs to sum to 100 and adhere to the multiple-of-5 constraint, allowing participants to focus on proportions rather than precise arithmetic. Finally, while participants received a fixed payment, the incentive structure relied on their psy- chological desire to express genuine opinions on public issues, a common assumption in public opinion polls. sues. 5 POLL RESULTS In this section, we describe in detail the pairwise comparisons we did in each poll, the results, and the conclusions we derived from them. 5.1 Comparing specific utility models In the first set of polls, we assumed, based on many theoretical and empirical works in participatory budgeting, that agents’ utility models are one of f;, £, or Leontief. We aimed to check which of these three utility models is more prominent. To this aim, participants were shown two randomly generated budget allocations: One was constructed to be closer to the par- ticipant’s ideal allocation according to one utility model (e.g., f), while the other was closer according to a different utility model (e.g., £)). Participants had to choose between two allocations that differ according to the two utility models under consideration, revealing which model better captures their preferences. Formally, the comparison pairs were generated using an algorithm that selects allocation pairs where two utility models predict opposite preferences. The full algorithm appears in section B. We applied this algorithm three times: £; versus Leontief, f; versus &, and f, versus Leontief. In all three polls, we used k = 10. An example of this process is provided in section B. Our original plan was to partition the participants into three groups: the "f people" (those whose preferences are based on f; metric), the "f people", and the "Leontief people". To our surprise and dismay, most participants did not belong to any of these groups! To understand why, note that a person whose preferences are based on f; will always prefer the allocation that is better according to £, to the allocation that is better according to some other metric (and worse according to f,). However, in the two polls involving £;, only less than 10% of the participants chose the ¢,-preferred allocation in 100% of the pairs. Similar results were observed for the other two utility models. Even when we required only 90% or 80% consistency, the number of consistent participants in each poll remained below 41%. Further comparison results can be found in Table 1, which shows that at higher thresholds of agreement (80%, 90%, 100%), no model consistently dominates. Support for each option drops sharply at these levels, indicating that there is no uni- versally preferred metric. Moreover, out of the 251 total participants, 34 completed all three relevant polls. Among them, 9 participants consistently selected the option aligned with the ¢, metric, 2 preferred f, and 10 favored the Leontief ratio. Surprisingly, 12 participants exhibited non-transitive preferences — that is, they selected a different preferred metric in each of the three surveys. For instance, one participant favored ¢; over Leontief in the first poll, choosing the £, option in 80% of the comparisons. In the second poll, they preferred £, over f;, selecting f) in 70% of the cases. However, in the third poll, they reversed again, favoring Leontief over & in 60% of the comparisons. A detailed summary of metric-based comparisons can be found in Appendix B. We concluded that none of the three utility models we checked can adequately explain people’s preferences. We could go on and check other specific utility models. Instead, we decided to take a step backwards and check more general properties of utility models, as we explain in the following subsections. 5.2 Single-Peaked preferences As a result of this finding, we proceeded to explore whether another function might account for the participants’ choices. We aimed to investigate whether the participants’ utility model satisfies two much more basic and general: "single peaked" and "peak linear". --- PAGE BREAK --- A utility function is called single-peaked (also known as star- shaped) if the utility of an allocation strictly decreases as the alloca- tion moves away from the agent’s ideal allocation ("peak") in any direction. Denote the ideal peak of agent i by pi = arg max u;(q) qehm Then for any distribution q # p;, the agent strictly prefers any distribution on the line segment between q and p; over q itself. That is, for all A € (0,1), uj (pi) > ui(Api + (1 —A)q) > ui(q) To determine whether this property indeed holds, poll questions were generated by forming convex combinations of each partic- ipant’s ideal budget and random allocations, with weights A € {0.1,0.2,...,0.9}. The detailed generation algorithm is provided in Appendix C, and an illustrative example appears in table 3. Here we were pleased to see, in contrast to the previous polls, a high degree of consistency. Overall, 88.8% of the answers (out of the 10n questions) showed preference to the weighted average vector over the purely random one. We also examined consistency levels across different values of A. Although we did not observe a clear increase in consistency as A grew larger, the overall percentages remained relatively high throughout. A detailed table of consistency rates per A is provided in table 4. We conclude that a large majority of the agents have a single-peaked utility function. Note that, for most values of A, the average vector has entries that are not multiples of 5. We suspected that this might create some mental bias. Therefore, we conducted a variant of this poll, in which all entries in the average vectors were rounded to the nearest multiple of 5. The algorithm itself along with an example can be found in section C. This modification did not yield a significant change in results, with consistency levels remaining nearly identical in both polls. 5.3. Peak Linear Encouraged by the positive results for single-peakedness, we went on to ask whether the agents’ preferences satisfy a stronger condition called peak linearity — the idea that moving halfway toward one’s ideal budget should yield exactly half the gain in utility compared to moving all the way. Formally, a utility function is peak-linear if for any distribution q and A € [0, 1], uj (Api + (1 — A)q) = Aui(pi) + (1 — A)ui(q) In the next poll, participants first evaluated three base vectors, each concentrating the majority of the budget on a single issue. Next, for each extreme vector g, convex combinations with the participant’s ideal budget p were generated using weights. Each combination was computed as Ap + (1 — A)q. At each A level, participants evaluated all pairwise comparisons between the resulting vectors, enabling the analysis of how proximity to the ideal allocation affects choice behavior. The detailed procedure for generating these combinations and constructing the questions appears in section D. If the utility function is indeed peak-linear, we would expect the ranking of the transformed vectors to mirror the ranking of the original extreme vectors for each participant. That is, if a participant prefers v; over v2, they should also prefer the A-weighted average of v, over that of v2. Indeed, the results show a high consistency rate of 78% (among all sets of all participants combined). It is lower than the single-peaked consistency rate of 88%, which makes sense since single-peaked is a stronger condition. We also computed the consistency rate for each A. The results are shown below: Percentile (A) Average Consistency 25% (A = 0.25) 70% (93/132) 50% (A = 0.5) 81% (107/132) 75% (A = 0.75) All percentiles 83% (110/132) 78% (310/396) (full details are in table 6). These results are reasonable: when A is larger, the average vector is closer to the extreme vector, so consistency is naturally higher. An illustrative example of inconsistency is provided in table 7. This example illustrates an inconsistent choice pattern, as the participant’s preferences over the A-weighted averages do not con- sistently mirror the ranking of the original extreme vectors, contrary to what would be expected under a peak-linear utility function. These findings suggest that while participants do not perfectly adhere to peak-linear preferences, there is a strong tendency toward consistency, particularly when the evaluated options are closer to their ideal budget allocation. table 8 shows that, when we consider only single-peaked agents, the fraction of peak-linear agents is higher. This makes sense, as peak-linear is a stronger condition than single-peaked. 5.4 Checking symmetry In the next set of polls, our aim was to check whether people’s utility functions are compatible with any f metric. Under the ¢, metric family, only the size of the deviation matters — not where in the budget it occurs, nor whether it represents an increase or decrease in funding. In other words, shifting 10 units away from the ideal in education is treated identically to shifting the same amount in health or defense. Likewise, adding 10 is seen as no different from subtracting 10 (see an example in section E) If participants were using pure f, logic, both options would be perceived as equally distant from the ideal regardless of whether deviations occur in different projects (project symmetry) or have opposite signs (sign symmetry). To directly test these theoretical assumptions, we designed two additional polls in which both options were equally distant from the ideal allocation, but differed in whether the deviation occurred in the same or different projects, or whether the signs of the deviations were reversed. To examine whether participants’ preferences are symmetric across projects, we generated pairs of allocations by rotating de- viations from the ideal budget. The full algorithm is provided in section E. This allows us to test whether participants’ choices re- main consistent when the same deviations are applied to different projects. Here, we used k = 4, which resulted in 12 questions overall. To illustrate, suppose the ideal budget is p = [30, 30, 40]. --- PAGE BREAK --- | q | 2 Original (50, 34, 16] | [20, 25,55] Deviation [20, 4, -24] | [-10, -5, 15] Rotated Deviation 1 | [-24, 20,4] | [15, -10, -5] Rotation | [6, 50,44] | [45, 20, 35] Rotated Deviation 2 | [4, -24, 20] | [-5, 15, -10] Rotation 2 [34, 6, 60] | [25, 45, 30] To test for sign symmetry, we implemented an algorithm that constructs poll sets by mirroring each deviation from the participant’s ideal budget. The full algorithm is provided in section E. Here k = 6, resulting in 12 questions overall. The purpose of these polls was to investigate whether participants responded consistently to these manipulations: if their choices were insensitive to position or sign, this would support the use of an £p-style distance function. Our results show that participants were not consistent in their choices. The average consistency rate for project symmetry (aver- aged over all n- k poll sets) was only 40.9%, indicating that par- ticipants usually considered positionally shifted alternatives as not equivalent. In the case of sign symmetry, the average consistency rate was somewhat higher at 60.8%, but still suggests partial sensitivity to the direction of deviations. In addition to checking the average consistency rate over all nk sets, we also checked the consistency rate for each participant. Only 10% of the participants showed 100% sign-consistency, and no participants showed 100% project-consistency. The figures for lower consistency rates were also quite low (see full details and an example in section E ). This inconsistency suggest that the £, model, as well as any other utility model that treat les symmetrically or treats increases and decreases symmetrically, may not adequately represent people’s preferences. 5.5 Consistency in Asymmetry among Projects Following our negative results for project symmetry and sign symme- try, we designed an additional poll to examine more closely whether individuals have a consistent preference for one project over the other, or for one “sign” over the other. This could support a certain weighted version of f,-based utilities. For checking the consistency in asymmetry among projects, we asked the subjects to rank three different vectors, whose distances from the ideal vector are (2x, —x,—x) and two rotated variants of it (namely (—x, 2x, —x) and (—x, —x, 2x)) for different, positive and negative values of x. If the subject’s utility function is based on weighted f, metric such as Dy a; |p; — q;|", then the ranking should be the same for all x. The algorithm used to generate the comparison pairs is detailed in section F, and a concrete example of the resulting allocation options is shown in table 9. In this poll, unlike in all the previous ones where participants were asked to choose a single option, they were asked to rank the alternatives, with | indicating the most preferred option and 3 the least preferred. An example can be seen in Figure 3 In this poll, a total of 37 participants took part. Less than 20% of the participants showed a consistent ranking of all 3 projects. Even when checking consistency in two of the three pairwise comparisons (A vs. B, B vs. C, C vs. A), only 43% of participants were consistent (full details are provided in section F). To further investigate the potential sources of this inconsistency, we examined a question that was inconsistent for this participant with the ideal budget [20, 20, 60]. In this question, the participant chose the option [12, 36, 52] over the alternative [36, 12,52], and also chose [28, 4, 68] over the alternative [4, 28, 68]. An explanation could be that the agent has a threshold value of 12 for issue C; that is, if the budget is lower than 12, this option will not be chosen. This also aligns with his choice in another question, where he preferred the budget [28, 28, 44] over [4, 28, 68]. 5.6 Consistency in Sign Asymmetry To check the consistency in asymmetry between signs, we checked whether individuals prefer two small decreases accompanied by one large increase as opposed to one large decrease accompanied by two small increases (e.g. (—x, —x, 2x) vs. (x, x,-2x) for some positive x). The core question is whether a concentrated loss in one category, balanced by distributed gains in others, is treated as equivalent to a concentrated gain funded by distributed losses. If the subject’s utility function is based on an ¢, metric with a different weight for increases and decreases, such as Dy a-max(p; — qj,0) +b max(q; — p;,0), then the ranking should be the same for all x and for all rotations of the difference vectors. To test this, the algorithm generates comparison pairs using a primary method that constructs two mirror-image scenarios: one fea- turing a concentrated loss and the other a concentrated gain. For each target category and each magnitude level, deviation vectors are ap- plied to the participant’s ideal budget to create candidate allocations. However, if this primary method generates an allocation with values outside the valid range of [0, 100], a fallback procedure is triggered. This fallback mechanism ensures a full set of 12 comparison pairs is generated by applying a set of predefined, fixed difference vectors that are circularly rotated for each target category. Here, our results are inconclusive. On one hand, only 1/3 of participants (11 out of 33) demonstrated full consistency across all three categories. If we allow for the possibility of a single mistake, then more than 50% of the participants could be consistent with (1). We conclude that Model (1) provides only a partial explanation of participants’ utilities, suggesting that further investigation is needed to assess its adequacy. It appears that participants’ preferences depend not only on the magnitude of change but also on the identity of the category it- self. Each category exhibits a clear “directional tendency”, either consistently favoring distributed decreases or consistently favoring concentrated ones. Such consistency indicates that participants hold a coherent priority structure for each category. It is also possible that each topic triggers a different sensitivity to the distribution of changes. This implies that simple symmetric models are limited and that utility functions with differentiated weights across topics should be considered. Next, we aim to investigate whether those who did not display consistency still exhibit monotonicity. That is, while their preference between a concentrated or distributed change may not be consistent across different topics, it might be monotonic with respect to the magnitude of the change. Among those who were not consistent, 11 displayed full monotonicity — meaning they changed their direction of preference at most once. If we also include the fully consistent participants, we find that 22 out of 34 people exhibited monotonicity. To formally test this hypothesis, we propose a more generalized utility function that can capture non-linear sensitivities to the size of gains and losses: m U(p.q) = > Lay -max(0,qy ~ pj)" ~ a; - max(0, py ~ 43)") j=l In this expanded model, the exponents r and s allow for the utility of a budget change to vary with its size. The parameters allow it to capture a consistent, structured preference pattern (even a non- linear one) across different magnitudes of change. For example, this structure can model a situation where a participant’s preference for a concentrated versus a distributed loss might flip once the magnitude of that loss crosses a certain threshold. Such behavior would violate the assumptions of the simpler linear model (e.g., Equation 1) but could still be described as a consistent, monotonic preference pattern under this more flexible, non-linear framework. A future poll would be designed specifically to estimate the parameters r and s, and thereby test whether participants’ choices, which appear inconsistent at first glance, actually adhere to a more nuanced, yet still structured, utility model. 5.7 Comparing Biennial Budgets Our motivation for the next poll was to test whether participants’ preferences correspond to any metric. To this aim, we wanted to check whether their distance metric satisfies the triangle inequality: Ix + yll < Ilxll + llyll However, since budget allocations are vectors that must sum to a fixed total, it is not straightforward to define or interpret the addition consistent people preferred a large increase to a large decrease in Education, and preferred a large decrease to a large increase in Cultural events, which can be understood in a similar way. --- PAGE BREAK --- of two budget vectors. To address this challenge, we reformulated the problem in terms of a biennial budget, which allows us to investigate whether an additive structure might hold across consecutive years rather than within a single budget vector. Importantly, this is an open empirical question: we do not assume in advance that such an additive relationship will actually be observed in participants’ choices. Specifically, if budgets are allocated in two consecutive years, one can measure the distance between each year’s chosen allocation and the participant’s ideal budget. The hypothesis is that the total utility across two years corresponds to the sum of the utilities in each year separately. If this additive assumption holds, then the two- year outcome can be evaluated simply by summing the distances. However, if participants systematically prefer one year over another regardless of the summed utilities, this would suggest deviations from the additive model. A further layer of analysis concerns whether individuals value the sum of ideal allocations across years, or whether they prefer to balance allocations by smoothing deviations across consecutive years. In the latter case, the sum of distances would no longer be an adequate representation of preferences. This distinction is crucial for understanding whether intertemporal preferences in participatory budgeting align with additive utility models or reflect balancing heuristics. We therefore set out to examine empirically whether participants prefer to receive their ideal budget allocation immediately or are willing to postpone it to the following year. The poll consisted of a simple repeated choice task presented ten times. In each task, participants were asked to choose which budget they preferred for the current year, while the unchosen budget would be automatically allocated in the subsequent year. This poll contains 12 questions generated by three distinct al- gorithms. The order of the questions follows a cyclic pattern with respect to the type of algorithm. Sub-poll 1; In this setting, the participant chooses between receiv- ing their ideal budget in the first year (and a random budget in the second year) or receiving the ideal budget in the second year (and the same random budget in the first year). Sub-poll 2: Here, the first-year budget is fixed in advance. The participant chooses the budget for the second year: either their exact ideal budget, or an alternative budget such that the two-year average (between the first- and second-year budgets) equals the participant’s ideal budget. Sub-poll 3: In this case, the second-year budget is fixed in ad- vance. The participant chooses the budget for the first year: Either their exact ideal budget or an alternative budget that ensures the two-year average is equal to the participant’s ideal budget. The poll generation algorithm and an example of questions for a participant are provided in section 5.7 Our results here are mixed (see section H for detailed results). In sub-polls 2 and 3, over 60% of the subjects (27 and 26 out of 39) consistently preferred to get their ideal budget, rather than a balancing budget. This indicates that a biennial budget can be used to compare sums of distances. On the other hand, in sub-poll 1, over 60% of the subjects (24 out of 39) consistently (in all 4 questions) preferred their ideal budget to be implemented in year 1. This hints that utilities in different years are not additive using a simple sum, but may be additive using a weighted sum. 5.8 Triangle Inequality Based on these results, we want to examine the primary objective of the triangle inequality. We construct a new survey consisting of 14 questions. The purpose of the first two questions is to filter out participants who balance the budgets across the two years — that is, the survey will only include individuals who do not balance between years (meaning they choose their ideal budget in one year and a random budget in the other, rather than selecting a random budget in one year and a budget that balances to the average in the other). After restricting the poll to these participants, we present the remaining 12 questions of the survey. Each question asks to compare two biennial budgets: e Option 1: A concentrated change, where the entire deviation from the ideal budget occurs within a single year. e Option 2: A distributed change, where the same overall de- viation is divided evenly between the two years, so that each year deviates only partially from the ideal. The algorithm tests the triangle inequality by presenting choices that compare a single concentrated change to a split change. Let q be the change vector and q = qi + qz. The poll contrasts (p, P+) vs. (p+qi p +42); So participants’ preferences reveal whether HlOll + Hall = laa + gall s llaall + Iaell holds. To demonstrate, assume the ideal budget is p = [30, 30, 40] and the base difference vector is q = [-20, 10, 10]. Decompose as qi = [-10, 10, 0], — q2 = [-10, 0, 10]. Option 1 (concentrated change): Year 1: p = [30, 30, 40], Year 2: p + q = [10, 40, 50]. Option 2 (split change): Year 1: p + qi = [20, 40, 40], Year 2: p + q2 = [20, 30, 50]. The generation procedure, including the precise algorithm, is provided in Appendix I. We plan to implement this poll in future work. 6 DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK We introduce a systematic polling methodology that uses structured pairwise comparisons to directly elicit preferences over budget allo- cations. This approach enables us to empirically test a wide range of utility function properties, including distance metrics, symme- try assumptions, and intertemporal preference,s while maintaining methodological rigor and minimizing cognitive burden on partici- pants. --- PAGE BREAK --- We are already working on polls for checking more nuanced properties of utility functions. Further directions for future work include: Demographic Considerations It is possible that demographic characteristics of participants, such as age, education level, or political orientation, influence how they interpret budget scenarios or perceive similarity between allocations. These factors could introduce heterogeneity in responses that is not captured by the distance function alone. Narrative and Framing Effects [Throughout the paper, we focused on national budget allocation, but we also made experiments with municipal budget allocation. The results were qualitatively similar (particularly, a large majority of the subjects showed consistency with single-peaked and even peak- linear preferences). However, there were interesting quantitative ifferences (e.g. in the number of subjects showing sign symmetry or project symmetry). Some of these differences may be explained y the perception that municipal budgets feel less critical or conse- uential to participants compared to national budgets. The question of how exactly the narrative framework of the survey influences articipant responses is worth further study. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS We are grateful to Prof. Ralph L. 2510.24855v1 [cond-mat.soft] 28 Oct 2025 arXiv Soft Matter ARTICLE TYPE Cite this: DOI: 00.0000/xxxxxxxxxx Impacting spheres: from liquid drops to elastic beads! Saumili Jana!, John Kolinski?:?, Detlef Lohse*?, and Vatsal Sanjay°+ Received Date Accepted Date A liquid drop impacting a non-wetting rigid substrate laterally spreads, then retracts, and finally DOI: 00.0000/xxxxxxxxxx jumps off again. An elastic solid, by contrast, undergoes a slight deformation, contacts briefly, and bounces. The impact force on the substrate — crucial for engineering and natural processes — is classically described by Wagner's (liquids) and Hertz’s (solids) theories. This work bridges these limits by considering a generic viscoelastic medium. Using direct numerical simulations, we study a viscoelastic sphere impacting a rigid, non-contacting surface and quantify how the elasticity number (1, dimensionless elastic modulus) and the Weissenberg number (Wi, dimensionless relaxation time) dictate the impact force. We recover the Newtonian liquid response as either El + 0 or Wi — 0, and obtain elastic-solid behavior in the limit Wi — co and El # 0. In this elastic-memory limit, three regimes emerge — capillary-dominated, Wagner scaling, and Hertz scaling — with a smooth transition from the Wagner to the Hertz regime. Sweeping Wi from 0 to co reveals a continuous shift from materials with no memory to materials with permanent memory of deformation, providing an alternate, controlled route from liquid drops to elastic beads. The study unifies liquid and solid impact processes and offers a general framework for the liquid-to-elastic transition relevant across systems and applications. 1 Introduction Impacts of spherical bodies on rigid substrates span two classi- cal limits that have long been treated separately: liquid drops and elastic solids. Both occur widely in nature and technology, where the normal force on the substrate is often the quantity of interest because it can damage engineered surfaces! Drop impact governs processes from inkjet printi and spray cool- to forensics") pesticide deposition"4| and soil ‘ Impacts of elastic solids arise in hardness testing) granular media and suspensions) sports), and everyday bounc- ing of soft rubber balls. Despite this breadth, a unifying framework for the impact force across liquid and solid limits has remained elusive. A falling liquid drop, after impact on a rigid surface deforms and laterally spreads until it reaches its maximum extent. Viscoelastic media — here, soft elastic gels — bridge liquids and solids: when deformed they support both viscous flow and recov- erable elastic stress24. Compared with Newtonian liquids, their rate-dependent rheology can markedly alter spreading, pinch-off, and rebound on impact2223) Such soft media are relevant to inkjet printing24) drop deposition) and spray atomization Soft solids such as hydrogels, comprising cross-linked networks with tunable elasticity, are widely used as biocompatible materials in rapid pro- totyping—“ and drug delivery see Chen et al.24l for background. In this work we parameterize the gel’s elastic response using the elastic modulus G which is the proportionality constant be- tween strain and elastic stresses, and the relaxation time that sets the decay timescale of those elastic stresses. Upon non- dimensionalizing the governing equations (section|2.1), two mate- rial control parameters emerge. The elastocapillary number _ GRo Y Ec (3) compares the elastic modulus to the Laplace pressure, while the Deborah number 4) compares the elastic-stress relaxation timescale to the inertio- capillary process time. Here + represents the coefficient of surface tension. Combining these parameters yields the elasticity number Ec G = = — 5 We = ane (5) El which compares elastic to inertial stresses. The impact inertia is expressed by the Weber number _ piVe Ro y We (6) comparing inertial to capillary forces. Another important dimen- sionless control parameter of the system is the Ohnesorge number 7 Oh = ——— (7) vpiyRo which is the ratio of inertio-capillary and the visco-capillary timescales. In this study, we simulate impacts of soft gel spheres on a rigid, non-contacting substrate using a volume-of-fluid, finite-volume framework. By varying the elastocapillary number (Ec) and the Deborah number (De), we traverse smoothly from liquid-like to solid-like response and compare the resulting force scalings with Wagner's (liquids) and Hertz’s (elastic solids) theories. We develop an expression for the peak force that transcends the two regimes, using a function of the elasticity parameter to compare the shear modulus with the impact stress. Consistent with these limits, we recover Newtonian-liquid behavior for De = 0 or Ec = 0, while for De — oo at sufficiently large Ec the dynamics converge to those of an elastic solid. 2| Journal Name, [year], Ivol.}1f17] 2 Numerical Framework 2.1 Problem description and governing equations We consider an axisymmetric sphere of radius Ro approaching a rigid substrate with initial velocity Vo. First, we derive scaling expressions for Finax in the two extreme regimes — an elastic contact limit versus a hydrodynamic impact limit —- and then combine these results to propose a single predictive expression for the dimensionless maximum impact force. 4.1 Purely Elastic Limit: Hertz Contact Theory Consider a solid elastic sphere of radius Ro, mass m, and elastic modulus G (shear modulus, assuming an incompressible mate- rial) impacting a rigid flat surface with speed Vo. Upon contact, the sphere deforms and a normal force F develops according to Hertz’s contact law. The vertical momentum of the drop’s center of mass is redirected into a radial outflow along the substrate, causing a small “wetted” area to grow outward from the impact point This Wagner-type mechanism - a thin spreading lamella initiated at the contact point! — contrasts sharply with the distributed Hertzian contact of an elastic solid. It produces a pronounced impulsive force at touchdown, as the drop’s momentum is arrested over a short time and small area. The first force peak thus originates from pure inertial impingement of the liquid on the surface®| We have analyzed this case in past, for details see the references Zhang et al.) Sanjay et al.) Sanjay and Lohse®, During the very early stage (t ~ tp = Do/Vo), the normal force rises sharply to its first maximum Fix as the drop’s inertia is transferred to the substrate. At this moment the deformation is still localized: the contact radius has grown only to the order of the drop’s initial radius. In fact, experiments confirm that at the peak force time tmax, the spread diameter Dy(tmax) is approx- imately equal to the initial drop diameter Do, consistent with early-time self-similarity of the impact“) Wagner's inviscid theory predicts that the peak force scales with the inertial pressure on the drop’s footprint. Sanjay and Lohse", 4.3 Predictive Interpolating Model for Maximum Impact Force For intermediate conditions (El ~ O (1)), the sphere’s deforma- tion and the fluid’s inertia both contribute, and the peak force deviates from either pure Hertz or Wagner scaling alone. We there- fore express the dimensionless peak force as a weighted transition between the two asymptotic contributions following the approach of Sanjay & Lohse (2025)5) Finax pve Re =5.3f(El) BP? +(1— (en) (3 +324), (0) with a smooth transition function f (£1) defined as a tanh function in log,, El, centered at El ~ O(1). The coefficients are fixed a priori: the Hertz prefactor 5.3 follows directly from the elastic analysis above (without fitting), while the constants 3.24 (Wag- ner plateau) and 3.2 (the Wet capillary correction) are taken from the Newtonian impact model of Sanjay & Lohse (2025)5) This construction ensures a continuous interpolation between the Hertz and Wagner limits. In spirit it follows the additive scaling approach of Sanjay & Lohse (2025)5! for drop impacts, but unlike their model - which includes separate viscous regimes — here only the two primary regimes (elastic vs. inertial) are needed. The re- sulting formula smoothly bridges the two asymptotes and correctly reproduces the peak-force scaling in both limits (this predictive curve is plotted in fig. [4p for comparison). 5 Influence of Elastic Stress Relaxation The results in §Blestablished the two asymptotic force scalings for impacts with permanent memory (De — oo): a Wagner plateau at small elasticity number and a Hertz law at large elasticity number (figure|4p. These two limits also bound impacts when the material memory is finite: relaxing the memory shifts the response continu- ously from solid-like to liquid-like, with the transition controlled by the non-dimensional relaxation time. We quantify the memory effect with the Weissenberg number _ _ pee, GBD which compares the elastic relaxation time to the impact time Ro/Vo (see . While De compares \ to the inertio-capillary time, Wi is the more natural process-time measure here and increases with the degree to which elastic stresses persist during impact“ Thus Wi = 0 (De = 0) recovers a Newtonian liquid, whereas Wi — 00 (De — ov) yields an elastic-memory limit. Figure[5] (fixed We = 100 and El = 40) visualizes the progres- sive loss of elastic behavior as Wi decreases from Wi — oo to 0. In the large-Wi limit, the bead contacts briefly and rebounds; the force trace is nearly symmetric with a large peak, characteristic of Hertz-like loading. Reducing W: increases the contact time and skews F'(t) towards a liquid-like evolution with a much smaller peak. At Wi = 0 the material has no memory and behaves as a Newtonian liquid: the sphere spreads and flows, and F(t) exhibits the familiar asymmetric shape. To quantify the role of memory, we plot Finax/(piVo Ro) versus El = Ec/We = G/(aiVi) for several Wi at We = 100 in fig. [6] At Wi = 0, the data follows the Newtonian liquid level established in 8B] On the other hand, as Wi — ov, the points converge to the elastic-memory master curve of §[3| namely the Hertz scaling Finax/(p1 Vo R3) = 5.3EP/ at large El. Between these limits, weaker memory (smaller W7) delays the transition to Hertz scaling, while stronger memory (larger Wi) makes the elastic response apparent already for softer spheres. Notably, even at Wi — oo the plateau persists for El < 1, because the modulus is introduced exclusively through £1: vanishing G implies a liquid-like bound irrespective of memory. Taken together with 83] these results show that both material stiffness (via El) and material memory (via Wi) govern the peak impact force: the Wagner and Hertz laws remain the bounding asymptotes, while Wi sets how rapidly the system transitions between them. Conclusions & outlook In this work, we investigate the impact of a viscoelastic sphere on a non-contacting rigid surface and chart a continuous tran- sition in impact dynamics from liquid-like to solid-like behavior by tuning the material parameters. The primary peak force Finax (associated with the inertial impact) smoothly crosses over from Wagner's inertial-drop scaling to Hertz’s elastic-contact scaling as the elasticity number El = Ec/We increases. For small El (liquid- ike response), we reproduce Finax/(piVo Rj) + 3.24 matching the constant plateau from Wagner’s theory. In contrast, for large El (elastic-dominated regime), Finax/(p1 Ve Ré) grows following a ower-law ~ 5.3EI°/°, consistent with Hertz’s prediction for elas- tic spheres. These two limiting behaviors bound the force response, and the transition between them is gradual rather than abrupt. The Weissenberg number Wi = De V/We, which quantifies the olymer’s relaxation time relative to the impact time, governs this memory-driven crossover: as Wi increases from 0 (no elastic memory) to co (permanent memory), the peak-force scaling shifts continuously from the Wagner limit to the Hertz limit. Thus, by adjusting Wi, one can smoothly interpolate between liquid-drop and elastic-solid impact outcomes. The modeling choices in this work were made to isolate the physics of the liquid—-to-elastic transition and enable direct com- parison to the classical limits. 2510.24851v1 [quant-ph] 28 Oct 2025 arXiv Pairing-induced phase transition in the non-reciprocal Kitaev chain Pietro Brighi and Andreas Nunnenkamp Faculty of Physics, University of Vienna, Boltzmanngasse 5, 1090 Vienna, Austria (Dated: October 30, 2025) Investigating the robustness of non-reciprocity in the presence of competing interactions is central to understanding non-reciprocal quantum matter. In this work, we use reservoir engineering to induce non-reciprocal hopping and pairing in the fermionic Kitaev chain, and reveal the emergence of a pairing-induced phase transition. The two phases appear in the spectrum of the non-Hermitian Kitaev Hamiltonian describing the dynamics of correlations, separated by an exceptional point. In the non-reciprocal phase, dynamics are characterized by directionality and slow relaxation, and the steady state supports non-reciprocal density and spatial correlations. At strong pairing, we uncover an unexpected density wave phase, featuring short relaxation times, a modulation in particle occupation and strikingly different correlation spreading depending on pairing non-reciprocity. Our work highlights the non-trivial breakdown of non-reciprocity due to superconducting pairing and invites experimental investigation of non-reciprocal fermionic systems. Introduction — Systems where the degrees of freedom affect one another in a non-reciprocal way give rise to fascinating phases and phase transitions [1—4], interest- ing dynamical phenomena [4—7| and amplification [8, 9]. In the context of open quantum systems, reservoir en- gineering [10] has been proposed as a practical route to non-reciprocity [11]. In particular, non-reciprocal ho ping has received considerable attention [8, 9, 12-14], due to the presence of the non-Hermitian skin effect [15-17] and of non-Hermitian topology [18-22]. In spite of these efforts, a deeper understanding of non- reciprocal quantum matter calls for the investigation of minimal models, where competing terms challenge non- reciprocal hopping. In this context, the role of particle- particle interactions has been explored both within the no-click limit of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians [23-31] and at the Lindblad master equation level [4, 6, 7]; these sys- tems, however, often lack analytically tractable solutions, and one has to resort to numerical methods, which are limited in system size. Here, instead, we consider the quadratic supercon- ducting pairing interaction as the process competing with non-reciprocal hopping. Using reservoir engineer- ing, we introduce a version of the celebrated Kitaev chain [32] where both hopping and pairing can be made non-reciprocal. This is qualitatively different from the behavior of the bosonic Kitaev chain, which supports non-reciprocity even in absence of reservoir engineer- ing [33, 34], as recently tested experimentally [35, 36]. Our reservoir engineering approach overcomes the lim- itations of the no-click limit used in recent studies of the non-Hermitian Kitaev chain, where non-reciprocal hopping or pairing [37-40], imaginary chemical poten- tial [19, 41-46] or interactions [47] have shown the pres- ence of various topological phases and edge modes en- hancement. Our work explores a direction different from that of previous reservoir engineering schemes for the Kitaev chain, mostly focused on steady state prepara- tion [48], or on stability of the Majorana modes to cou- pling with the environment [49, 50]. Studying the dynamics and steady state under open boundary conditions, we identify a pairing-induced phase transition. At weak pairing, the system exhibits a non- reciprocal phase characterized by directional dynamics, slow relaxation, and steady-state non-reciprocity. At the critical point, a density-wave phase emerges from the breakdown of non-reciprocity, featuring a modulation of particle density both in dynamics and steady state, as well as short relaxation times. This phase further hosts two different regimes, depending on pairing non- reciprocity. These findings show that introducing pair- ing interactions in non-reciprocal hopping models quali- tatively affects the many-body dynamics and phase tran- sitions, remaining in the domain of quadratic, solvable, problems. Let |r,) be a right eigenvector of H, and let (¢| be a left eigenvector of Ht, with eigenvalues E,, and E*,, respectively. The vector- ized rank-one matrix ||Rin)) = vec(|rn)(ém|), then, is a right eigenvector of H with eigenvalue Eym = En — E;, H||Rmn)) = Arn) (m| — Irn) Cm|Ht =Enn||Rnm))- (6) Pairing-induced phase transition — From the transi- ion in the spectrum of H, then, we expect to observe a qualitative transition in the dynamics of the system, originating from the competition between non-reciprocal hopping and pairing. On one hand, non-reciprocal hop- ing induces directional particle motion [7] and their ac- cumulation on one side of the chain [4, 13]. On the other, pairing injects pairs of particles everywhere in the chain, thus conflicting with non-reciprocity in the steady state, similar to the effect of incoherent gain discussed in Ref. [13]. In the following, we will show results for the non-reciprocal Kitaev chain in OBC, where the pairing- induced transition is sharpest. The interested reader can find details about the transition in PBC in the End Mat- er and Supplemental Material [54]. To observe the transition, we consider a simple pure initial state po = |Wo)(¥ol, Wo) = ek o|Vac), where a single fermion is initialized in the middle of the chain, and investigate its density dynamics (f,(t)) obtained from Eq. In the pairing-dominated regime at large A = 10w short time dynamics reveal a qualitatively different be- havior characterized by the emergence of a density wave attern (b),(d). The density modulation originates and spreads ballistically from defects breaking translational invariance, i.e. the boundaries and the particle at j = g. While for I, = 0 the density wave is reciprocal, for non- reciprocal pairing it spreads only along the right branch of the defect wavefront, resulting in a non-reciprocal den- sity wave pattern. At large A > w, the steady state presents a density wave order, akin to the one observed in dynamics, pen- etrating in the bulk from the boundaries up to a char- acteristic lengthscale pw. This feature is due to the pairing interaction and is completely absent in other sce- narios where non-reciprocity is destroyed e.g. by incoher- ent gain [4, 13]. Coherent pairing leads to the emergence of density modulation on both ends of the chain, while purely non-reciprocal pairing results in density wave or- der only close to the left boundary. As we report in panel (e) Epw grows linearly with A and has small finite size effects, thus suggesting that at large A a considerable fraction of the chain presents density wave order. We note that a non-reciprocal density-wave pattern has been observed in purely dissipative non-reciprocal bosonic sys- tems [57]. In the density wave phase correlations decay symmet- rically, ¢g = ¢r. Depending on the nature of the pairing interaction, coherent or non-reciprocal, two opposite be- haviors emerge. Coherent pairing promotes long-range correlations with ¢ x A, while for T,, = 2A correlations are extremely short-ranged, yielding saturating ¢ for in- creasing A. Conclusion — In this work, we investigated the break- down of non-reciprocity due to superconducting pairing. We reveal a phase transition corresponding to a qual- itative change in the spectrum of the dynamical non- Hermitian Kitaev matrix. The non-reciprocal nature of the dominant processes determines the behavior of the system: directional dynamics and inhomogeneous parti- cle density on one hand and pairing-induced density wave order on the other. The non-reciprocal phase is further --- PAGE BREAK --- characterized by long relaxation times, typical of non- reciprocal systems [14, 58] with emergent large length- scales. The density wave phase, instead, presents fasci- nating spatial correlations, whose spreading is tunable by pairing non-reciprocity. Our results contribute to the understanding of non- reciprocal quantum matter and directly connect with re- cent studies on non-reciprocal fermionic systems [4, 13, 14]. In particular, the non-reciprocal Kitaev chain pro- vides a tractable framework to investigate the behavior of non-reciprocal fermions beyond the phase diagram pre- sented in this work, and the non-trivial behavior of cor- relations invites a more detailed analysis of the effect of non-reciprocal pairing. Our results are based on the Lindblad master equation, and therefore do not suffer from any postselection limitation, making our model par- ticularly appealing for experimental investigation. In this regard, an implementation of our model in quantum dots coupled to common leads [59] would be of great. interest in the ongoing discussion on the so-called poor man’s Majoranas [60-64].
